teile.einleitung: The cursus honorum was the career path of offices in ancient Rome. Anyone who wanted to become a politician had to go through the offices in a fixed order. The goal was the highest office, the consulship.
wichtigste: The most important offices followed in the order quaestor, praetor, consul.
In 180 BC the Lex Villia annalis set a minimum age for the offices.
Between two offices there had to be a break of two years, the biennium.
Quaestors were responsible for the state's finances.
Praetors mainly took care of the administration of justice.
Aediles looked after markets, public buildings and games.
Censors assessed the citizens and drew up the list of senators.

abschnitte.text: **Cursus honorum** means “course of honours”. In the Roman Republic there was a fixed order of offices. First you became **quaestor**, then **praetor** and finally **consul**. In between you could become **aedile**. The offices were usually limited to **one year** and were held by several people together.

The law **Lex Villia annalis** of **180 BC** set a **minimum age** for the offices. Nobody was meant to reach a high office too young. Between two offices there had to be a break of **two years**. This break is called the **biennium**. That way nobody could gain too much power too quickly.

The **quaestors** were responsible for the **state finances**. They managed the state treasury or accompanied governors to the provinces. The **aediles** looked after **markets**, **public buildings** and **games**. With splendid games they could become popular with the people. That helped them in later elections.

The **praetors** were mainly responsible for the **administration of justice**. They led court cases and could also command troops. At the top stood two **consuls**. They led the state and the army. In Rome the year was even named after the two consuls.

A special office was that of **censor**. It was usually held by former consuls. The censors **assessed the citizens** by their wealth and drew up the **list of senators**. Some Roman ideas are still familiar today. In Switzerland the office of **President of the Confederation** changes every year, and the Federal Council decides together as a collegiate body.

gewusst: Our word “census” for a population count comes from the Roman censor.
The word “candidate” comes from the white toga, the “toga candida”, worn by Roman applicants for office.

teile.einleitung: Epicureanism is a philosophy that goes back to the Greek Epicurus. It teaches how to lead a happy and calm life, without fear of the gods or of death.
wichtigste: Epicurus was born around 341 BC on the island of **Samos**.
He strove for **ataraxia**, peace of mind.
For him, pleasure meant the **absence of pain and unrest**.
You do not need to fear death, because we do not experience it while we exist.
The gods exist, but do not care about humans.
The Roman poet **Lucretius** spread the teaching in “De rerum natura”.

abschnitte.text: Epicurus was born around 341 BC on the island of **Samos**. In Athens he founded a school called the **Garden**. Friends lived and learned there together. Unusually for the time, women and slaves were also allowed to take part. Epicurus died around 270 BC, but his teaching lived on for centuries.

For Epicurus the aim of life is **pleasure**. But by this he did not mean wild partying. For him, pleasure is the **absence of pain and unrest**. Anyone who lives without fear and worries reaches **ataraxia**, peace of mind. This includes a simple life, friendship and thinking. Too much luxury, according to Epicurus, tends to bring new worries.

Epicurus took over the **atomic theory** of Democritus: everything is made of atoms. According to his teaching the **gods exist**, but **they do not care about humans**. So there is no need to fear them. Nor should we be afraid of **death**. As long as we exist, death is not there, and when death is there, we no longer exist.

The teaching of Epicurus was summed up in four maxims, the **tetrapharmakos**, the “fourfold remedy”. They run roughly: God is not to be feared, death is not to be feared, the good is easy to obtain, the bad is easy to endure. These sentences were meant to work like a cure for fear.

In Rome the poet **Lucretius** spread the teaching in his long poem **“De rerum natura”**, “On the Nature of Things”. It explains atomic theory in verse. Only a few of Epicurus' own writings survive. Today a person who enjoys life is sometimes called an “epicure”, which does not quite fit Epicurus' modest teaching.

gewusst: According to ancient reports Epicurus wrote about 300 works, but mainly a few letters and maxims survive.
The word “tetrapharmakos” is made up of “tetra” for four and “pharmakon” for medicine.

teile.einleitung: **Spinosaurus** was a large predatory dinosaur of the Cretaceous. On its back it carried a tall **sail**. It lived in North Africa and hunted mainly fish.
wichtigste: Spinosaurus had a large sail on its back.
It ate mainly fish.
Its snout was long and narrow.
It lived in North Africa, often in and by the water.
According to present knowledge, it was the longest predatory dinosaur.
The first bones, in Munich, were destroyed in the war.
Its name means spiny lizard.

abschnitte.text: On the back of Spinosaurus stood very long bony projections of the vertebrae. Skin stretched between them, and so a large **sail** was formed. What it was for is not entirely certain. Perhaps it was for showing off or for being recognised by other animals. From these thorn-like bones comes its name: **Spinosaurus** means **spiny lizard**.

The snout of Spinosaurus was **long and narrow**, similar to that of a crocodile. Its teeth were cone-shaped and well suited to holding slippery prey. It ate mainly **fish**. That is why it often stayed **in and by the water**, in rivers and swamps.

According to present knowledge, Spinosaurus was the **longest predatory dinosaur**, longer than Tyrannosaurus rex. Experts estimate its length at about 15 metres. Because only a few bones have been found, such figures are uncertain, however. It lived about 100 million years ago in **North Africa**.

The first bones were found at the start of the 20th century in **Egypt**. The German researcher **Ernst Stromer** described the animal and took the bones to **Munich**. In the **Second World War**, the museum was hit in a bombing raid, and the bones were **destroyed**. Luckily there were drawings and photographs of them. Later, new bones were found in Morocco.

gewusst: Of the first Spinosaurus bones, destroyed in the war, only drawings and photographs have remained.
New finds show that Spinosaurus had a broad, fin-like tail that helped in swimming.

teile.einleitung: Stone tools are the oldest tools of humankind. Over millions of years, our ancestors made knives, scrapers, points and axes from them. Because stone lasts so long, these finds tell us a great deal today about life in the Stone Age.
wichtigste: Stone tools existed over millions of years, from the Old Stone Age to the New Stone Age.
Flint, also called silex, was especially popular because it breaks with sharp edges.
The hand axe is regarded as the typical all-purpose tool of the Old Stone Age.
The oldest known hand axes are about 1.75 million years old.
Besides stone, people also used bone, antler and wood.
In the New Stone Age, trees were felled with ground stone axes.
The bow and arrow made it possible to hunt animals from a long way off.

abschnitte.text: A stone tool is an object of stone that people deliberately worked in order to use it for a task. The oldest known stone tools come from Africa and are over three million years old. At that time, early hominins still lived there, not modern humans. A whole era is named after this material, the **Stone Age**. It is divided into the **Old Stone Age**, the Middle Stone Age and the New Stone Age.

**Flint**, which occurs in limestone, was best suited. With a hard hammerstone or a piece of antler, pieces were struck off a nodule. This produces flakes with edges that can be sharper than a modern kitchen knife. These flakes are called **flakes** or blades. By fine pressing along the edge, they could be shaped even more precisely.

The **hand axe** is a large tool, worked all round, that is held in the fist. With it you could cut, scrape, chop and dig, much like with a pocket knife. Later, people made narrow, long **blades**, which were used mainly for cutting meat, hide and plants. Scrapers were needed to clean animal skins, and borers to make holes in leather or wood.

For hunting, people fixed pointed stones to spears. A great invention was the **bow and arrow**, because with it you could shoot far and accurately. At the front of the arrow sat a small stone point, which was fixed with birch pitch and sinews. From bone, people carved **harpoons** with barbs to catch fish. There were also needles of bone, with which clothes of fur were sewn.

In the **New Stone Age**, people settled down and cleared forests for their fields. For this they needed powerful **stone axes**, whose blade was ground smooth. The blade sat in a wooden shaft or in an intermediate piece of red deer antler. Such axes have been found in many **pile-dwelling settlements** on Swiss lakes, for example on Lake Zurich and Lake Biel.

In Switzerland too, archaeologists have discovered many stone tools. In the New Stone Age, flint was even quarried in small **mines**, for example on the Lägern near Otelfingen in the canton of Zurich. Good flints were in demand and were traded over long distances. Many finds can be seen today in museums, for example in the **Swiss National Museum** in Zurich.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for flint, a very hard stone that breaks with sharp edges.
A large stone tool that is held in the hand and used for many tasks.
A chip of stone that is struck off a larger stone during working.
A throwing spear with barbs, used to catch fish or other water animals.

gewusst: Freshly struck flint edges are so sharp that researchers can still cut meat with them today.
With two flints, or flint and iron ore, you can strike sparks, which is where the name flint comes from.
The hand axe was used almost unchanged for over a million years.

teile.einleitung: Maat is a central concept of ancient Egyptian religion. It stands for truth, justice and the right order of the world and was also worshipped as a goddess.
wichtigste: Maat means truth, justice and world order.
The opposite of Maat is called Isfet, chaos and injustice.
The pharaoh was to realise Maat and ward off chaos.
The goddess Maat was regarded as a daughter of the sun god Re.
Wisdom teachings explained how to live according to Maat.
The judgement of the dead took place in the Hall of the Two Truths.

abschnitte.text: The ancient Egyptians believed that the world has a **right order**. They called this order **Maat**. It included nature, society and the whole cosmos. The opposite was **Isfet**: lies, violence and **chaos**. The Egyptians saw the world as a constant struggle in which Maat had to be defended against Isfet.

The **pharaoh** was regarded as the guarantor of the world order. He was to **realise** Maat and ward off chaos. This included ruling justly, honouring the gods and protecting the land. On **temple reliefs** one sees the king symbolically offering the gods a small figure of Maat.

Maat was also worshipped as a **goddess**. She was regarded as a daughter of the sun god **Re** and accompanied him on his journey in the **solar barque**. She can be recognised by an **ostrich feather** on her head. The feather became a sign of truth and justice.

abschnitte.titel: Maat in daily life and the afterlife
abschnitte.text: Every single person was also to live according to Maat. **Wisdom teachings**, such as the teaching of **Ptahhotep**, gave advice for right behaviour. They stress modesty, justice and measured speech. After death every person had to answer in the **judgement of the dead**. It took place in the **Hall of the Two Truths**, where it was decided whether one would live on in the afterlife.

gewusst: In the judgement of the dead, according to Egyptian belief, the heart of the deceased was weighed against the feather of Maat.
Judges and high officials were regarded in Egypt as servants of Maat.

teile.einleitung: Greek mythology is the collection of the myths of the ancient Greeks about gods, heroes and monsters. With these stories people explained the world, nature and their own origins. Many of these myths are still told today in books, films and games.
wichtigste: According to the Greeks' belief, the most important gods lived on Olympus.
Zeus was the supreme god, Poseidon ruled the sea and Hades the underworld.
The hero Heracles had to perform twelve difficult labours.
In the myth the Greeks captured Troy with a wooden horse full of warriors.
Homer is said to have written the Iliad and the Odyssey.
Odysseus wandered for ten years after the Trojan War.
The Titan Prometheus brought fire to humans and was punished for it.

abschnitte.text: A **myth** is an old story about gods, heroes and the beginning of the world. The Greeks first passed these stories on by word of mouth. Later poets such as **Homer** and Hesiod wrote them down. The myths explain, for example, why there are seasons or where fire comes from. At the same time they show which qualities the Greeks admired, such as courage, cleverness and loyalty.

Before the gods of **Olympus**, the **Titans** ruled. Zeus and his siblings defeated them in a great battle. After that Zeus, Poseidon and Hades divided up the world: the sky, the sea and the underworld. The Titan **Prometheus** stole the fire of the gods and brought it to humans. As a punishment he was chained to a rock, where an eagle ate his liver every day.

The strongest hero was **Heracles**, a son of Zeus, whom the Romans called Hercules. He had to complete **twelve labours**, for example defeating the Nemean Lion and cleaning out the huge stable of Augeas in one day. The hero **Theseus** found his way into the labyrinth on Crete and killed the **Minotaur** there, a monster with a bull's head. So that he could find his way out again, the king's daughter Ariadne gave him a ball of wool thread.

According to the myth, the Greeks fought for ten years against the city of **Troy**. The reason was that the Trojan prince Paris had abducted the beautiful Helen. The greatest Greek hero was **Achilles**, who was vulnerable only at the heel. That is why we now say **Achilles heel** for a weak spot. In the end the Greeks built a wooden horse, hid warriors inside it and so captured the city.

The clever hero **Odysseus** had thought up the trick with the horse. On the voyage home to Ithaca he wandered for another **ten years**. He outwitted the one-eyed giant Polyphemus and resisted the song of the Sirens. Homer's **Odyssey** tells of this journey, and even today a long, difficult journey is called an odyssey.

Many words and sayings come from Greek mythology, for example **panic** from the shepherd god Pan, or echo from a nymph. Constellations such as Hercules, Perseus or Andromeda bear names from the myths. Artists have painted the stories and carved them in stone for centuries. Even today books, films and games about Greek heroes appear.

begriffe.erklaerung: An old story about gods, heroes and the origin of the world.
A powerful family of gods that ruled before Zeus.
A building with many winding passages in which you get lost.
A vulnerable or weak spot, named after the hero Achilles.

gewusst: In the 19th century Heinrich Schliemann searched for Troy and dug up an ancient city in the hill of Hisarlik in present-day Turkey.
The Achilles tendon at your heel is named after the hero Achilles.
The word museum comes from the Muses, the goddesses of the arts in Greek myth.

teile.einleitung: Eratosthenes was a Greek scholar who lived in Alexandria in the 3rd century BC. He is famous because he worked out the size of the Earth using shadows and geometry.
wichtigste: Eratosthenes headed the famous **Library of Alexandria**.
Around 240 BC he determined the **circumference of the Earth** with astonishing accuracy.
In **Syene** the Sun stood almost straight overhead at noon on the summer solstice.
He assumed that the Sun's rays reach the Earth **parallel** to each other.
His calculation gave **250,000 stadia**.
With the **sieve of Eratosthenes** you can find prime numbers.
He is regarded as the founder of **geography**.

abschnitte.text: Eratosthenes was born around 276 BC in **Cyrene** in North Africa. Later the king of Egypt brought him to **Alexandria**. There he **headed the library**, the largest collection of books in the world at that time. He worked on mathematics, astronomy, history and poetry. He is also regarded as the founder of **geography**, the description of the Earth.

Eratosthenes heard that in **Syene**, present-day Aswan, at noon on the summer solstice the Sun stood almost straight overhead. The wells then cast no shadow. In Alexandria, however, a stick cast a short shadow at the same time. Eratosthenes assumed that the Sun's rays reach the Earth **parallel** to each other. So the difference had to be due to the curve of the Earth.

The angle of the shadow in Alexandria was about **one fiftieth of a full circle**. So the distance between the two cities had to be one fiftieth of the Earth's circumference. Eratosthenes took this distance to be **5,000 stadia**. 5,000 times 50 gives **250,000 stadia**. Exactly how long a stadium was is not certain, but the result was probably close to today's value of **about 40,000 km** at the equator.

Eratosthenes also invented a simple method for finding **prime numbers**. You write down all the numbers up to a limit. Then you cross out all the multiples of 2, then of 3, of 5 and so on. What is left are the prime numbers. Up to 30, **10** numbers remain: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29.

gewusst: Eratosthenes was nicknamed “Beta”, because he was considered second best in many subjects.
Many children still learn the sieve of Eratosthenes in maths lessons today.

teile.einleitung: Cuneiform is one of the oldest scripts in the world. It arose more than 5,000 years ago in Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris in present-day Iraq. Its signs were pressed into soft clay with a stylus and look like lots of little wedges.
wichtigste: Cuneiform arose more than 5,000 years ago in Mesopotamia.
It was mostly written on clay tablets.
A stylus made of reed served as the writing tool.
The signs consist of wedge-shaped strokes, hence the name.
Simple picture signs gradually became abstract signs.
It was used for about 3,000 years for several languages, such as Sumerian and Akkadian.
The Behistun Inscription in Iran helped with the decipherment in the 19th century.

abschnitte.text: Cuneiform is a script whose signs consist of small **wedge-shaped** impressions. It was invented by the **Sumerians** in Mesopotamia, in the area of present-day Iraq. The oldest finds come from the city of **Uruk** and are more than 5,000 years old. Together with the Egyptian hieroglyphs it is one of the oldest scripts of humankind.

The scribes pressed the signs with a **stylus** of reed into a soft **clay tablet**. Because the reed had an angular tip, strokes with one thick and one thin end were made, that is, wedges. Afterwards the tablet was left to dry in the sun or fired in a kiln. Many tablets are only the size of the palm of a hand, so that they could be held easily.

At the beginning the script was used mainly to count and record goods such as grain, beer or sheep. The first signs were simple **picture signs**, for example a head or an ear of grain. In time the pictures were simplified, turned and became **abstract signs** made of wedges. Many signs now no longer stood only for a thing but also for a syllable. So whole sentences, laws and stories could be written down.

Cuneiform was used for about **3,000 years**. At first it was used to write **Sumerian**, later mainly **Akkadian**, the language of the Babylonians and Assyrians. Other peoples such as the Hittites and the Persians also used cuneiform for their languages. In cuneiform, among other things, the Epic of Gilgamesh and the laws of King Hammurabi have come down to us. Around the turn of the era it was slowly displaced by alphabetic scripts and fell into oblivion.

For a long time nobody could read cuneiform any more. The key was provided by the **Behistun Inscription**, a huge rock inscription in present-day Iran that the Persian king Darius I had made. It contains the same text in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. In the 19th century researchers such as the Briton **Henry Rawlinson** managed to compare the texts and decipher the script.

Today hundreds of thousands of cuneiform tablets are known. That so many survive is due to the material: **clay** becomes very durable when dried or fired. When a palace or a library burned down, the tablets were even hardened in the process. A famous collection comes from the library of the Assyrian king **Ashurbanipal** in Nineveh. The tablets tell us about trade, school, medicine and astronomy in the Ancient Near East.

begriffe.erklaerung: The land between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris, roughly present-day Iraq.
A flat slab of clay into which signs could be pressed.
A pen for scratching or pressing writing.
Finding out how an unknown script is read.
An early people in Mesopotamia who invented cuneiform.

gewusst: The first cuneiform texts were not stories but lists of goods and accounts.
Pupils in Mesopotamia practised writing on clay tablets that could be smoothed and used again.
Swiss museums and universities also own cuneiform tablets, which researchers are still studying today.

teile.einleitung: Vercingetorix was a Gallic chieftain of the tribe of the Arverni. In 52 BC he led the great uprising of the Gauls against Julius Caesar and the Romans.
wichtigste: Vercingetorix led the great uprising against Rome in 52 BC.
At Bibracte, an assembly of the Gauls chose him as commander in chief.
He had villages and supplies burned to weaken the Romans.
At Gergovia he repelled an attack by Caesar.
After the defeat at Alesia he surrendered and was later executed in Rome.
In France today he is regarded as a national hero.

abschnitte.text: From 58 BC, Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, present-day France. In **52 BC**, many Gallic tribes rose up together. Their leader was **Vercingetorix** of the **Arverni** tribe. At **Bibracte**, an assembly chose him as **commander in chief**. Even the powerful **Aedui** had to accept his leadership. It was the last great attempt to drive the Romans out.

Vercingetorix knew that the Romans were very strong in open battle. So he had **villages and supplies burned**. The Romans were to find neither grain nor fodder for their animals in Gaul. This way of waging war is called the **scorched-earth tactic**. It was hard on his own people, but was meant to starve out the enemy.

At **Gergovia**, a town of the Arverni, Caesar attacked. Vercingetorix repelled the attack, and Caesar had to break off the siege. It was one of his rare defeats. Later, however, Vercingetorix was shut in at **Alesia**. The Romans built ramparts around the town, and a Gallic relief army could not free him. In the end he had to surrender.

After his **surrender**, Vercingetorix was taken to **Rome**. He remained a prisoner for several years. At Caesar's **triumphal procession**, he was paraded before the people. After that he was executed, as was usual for defeated leaders at that time.

In the 19th century, Vercingetorix became the **national hero of France**. Emperor **Napoleon III** had excavations carried out at Alesia and a large statue erected there. In **Clermont-Ferrand** in the Auvergne, an equestrian monument stands on the Place de Jaude. It is by **Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi**, who also created the **Statue of Liberty** in New York.

gewusst: What we know about Vercingetorix comes mainly from Caesar's own account of the Gallic War.
The Helvetii from the area of present-day Switzerland also fought against Caesar, as early as 58 BC at Bibracte.

teile.einleitung: The Achaemenid Empire was the first great Persian empire and one of the largest empires of antiquity. It was founded around 550 BC by Cyrus II and, in the time of Darius I, stretched from Egypt to the Indus. It is named after Achaemenes, the legendary ancestor of the royal family.
wichtigste: Cyrus II founded the empire around 550 BC.
The heartland of the Persians lay in present-day Iran.
Governors, the satraps, administered the individual provinces.
The Royal Road from Sardis to Susa served messengers and merchants.
Darius I had the magnificent residence city of Persepolis built.
In the 5th century BC, the Persians fought against Greek city states in the Persian Wars.
Alexander the Great conquered the empire around 330 BC.

abschnitte.text: The Persians originally lived in the south of present-day **Iran**, in the region of Persis. Their king **Cyrus II** defeated the Medes around 550 BC and took over their empire. After that he conquered Lydia in present-day Turkey and, in 539 BC, the rich city of Babylon. Cyrus mostly let the conquered peoples keep their religion and customs. That is why, for example, the Jews were allowed to return from Babylon to their homeland.

Under Cyrus's son Cambyses II, Egypt was conquered in 525 BC. Under **Darius I**, who ruled from 522 BC, the empire stretched from Egypt and present-day Turkey to the **Indus** in present-day Pakistan. Many peoples with different languages lived in it. For administration, Aramaic was often written, and on inscriptions also Old Persian in cuneiform.

The empire was divided into provinces, which were administered by governors, the **satraps**. They collected taxes and kept order. The **Royal Road** ran about 2,500 kilometres from Sardis to Susa. At stations, fresh horses stood ready, so that messengers covered the route in a few days. Darius I also introduced a uniform gold coin, the **daric**.

Around 518 BC, Darius I had the palace city of **Persepolis** built. On huge stone reliefs you can see envoys of many peoples bringing gifts to the king. At the New Year festival, delegates from the whole empire gathered here. In the older capital **Pasargadae**, the tomb of Cyrus II still stands today. Both sites are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

When Greek cities in Asia Minor rose up, the **Persian Wars** came about. The Persians lost to the Greeks at Marathon in 490 BC and in the naval battle of Salamis in 480 BC. The empire nevertheless remained powerful for about another 150 years. From 334 BC, **Alexander the Great** attacked and defeated King Darius III. Around 330 BC the Achaemenid Empire was at an end, and the palace of Persepolis went up in flames.

begriffe.erklaerung: A governor who administered a province of the Persian Empire in the name of the king.
A long road through the Persian Empire with stations for messengers and horses.
A gold coin that Darius I introduced for the whole empire.
The magnificent palace city of the Persian kings in present-day Iran.

gewusst: The Greek historian Herodotus praised the Persian messengers so highly that his sentence stands today above the main post office of New York.
On the so-called Cyrus Cylinder of clay, Cyrus II reports the conquest of Babylon, and it lies today in the British Museum.
The ruins of Persepolis were so impressive that travellers admired them for centuries.

teile.einleitung: In ancient Rome an insula was a multi-storey block of rented flats. Most people in the city of Rome lived in such buildings, often cramped and with little comfort.
wichtigste: An insula was a multi-storey block of flats to rent.
The Latin word “insula” actually means island.
On the ground floor there were often shops and workshops.
Poorer people usually lived right at the top.
Fire and collapse were great dangers.
Augustus limited the height to about 20 metres.

abschnitte.text: “**Insula**” is Latin and means **island**. A block of flats was surrounded on all sides by streets, like an island by water. That is how it got this name. In an insula many families lived as **tenants**. Wealthy Romans, by contrast, lived in a house of their own, a **domus**. In the city of Rome there were far more insulae than single houses.

On the **ground floor** of many insulae there were small **shops**, snack bars and **workshops**. They opened directly onto the street. Above them lay the flats. The lower flats were larger and more expensive. The **upper floors** were cramped and cheap. People with little money lived there.

The buildings were partly made of **wood**, and people cooked and heated with open fires. So fires broke out often. Anyone living at the top could easily be trapped in a **fire**. Some blocks of flats were also badly built and **collapsed**. Emperor **Augustus** therefore allowed a height of at most 70 Roman feet, that is, about **20 metres**.

There was no **running water** in the upper flats. People carried water up in jugs from the public **fountain** in the street. Most flats also had no **toilet** of their own. People went to public **latrines**, where many sat side by side. To wash, they visited the public baths.

In Rome itself only a few remains of insulae survive. They can be seen especially well in **Ostia**, the old port city of Rome. There the brick walls of multi-storey blocks of flats still stand. One can recognise shops, stairwells and courtyards. They show how ordinary people lived in antiquity.

gewusst: Some insulae in Rome probably had five or more storeys.
Even in antiquity poets complained about high rents and noise in Rome.

teile.einleitung: The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest stories in the world. It comes from Mesopotamia and tells of a king who has adventures, loses a friend and searches for eternal life.
wichtigste: Gilgamesh is **a king from an ancient legend**.
He ruled over the city of **Uruk**.
According to the epic he is **two thirds** divine.
His best friend is called **Enkidu**.
After Enkidu's death Gilgamesh searches for **eternal life**.
The wise Utnapishtim tells **of a great flood**.
The oldest Gilgamesh stories were written down in **Sumerian**.

abschnitte.text: The **Epic of Gilgamesh** comes from **Mesopotamia**, the land between the Euphrates and the Tigris in present-day Iraq. The oldest stories about Gilgamesh were written down in **Sumerian**. Later they were combined into a long epic in the Akkadian language. It was written in **cuneiform** on clay tablets. Many tablets were found in the 19th century in the ruins of the city of **Nineveh**.

Gilgamesh is **a king from an ancient legend**. He rules over the city of **Uruk**. According to the epic he is **two thirds divine** and one third human. At the beginning he is strong but arrogant, and the people suffer under him. So the gods create an equal companion for him: the wild **Enkidu**.

After a fight, Gilgamesh and Enkidu become **best friends**. Together they go into the **Cedar Forest** and defeat its guardian **Humbaba**. Then they also defeat the **Bull of Heaven**, which the goddess **Ishtar** has sent. But the gods decide that Enkidu must die for it. Gilgamesh is deeply sad about this.

After the death of his friend, Gilgamesh becomes afraid of his own death. He searches for **eternal life** and travels to the wise **Utnapishtim**. He tells him **of a great flood** that he survived in a boat. The story resembles the story of Noah in the Bible. Utnapishtim reveals to Gilgamesh a **plant of youth**.

On the way home Gilgamesh bathes in a spring. Then **a snake** steals the plant of youth. Gilgamesh has to accept that he cannot become immortal. He returns to Uruk and looks at the mighty **city walls** that he built. They remain as his work, even though he himself must die.

gewusst: When the researcher George Smith deciphered the flood story on a clay tablet in 1872, it caused a great stir.
The Epic of Gilgamesh is more than a thousand years older than the poems of Homer.

teile.einleitung: **Triceratops** was a large plant eater of the Cretaceous. It had three horns on its head and a large neck frill. It lived in North America, at the same time as Tyrannosaurus rex.
wichtigste: Triceratops means three-horned face.
It lived in the Cretaceous in North America.
Behind its head it carried a large neck frill.
Its mouth at the front was like a parrot's beak.
A large Triceratops was about 8 metres long and much heavier than a car.
It lived at the same time as Tyrannosaurus rex.

abschnitte.text: The name **Triceratops** means **three-horned face**. Above the eyes it had two long horns, and on the nose a shorter one. Behind the head it carried a large **neck frill** of bone. Its skull is among the largest skulls of any land animal.

Triceratops probably needed its **horns for defending and fighting**. It lived at the same time as **Tyrannosaurus rex**, a dangerous predatory dinosaur. Bones of Triceratops with bite marks of a T. rex have even been found. Probably the animals also fought one another with their horns.

At the front, the mouth looked like a **parrot's beak**. With it, it could bite off tough plants. Further back in the mouth it had many teeth that worked like scissors. Worn teeth were continually replaced by new ones.

A large Triceratops was about **8 metres** long. It was **much heavier than a car**, probably several tonnes. It lived at the end of the **Cretaceous** in **North America**, about 66 to 68 million years ago. It is among the last dinosaurs before the great extinction.

gewusst: Triceratops is among the last dinosaurs that lived before the great extinction 66 million years ago.
Many skulls of Triceratops have been found, but only a few complete skeletons.

teile.einleitung: Abu Simbel is a place in the south of Egypt with two gigantic rock temples. Pharaoh Ramesses II had them cut directly into a mountain on the Nile in the 13th century BC. In the 20th century they were moved in a great rescue operation.
wichtigste: Abu Simbel consists of two rock temples, a large one and a small one.
The temples were cut out of a sandstone mountain on the bank of the Nile.
The small temple is dedicated to the goddess Hathor and to Nefertari, the chief wife of Ramesses II.
The Basel man Johann Ludwig Burckhardt rediscovered the large temple for Europe in 1813.
From 1964 to 1968, the temples were taken apart and rebuilt about 65 metres higher.
Since 1979 they have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Ramesses II was one of the most powerful pharaohs of Egypt. He had the two temples built in Nubia, in the far south of his empire. In front of the **large temple** sit four huge statues of the pharaoh, each about 20 metres tall. The **small temple** next to it is dedicated to the goddess **Hathor** and Queen **Nefertari**. Six statues stand on its front. Neither temple was built of masonry, but cut out of the **sandstone** of the mountain.

The large temple reaches deep into the mountain. At the very back lies the innermost sanctuary with statues of gods. Twice a year, the rising sun shines through the long passage as far as these figures. This shows how well the ancient Egyptians knew the course of the sun. Even today many people come on these days to see the spectacle.

abschnitte.titel: A Basel man in the sand
abschnitte.text: In time, the desert wind blew a lot of sand in front of the temples. In Europe, nothing was known of them for a long time. In 1813, the Basel researcher **Johann Ludwig Burckhardt** came by. He travelled through the Orient under the name Sheikh Ibrahim. He saw the heads of the statues sticking out of the sand. A few years later, other researchers uncovered the entrance.

In the 1960s, Egypt built a huge **dam** at Aswan. Behind it, a large reservoir was formed that would have flooded the temples. Under the leadership of **UNESCO**, many countries helped with the rescue. From **1964 to 1968**, the temples were sawn into over a thousand blocks. About **65 metres higher** and somewhat further inland, they were put back together. Over them, artificial hills were built so that everything looks like a mountain again.

The rescue of Abu Simbel was a model for the cooperation of many states. It furthered the idea that some places belong to all humankind. In **1979**, the Nubian monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae were added to the **World Heritage** list. Today Abu Simbel is one of the best-known travel destinations in Egypt.

gewusst: The temples were moved so precisely that sunlight still falls into the innermost sanctuary, though about a day later than before.
A Swiss man, Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, made Abu Simbel known in Europe.

teile.einleitung: Constantine the Great was a Roman emperor who changed the empire greatly. He was the first emperor to favour Christianity and founded the city of Constantinople.
wichtigste: Constantine bears the epithet “the Great”.
In 312 he defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge.
In 313 the Edict of Milan allowed Christians to practise their faith freely.
In 321 he made Sunday a day of rest.
He expanded Byzantium into the city of Constantinople, present-day Istanbul.
His mother Helena is honoured as a saint.

abschnitte.titel: The victory at the Milvian Bridge
abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 4th century several men quarrelled over power in the Roman Empire. In **312** Constantine defeated his opponent **Maxentius** at the **Milvian Bridge** in Rome. After that he ruled the west of the empire. According to the story, before the battle he saw a **Christian sign** in the sky. He had it painted on the shields of his soldiers.

Constantine was the first Roman emperor to support **Christianity**. With the **Edict of Milan** of **313**, all people in the empire were allowed to practise their religion freely. With that the great persecutions of Christians were largely over. Constantine had churches built and took an interest in disputes among Christians. Shortly before his death in 337 he was **baptised**.

Constantine greatly expanded the old city of **Byzantium** on the **Bosporus**. He gave it his own name: **Constantinople**. The city became a new capital of the empire. It lay conveniently between Europe and Asia. Today the city is called **Istanbul** and lies in Turkey.

abschnitte.titel: Sunday as a day of rest
abschnitte.text: In **321** Constantine made **Sunday** a day of rest. On this day, for example, the law courts were to be closed. To this day Sunday is a day off in many countries, including Switzerland.

In Rome, next to the **Colosseum**, stands the **Arch of Constantine**. This large triumphal arch recalls the victory of 312. Constantine's mother **Helena** was a Christian and is honoured today as a saint. Because of his great changes Constantine received the epithet **“the Great”**.

gewusst: Constantine was proclaimed emperor by his soldiers in 306 in present-day York in England.
Constantinople remained the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire for over 1,000 years.

teile.einleitung: The First Council of Nicaea was a great gathering of bishops in AD 325. There the Christians argued about how God the Father and Jesus Christ relate to each other, and agreed on a common creed.
wichtigste: The council took place in **AD 325**.
It was summoned by **Emperor Constantine**.
It condemned the teaching of **Arianism**.
The creed calls Father and Son **homoousios**, that is, of the same substance.
The council made an important ruling about the date of **Easter**.
The young deacon **Athanasius** took part.
The town of Nicaea is now called **Iznik** and lies in Turkey.

abschnitte.text: At the start of the 4th century **Emperor Constantine** had allowed and supported the Christian faith in the Roman Empire. But among Christians there was a fierce dispute. Constantine wanted to secure unity in the empire. So in **AD 325** he invited the bishops to **Nicaea** in Asia Minor. Several hundred bishops came, mostly from the east of the empire. This gathering is counted as the first **ecumenical council**, that is, a gathering of the whole Church.

A priest from Alexandria named **Arius** taught that the Son of God was created by the Father and was not equal to him. This teaching is called **Arianism**. Many bishops objected to him strongly. The council condemned Arianism. Arius and some of his followers were sent into exile. But the dispute was far from over.

The council drew up a common **creed**. It states that the Son is **homoousios** with the Father, Greek for **of the same substance**. This meant that Father and Son share the same nature. In 381 the creed was expanded in Constantinople. In this form it is still spoken in many churches today, including Catholic and Reformed churches in Switzerland.

The council also dealt with the date of **Easter**. All Christians were to celebrate the festival on the same Sunday. It also decided rules for the order of the Church, for example on the consecration of bishops. As a young deacon, **Athanasius** was present. He later became bishop of Alexandria and fought against Arianism all his life.

The town of Nicaea lies in present-day **Turkey** and is called **Iznik**. It lies on a lake south-east of Istanbul. Later Iznik was famous for its colourful **ceramic tiles**. Remains of the old city walls can still be seen.

gewusst: In 787 a second council also took place in Nicaea.
Constantine himself was only baptised shortly before his death.

teile.einleitung: At **Carnac** in Brittany in France, thousands of large stones stand in long rows. They were set up in the New Stone Age. The stone rows of Carnac are among the best-known Stone Age monuments in Europe.
wichtigste: Carnac lies in the département of Morbihan in Brittany.
The three main groups are Le Ménec, Kermario and Kerlescan.
The stones are mostly dated to the 5th and 4th millennia BC.
At the ends of Le Ménec stands a stone oval, a cromlech.
In the village stands the burial mound Tumulus Saint-Michel.
Since 1991, the rows have been largely fenced off.
James Miln laid the foundation for the Museum of Prehistory.

abschnitte.text: The upright stones are called **menhirs**. At Carnac they stand in long, almost parallel rows over several kilometres. The three main groups are called **Le Ménec**, **Kermario** and **Kerlescan**. At the ends of the rows of Le Ménec stands a stone oval, a so-called **cromlech**.

The stone rows are mostly dated to the **5th and 4th millennia BC**. So they are older than Stonehenge in its well-known form. What they were for is not known for certain. Perhaps they were a place for celebrations or rituals, perhaps they had to do with the course of the sun.

In the village of Carnac stands the large New Stone Age burial mound **Tumulus Saint-Michel**, on which a chapel stands today. A Breton **legend** tells that Saint **Cornelius** was pursued by Roman soldiers. He is said to have turned the soldiers into stone, and so the stone rows came about.

In the past, many visitors walked around between the stones. As a result the ground was worn away, and plants could no longer grow. Since **1991**, the rows have therefore been largely **fenced off**, to protect them from **erosion**. The Scottish researcher **James Miln** dug at Carnac in the 19th century and collected finds. His collection became the foundation of the **Museum of Prehistory** in Carnac.

gewusst: In total, about 3,000 menhirs stand at Carnac.
The word menhir comes from the Breton language and means “long stone”.

teile.einleitung: “All roads lead to Rome” is a well-known saying. It means that there are many different ways to the same goal. The saying recalls the huge road network of the ancient Romans.
wichtigste: The saying means: there are many ways to the goal.
In the Roman Empire, many roads led to Rome, because Rome was the capital.
The Latin word “via” means road.
The top layer of important Roman roads consisted of large flat stones.
A Roman mile was 1,000 double paces.
Mostly Roman soldiers built the roads.
In French the saying is “Tous les chemins mènent à Rome”.

abschnitte.text: Whoever says “All roads lead to Rome” means: you can reach a goal in **different ways**. What matters is that you arrive, not which way you choose. The saying exists in many languages. In French it is **“Tous les chemins mènent à Rome”**, in Italian “Tutte le strade portano a Roma”. Another well-known saying about Rome is: **“Rome was not built in a day”**.

**Rome** was the **capital** of a huge empire. So that soldiers, messengers and merchants could travel quickly, the Romans built a dense road network. Many roads began in Rome or led there. The most famous is the **Via Appia**, built from 312 BC. The Latin word **“via”** means road. In total, the Romans built tens of thousands of kilometres of roads.

abschnitte.titel: How a Roman road was built
abschnitte.text: An important Roman road consisted of several **layers**. At the bottom lay coarse stones, above them gravel and sand. At the very top, **large flat stones** were often laid. The road was slightly arched in the middle so that rainwater could run off. The roads were mostly built by **Roman soldiers** when they were not fighting.

The Romans measured distances in **miles**. A Roman mile was **1,000 double paces**, which is about one and a half kilometres. At the roadside stood **milestones** that showed the distance. In the Forum in Rome, Emperor Augustus had a golden milestone set up. It was regarded as the centre of the road network. Our word “mile” comes from the Latin “mille”, a thousand.

Roman roads also led through present-day Switzerland. They joined towns such as **Aventicum** (Avenches) and **Augusta Raurica** near Basel. Over Alpine passes such as the **Great St Bernard**, you reached Italy and so the direction of Rome. In some places, remains of these roads and Roman milestones can still be seen today.

gewusst: Many roads in Europe today still follow the course of old Roman roads.
The word “mile” comes from the Latin “mille passus”, a thousand double paces.

teile.einleitung: Typology is an important method in archaeology. Finds are ordered by their shape, and in this way you can tell from which period they come, even without written sources.
wichtigste: Typology means ordering and comparing objects by their shape.
The Swedish archaeologist Oscar Montelius is regarded as its founder.
An index form is a type of find that is typical of a particular period.
In the Iron Age, brooches are especially often used as index forms.
In 1885, Otto Tischler divided the La Tène period into Early, Middle and Late La Tène.
Paul Reinecke created stages such as Bronze Age A to D and Hallstatt A to D.

abschnitte.text: Tools, jewellery and vessels change their appearance over time, just as cars or telephones change today. **Typology** makes use of this. Similar objects are laid in a row, from the simple to the more developed piece. In this way a **relative chronology** is produced: you know what is older and what is younger, even if you do not know an exact year.

The Swedish archaeologist **Oscar Montelius** is regarded as the founder of the typological method. He arranged objects such as **axes** and **brooches** in rows according to the development of their shape. From this he created a chronology of the **Nordic Bronze Age**. His method is still used today and is continually refined.

An **index form** is a type of find that was in use only for a short time but was widespread. If you find an index form, you can place the whole find site in time. **Brooches** are especially suitable. These are clasps with which clothes were held together. Their shape changed quickly, almost like fashion.

**Otto Tischler** divided the **La Tène period**, the later Iron Age, in 1885 into Early, Middle and Late La Tène. He relied mainly on the brooches. **Paul Reinecke**, around 1900, divided the south German Bronze and Iron Age on the basis of typical combinations of finds. His stages such as **Bronze Age A to D** and **Hallstatt A to D** are still in use today in central Europe and Switzerland.

gewusst: The La Tène period is named after the find site La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel in Switzerland.
With a single well-dated brooch, a whole grave can sometimes be placed in time.

teile.einleitung: The Egyptian Book of the Dead is a collection of spells for life after death. The ancient Egyptians put it into the tomb with the deceased. It was meant to help them reach the afterlife safely.
wichtigste: The Book of the Dead is a **collection of spells for the afterlife**.
Its ancient Egyptian name translates as **“Book of Coming Forth by Day”**.
It was mostly written on **papyrus scrolls**.
At the judgement of the dead, the heart is weighed against the **feather of Maat**.
The god **Osiris** presides over the judgement of the dead.
The name “Book of the Dead” was given to it in 1842 by the researcher **Karl Richard Lepsius**.

abschnitte.titel: Spells for the way to the afterlife
abschnitte.text: The ancient Egyptians believed in a **life after death**. The way there was regarded as dangerous. The **Book of the Dead** contained many spells that were meant to protect and guide the deceased. Its ancient Egyptian name translates as **“Book of Coming Forth by Day”**. It was mostly written on **papyrus scrolls** and decorated with coloured pictures.

A famous scene is the **judgement of the dead**. There the **heart** of the deceased is laid on a scale. On the other side lies the **feather of Maat**, the sign of truth and justice. The jackal-headed god **Anubis** operates the scale. The god Thoth writes down the result. **Osiris**, the ruler of the afterlife, presides.

Before the court, the deceased speaks a **declaration of innocence**. In it he addresses **42 judges of the dead**. He assures them that he has done nothing evil, for example that he has not lied and not stolen. Whoever had a pure heart was allowed to enter the afterlife. According to the Book of the Dead, the heart of a guilty person was eaten by the monster **Ammit**.

The Egyptians were afraid that their own heart might testify against them before the court. That is why a **heart scarab** was often placed with the dead. This is an amulet in the shape of a beetle. On it was often written **Spell 30B** from the Book of the Dead. It asks the heart not to speak against its owner.

The collection was given the name **“Book of the Dead”** in **1842** by the German researcher **Karl Richard Lepsius**. He published a long papyrus scroll and numbered the spells. Researchers still use these numbers today. No Book of the Dead contains all the spells, and every scroll has its own selection.

gewusst: Rich Egyptians had a Book of the Dead made to their own wishes, with their name and their picture in it.
Some copies of the Book of the Dead are many metres long.

teile.einleitung: The First Triumvirate was an alliance of three powerful Romans in 60 BC. Caesar, Pompey and Crassus helped each other to push through their goals against the Senate.
wichtigste: The alliance consisted of **Caesar, Pompey and Crassus**.
It was made in **60 BC**.
“Triumvirate” means **league of three men**.
It was a **private agreement without an office**.
Pompey married **Caesar's daughter Julia**.
In 56 BC the three renewed their alliance at **Luca**.
Crassus fell in 53 BC **at Carrhae** against the Parthians.

abschnitte.text: The word **triumvirate** means **league of three men**. In **60 BC** three politicians joined forces: **Gaius Julius Caesar**, **Gnaeus Pompeius** (Pompey) and **Marcus Licinius Crassus**. Each of them on his own had met resistance in the Senate. Together they were strong enough to push through their plans. The alliance was **a private agreement without an office**, so not an official organ of the state.

**Pompey** was a famous general. He wanted **confirmation of his arrangements in the East** and **land for his veterans**. **Crassus** was known for his **enormous wealth**. He mainly wanted to help the **tax collectors of the province of Asia**, who had paid too much for their contracts. **Caesar** wanted to become consul and afterwards receive a province with an army of his own.

Caesar was elected consul for the year 59 BC and pushed through the wishes of his partners. To strengthen the alliance, Pompey married **Caesar's daughter Julia**. After that Caesar received the governorship of Gaul and began the Gallic War. When tensions arose, the three met in 56 BC at **Luca** and renewed their alliance.

In 54 BC Julia died, and with her an important bond between Caesar and Pompey was lost. A year later Crassus marched against the **Parthians** and fell in 53 BC **at Carrhae**. Now only Caesar and Pompey were left facing each other. Pompey drew closer to the Senate. In 49 BC a **civil war** began between the two.

gewusst: Later there was a **Second Triumvirate** of Octavian, Antony and Lepidus, which, unlike the first, was an official office.
The term “First Triumvirate” was only coined later; the Romans themselves did not call the alliance that.

teile.einleitung: The Assyrians were a people in ancient Mesopotamia, in the area of present-day Iraq. Their heartland lay on the River Tigris. In the 1st millennium BC, they built a great and feared empire.
wichtigste: The heartland of the Assyrians lay on the Tigris.
Their first capital Ashur has the same name as their chief god.
Ashurnasirpal II made Nimrud the capital in the 9th century BC.
Tiglath-Pileser III built the empire into a great power with provinces and a standing army.
Sargon II had the new capital Dur-Sharrukin built.
Defeated peoples were often resettled by force.
In the 7th century BC, the Assyrians conquered Egypt.

abschnitte.text: The Assyrians lived in the north of **Mesopotamia**, on the River **Tigris**. Their first capital was called **Ashur**, just like their chief god. They spoke a form of Akkadian and wrote in **cuneiform** on clay tablets. At first Ashur was a trading city. Later it grew into a great empire.

The kings built new capitals again and again. In the 9th century BC, **Ashurnasirpal II** made the city of **Nimrud** the capital. **Sargon II** later had the new city of **Dur-Sharrukin** built, which means “Fortress of Sargon”. After that, **Nineveh** became the most important city. The palaces were decorated with large stone reliefs that show military campaigns and hunts.

At the gates of the palaces stood huge figures of stone. They are called **lamassu**. A lamassu is a **winged bull with a human head**. It was supposed to protect the palace from evil powers. Many lamassu have five legs: from the front you see it standing, from the side striding. Today some stand in great museums of the world.

In the 8th century BC, King **Tiglath-Pileser III** built the empire into a **great power**. He divided it into **provinces** and created a **standing army**, that is, soldiers who were permanently in service. Defeated peoples were often **resettled by force**. In this way the rulers wanted to prevent uprisings. In the **7th century BC**, the Assyrians even conquered **Egypt**.

King Ashurbanipal collected a great **library** of clay tablets in Nineveh. Among them was the famous **Epic of Gilgamesh**. In 612 BC, Babylonians and Medes conquered Nineveh. Soon afterwards the empire fell. Archaeologists have excavated many of its palaces and writings.

gewusst: In the library of Ashurbanipal, over 20,000 clay tablets and fragments were found.
Even today there are people who call themselves Assyrians and speak a form of Aramaic.

teile.einleitung: Hellenism is an era of ancient times from the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BC to the year 30 BC. In this time Greek culture spread from Egypt to Persia.
wichtigste: Alexander's conquests introduced the era.
His death in 323 BC is usually taken as the beginning of the Hellenistic age.
His generals, the Diadochi, divided up the empire.
Large kingdoms were the Ptolemaic Kingdom and the Seleucid Empire.
Many people spoke the common Greek language, Koine.
With Cleopatra VII the last Hellenistic great kingdom ended in 30 BC.

abschnitte.text: **Alexander the Great** was king of **Macedonia**. As a teenager he was taught for about three years by the philosopher **Aristotle**. With his army he conquered the huge **Persian Empire** and marched as far as India. In **323 BC** he died, aged only 32, in **Babylon**. His death is usually taken as the beginning of the Hellenistic age.

After Alexander's death his generals fought over his empire. They are called the **Diadochi**, which means “successors”. They divided the empire into several kingdoms. The **Ptolemies** ruled in Egypt. The **Seleucid Empire**, with its capital **Antioch**, ruled large parts of Western Asia. In Macedonia the **Antigonids** ruled.

In the new kingdoms Greeks lived together with Egyptians, Persians and many other peoples. The Greek language spread as **Koine**, which means “the common” language. It was spoken from Egypt to Persia. The **New Testament** was also later written in Koine. Greek and Eastern cultures mingled in art, religion and science.

The city of **Alexandria** in Egypt became a centre of science. There was a famous **library** with a great many scrolls. Scholars researched mathematics, stars, medicine and language. Off the city stood the **Lighthouse of Pharos**, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

Little by little the **Romans** conquered the Hellenistic kingdoms. In **30 BC** **Cleopatra VII**, the last queen of the Ptolemies, died. Egypt became a Roman province, and with that the era usually ends. The term “**Hellenism**” was coined in the 19th century by the German historian **Johann Gustav Droysen**. From 1836 he published a “History of Hellenism”.

gewusst: Alexander founded many cities that he named Alexandria after himself. The best known lies in Egypt.
Hellenes is the name the Greeks gave themselves. The word Hellenism comes from it.

teile.einleitung: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a famous orator, politician and writer in ancient Rome. He lived from 106 to 43 BC, in the time of the late Republic. His speeches and letters survive to this day.
wichtigste: Cicero was a “homo novus”, a “new man”, because he was the first in his family to become consul.
In 70 BC he successfully prosecuted Verres, the governor of Sicily.
His first speech against Catiline begins with “Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?”
In 58 BC the tribune Publius Clodius Pulcher brought about his exile.
Many of his letters are addressed to his friend Atticus.
In 44 BC he dedicated the work “De officiis” to his son Marcus.
In 43 BC he was killed by soldiers while fleeing.

abschnitte.text: Cicero came from **Arpinum**, a small town south-east of Rome. His family was wealthy but not noble. He became a brilliant **lawyer** and **orator**. In 63 BC he became **consul**, the highest office of the Republic. Because he was the first in his family to get so far, he was called a **“homo novus”**, a new man.

In **70 BC** Cicero prosecuted **Verres**, the former governor of Sicily. Verres had plundered the province. Cicero won the trial. As consul he uncovered a conspiracy by the politician **Catiline**. His first speech against him begins with the famous words **“Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?”**. That means: “How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?”

During the conspiracy, men had been executed without a trial. Cicero was later blamed for this. In **58 BC** the tribune **Publius Clodius Pulcher** made sure that he had to go into **exile**. The very next year he was allowed to return. During this time Caesar, Pompey and Crassus were becoming ever more powerful.

Cicero wrote a great deal. Hundreds of **letters** survive, a large collection of them to his close friend **Atticus**. They show what life in Rome was like at that time. He also wrote books about philosophy and politics. In **44 BC** he dedicated to his son Marcus the work **“De officiis”**, on right conduct. His Latin was long held up as a model in schools.

After Caesar's murder, Cicero gave sharp speeches against **Mark Antony**. When Antony took power together with Octavian and Lepidus, Cicero was put on a list of enemies. In **43 BC** he was **killed by soldiers while fleeing**. With him died one of the last great defenders of the Republic.

gewusst: The name Cicero comes from the Latin word “cicer”, which means chickpea.
To this day many pupils read texts by Cicero in Latin lessons.

teile.einleitung: Heracles is the most famous hero of the Greek myths. He was unbelievably strong and had to carry out twelve difficult tasks, the twelve labours of Heracles.
wichtigste: Heracles was a son of the father of the gods, Zeus, and the mortal woman Alcmene.
So he was regarded as a demigod with enormous strength.
The myth tells of his twelve labours.
He defeated the Nemean Lion and the many-headed Hydra.
He cleaned the stables of Augeas in one day.
The Romans call him Hercules.

abschnitte.text: Heracles was a son of **Zeus**, the supreme god, and the mortal woman **Alcmene**. So he was a **demigod**. The goddess **Hera**, the wife of Zeus, was very angry about this. She persecuted Heracles all his life. Even as a baby he is said to have strangled two snakes that Hera had sent.

In the service of King **Eurystheus**, Heracles had to complete **twelve labours**. First he defeated the **Nemean Lion**, whose skin no weapon could pierce. Heracles strangled it and afterwards wore its skin as a cloak. Then he fought the **Hydra**, a water serpent with many heads. For every head cut off, two new ones grew. Only when the wounds were sealed with **fire** could he defeat it.

King **Augeas** had a great many cattle. His stables had not been cleaned for years. Heracles was to clean them out in **a single day**. He was clever: he diverted **two rivers** through the stables. The water washed out all the dung at once. To this day, a huge, dirty task is said to be like cleaning out the **Augean stables**.

The last and hardest labour took Heracles into the **underworld**. There the dog **Cerberus** guarded the entrance. Cerberus had three heads. Heracles overpowered him with his **bare hands** and brought him briefly up to the world above. Then he took him back again. Other labours included capturing a golden-horned hind and fetching golden apples.

The **Romans** took over many Greek myths. Heracles became **Hercules** for them. He was popular throughout the ancient world and was worshipped as a god. To this day a very strong person is said to be a Hercules. A hard task is called a **herculean task**. A constellation also bears his name.

gewusst: The “Pillars of Hercules” was in ancient times the name for the rocks on the Strait of Gibraltar.
According to the myth, after his death Heracles was taken up into Olympus and so became a god himself.

teile.einleitung: Divico was a leader of the Helvetii, a Celtic people in the area of present-day Switzerland. He is famous because he challenged the Romans twice: as a young commander and as an old man facing Caesar.
wichtigste: Divico was a **leader of the Helvetii**.
In 107 BC he defeated a **Roman army**.
The battle took place near **Agen** in present-day **France**.
The defeated Romans had to pass **under a yoke**.
In 58 BC Divico negotiated with **Caesar**; he was then **about 70 years** old.
Caesar demanded **hostages**, but Divico **refused**.

abschnitte.text: The **Helvetii** were a Celtic people who lived on the Plateau of present-day Switzerland. They were divided into several tribes. Divico belonged to the tribe of the **Tigurini**. What we know about him comes mainly from the accounts of the Roman **Julius Caesar**. Divico is one of the first people from the area of Switzerland whose name has been handed down.

In 107 BC the Tigurini marched south-west. Near **Agen** in present-day **France**, under Divico's leadership, they defeated a **Roman army**. The Roman commander was killed in the battle. The surviving Romans had to **pass under a yoke**. This was a gateway made of spears and was seen as a great humiliation.

About fifty years later, in 58 BC, the Helvetii wanted to emigrate to the west. Caesar stood in their way. After a first fight, the Helvetii sent the old Divico, then **about 70 years** old, to negotiate. Caesar demanded **hostages** and compensation. Divico **refused** and is said to have replied that the Helvetii were used to taking hostages, not giving them.

Later Divico was regarded in Switzerland as a hero who stood up to a great power. In the 19th century the Swiss poet **Conrad Ferdinand Meyer** wrote **a poem** about Divico's victory. Paintings too show the Romans passing under the yoke. But such pictures say more about the time they were made than about the exact events.

gewusst: The word “yoke” comes from the wooden beam used to harness oxen together.
Divico's proud answer to Caesar is found in Caesar's own account of the Gallic War.

teile.einleitung: **Stegosaurus** was a large plant eater of the Jurassic. On its back it carried two rows of large bony plates. At the end of its tail it had four pointed spikes.
wichtigste: Stegosaurus means roof lizard.
It ate plants and walked on four legs.
At the end of its tail it had four pointed spikes.
Its head was small and narrow, and its brain very small.
Most fossils were found in North America.
It lived much earlier than Tyrannosaurus rex.

abschnitte.text: On its back, Stegosaurus carried two rows of large, flat **bony plates**. The first researchers thought they lay flat like roof tiles. That is why it is called the **roof lizard**. Today we know that the plates stood upright. Probably they served **for showing off and impressing**, so that the animals recognised each other.

At the end of its tail, Stegosaurus had **four pointed spikes**. With powerful blows of the tail it could defend itself against predatory dinosaurs. Bones of predatory dinosaurs have even been found that were wounded by such spikes.

Stegosaurus walked on **four legs**. The hind legs were much longer than the forelegs, so its back was highly arched. The **head** was **small and narrow** and close to the ground. The **brain** was **very small** compared with the huge body. It ate low-growing **plants** such as ferns.

Stegosaurus lived in the **Jurassic**, about 150 million years ago. Most fossils were found in **North America**. Tyrannosaurus rex only lived at the end of the Cretaceous. So the two **never met**. Between them lies more time than between T. rex and us today.

gewusst: The brain of Stegosaurus was only about as big as a walnut.
A fully grown Stegosaurus was about as long as a bus.

teile.einleitung: The Urnfield culture shaped central Europe in the late Bronze Age. It gets its name from the custom of burying the ashes of the dead in urns in large cemeteries.
wichtigste: The Urnfield culture existed from roughly 1300 to 800 BC.
The dead were cremated, and their ashes were placed in urns in flat graves.
It corresponds roughly to the stages Hallstatt A and B after Paul Reinecke.
In Switzerland, the lakeshores were densely settled again.
A typical religious symbol is the bird sun barque.
The Lusatian culture with Biskupin also belongs to the circle of Urnfield cultures.

abschnitte.text: The people of this time cremated their dead. They put the ashes in **urns**, that is clay vessels, and buried them in **flat graves**. In this way large cemeteries with many urns arose. These **urnfields** gave the whole culture its name. The custom spread over large parts of Europe.

The Urnfield culture forms the **late Bronze Age** of central Europe, from about **1300 to 800 BC**. After it came the earlier Iron Age. The archaeologist **Paul Reinecke** divided this period into stages after the cemetery of Hallstatt. The early stages **Hallstatt A and B** still belong to the Bronze Age Urnfield culture.

In Switzerland, the lakeshores were densely settled again after a gap. Such **lakeshore settlements** existed for example at **Zurich Alpenquai** or at **Hauterive-Champréveyres** on Lake Neuchâtel. The houses stood on piles or on damp ground. Around 800 BC, these settlements came to an end.

A typical symbol is the **bird sun barque**: a boat with bird heads carrying a sun disc. It probably stands for the journey of the sun. From the late Bronze Age also come the **gold hats**, tall cones of thin gold sheet. Their patterns are interpreted as moon and sun calendars, for example in the **Berlin Gold Hat**.

In the east of central Europe, in Poland and eastern Germany, lived the **Lusatian culture**. It too buried its dead in urns and belongs to the circle of Urnfield cultures. Well known is the settlement of **Biskupin**, a fortified wooden settlement on a lake island. A part of it was rebuilt and can be visited.

gewusst: A gold hat is beaten from a single piece of gold sheet and is wafer thin.
The settlement at Alpenquai lies today in the middle of the city of Zurich beneath the lake bed.

teile.einleitung: Turkana Boy is one of the most famous fossils in the world. It is the almost complete skeleton of a child of the human species Homo erectus, who lived in East Africa about 1.5 million years ago.
wichtigste: Turkana Boy was found in 1984 in the north of Kenya.
The first bone was discovered by the Kenyan fossil hunter Kamoya Kimeu.
The skeleton is about 1.5 million years old.
He belongs to the human species Homo erectus, though some say Homo ergaster.
According to the present estimate, he was about 8 to 9 years old when he died.
After the find site, he is also called Nariokotome Boy.

abschnitte.text: In August 1984, **Kamoya Kimeu** discovered a small piece of a frontal bone. He was working in the team of the researchers **Richard Leakey** and **Alan Walker**. The find site lies about 5 kilometres west of **Lake Turkana** in the north of Kenya, in the dried-up river bed of **Nariokotome**. Over several digging seasons, the team then uncovered bone after bone.

67 bones and 12 teeth were found. For such an old fossil, that is a great deal. Especially valuable are the bones below the skull, that is the arms, legs, pelvis and vertebrae. For the first time, the **build** of an early human could be studied so exactly. That is why Turkana Boy is regarded as one of the most complete skeletons of an early human.

At first it was estimated that the boy was 11 to 13 years old. Later the **growth lines in the tooth enamel** were examined. Teeth grow in fine layers, similar to the annual rings of trees. These lines showed that he was only about **8 to 9 years** old. So early humans evidently became adult faster than we do today.

Turkana Boy is usually counted as the species **Homo erectus**, which means “upright human”. Some experts use the name **Homo ergaster** for the African finds. The skeleton shows a large, slender body with long legs, well suited to long-distance walking. His brain, at about 880 cubic centimetres, was clearly smaller than ours.

The skeleton used to be estimated at about 1.6 million years old. A more exact analysis of the rock layers gave an age of about **1.53 million years**. At that time there were no humans of our species in East Africa yet. Finds like this help us to understand how humans developed over a long time.

gewusst: For a fossil that is over a million years old, an almost whole skeleton is a great rarity.
Kamoya Kimeu was one of the most successful fossil hunters in Africa and found many important fossils.

teile.einleitung: Hadrian was emperor of the Roman Empire from AD 117 to 138. He travelled a great deal, had great buildings put up and secured the borders instead of conquering new lands.
wichtigste: Hadrian ruled as Roman emperor from AD 117 to 138.
He is one of the so-called “good emperors” or adoptive emperors.
He travelled for many years through almost all the provinces of his empire.
He had the Pantheon in Rome rebuilt.
His tomb on the Tiber is now the Castel Sant'Angelo.
Hadrian was the first emperor to wear a full beard permanently.

abschnitte.text: Hadrian's family came from the city of **Italica** in Hispania, present-day Spain. He was a relative of Emperor **Trajan**, who supported him. After Trajan's death in 117, Hadrian became emperor. He counts as one of the **adoptive emperors**, because these emperors often chose their successor by adoption. Hadrian himself later adopted Antoninus Pius as his successor.

No emperor before him travelled as much as Hadrian. He visited **provinces**, cities and army camps from Britain to Egypt. In doing so he checked the administration and the army. Hadrian no longer wanted to enlarge the empire, but to **secure its borders**. So he had frontier works built, such as the famous Hadrian's Wall in Britain.

In Rome Hadrian had the **Pantheon** rebuilt, a temple for all the gods. Its huge concrete dome has a round opening at the top, the oculus. It is still the largest dome of unreinforced concrete in the world. For himself Hadrian had a large round **tomb** built on the Tiber. Later it was converted into a fortress of the popes and is now called the **Castel Sant'Angelo**.

The emperors before Hadrian were mostly clean-shaven. Hadrian was the first emperor to wear a permanent **full beard**. He can be seen like this on many statues and coins. Hadrian admired **Greek culture**, and beards were usual among Greek philosophers. Many emperors after him also wore a beard, and so the beard came into fashion in Rome.

At **Tivoli** near Rome Hadrian had a huge complex built, the **Villa Adriana**. It was more a small town than a house, with palaces, baths, gardens and pools. Some parts recalled places that Hadrian had seen on his travels. Today the villa is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: The dome of the Pantheon is exactly as high inside as it is wide: a huge sphere would fit inside it.
Hadrian also wrote poems and was interested in architecture, art and philosophy.

teile.einleitung: Jean-François Champollion was a French linguist. He was the first to decipher the Egyptian hieroglyphs and is therefore regarded as the founder of Egyptology.
wichtigste: Champollion was born in 1790 in Figeac in southern France.
Even as a child he learned many ancient languages.
He knew Coptic, the youngest form of the Egyptian language.
In 1822 he announced his breakthrough in a letter to Dacier.
He recognised that hieroglyphs are partly phonetic signs and partly picture signs.
He died in 1832 at only 41 years old.

abschnitte.text: Champollion was born on 23 December **1790** in **Figeac** in southern France. Even as a child he learned many ancient **languages**, such as Latin, Greek, Hebrew and Arabic. His elder brother **Jacques-Joseph** supported him from his youth. Especially important for him became **Coptic**. It is the youngest form of the Egyptian language and continued to be used in the church.

In 1799 French soldiers found the **Rosetta Stone** in Egypt. On it stands the same text in three scripts: **hieroglyphs**, Demotic and **Greek**. Scholars could read Greek. So there was a key to the hieroglyphs. The English scholar **Thomas Young** also worked on it and made important first steps.

In hieroglyphs, royal names are written inside an oval, the **cartouche**. Champollion compared the names **Ptolemy** and **Cleopatra** and in this way found sound values of signs. He recognised that hieroglyphs are partly **phonetic signs** and partly **picture signs** for whole words or determinatives. In September **1822** he presented his findings in a letter to **Bon-Joseph Dacier**. This “Lettre à M. Dacier” is regarded as the birth certificate of **Egyptology**.

Only late in life could Champollion travel to Egypt himself. From **1828 to 1829** he led a Franco-Tuscan expedition with the Italian scholar **Ippolito Rosellini**. The researchers copied numerous inscriptions on the spot. So Champollion could test his method on real monuments. It was his only journey to Egypt.

Champollion died on 4 March **1832** in Paris at only **41 years old**. Many of his works were not yet printed. His brother Jacques-Joseph Champollion-Figeac published the Egyptian **grammar** and the **dictionary** after his death. Thanks to Champollion, researchers today can read thousands of ancient inscriptions.

gewusst: In Figeac there is today a museum about the scripts of the world that is named after Champollion.
The Rosetta Stone is today in the British Museum in London.

teile.einleitung: The Empire of Aksum was a powerful kingdom in north-eastern Africa. It lay in the area of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea. In the first centuries AD it was an important trading empire.
wichtigste: Aksum lay in the area of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea.
King Ezana adopted Christianity in the 4th century.
Aksum minted its own gold coins.
The old written language is called Ge'ez.
Aksum traded through the port of Adulis on the Red Sea.
Mani counted Aksum, along with Rome, Persia and China, among the greatest empires in the world.

abschnitte.titel: An empire on the Red Sea
abschnitte.text: The capital **Aksum** lay in the highlands of present-day Ethiopia. The empire reached as far as the **Red Sea**. There lay the important port of **Adulis**. Through it, Aksum traded with Egypt, the Roman Empire, Arabia and India. Goods sold included ivory, gold and frankincense.

Aksum showed its power with its own **gold coins**. Only a few empires of that time minted such coins. On them were the names and pictures of the kings. The written language of the empire was **Ge'ez**. It is still used today in the services of the Ethiopian church.

In the **4th century**, King **Ezana** adopted **Christianity**. This makes Aksum one of the first empires in the world with a Christian ruler. On his coins, a cross soon replaced the old signs of sun and moon. Christianity shapes Ethiopia to this day.

Aksum is famous for its huge **stelae**, tall stone pillars made from a single block. Some are decorated with windows and doors, like skyscrapers of stone. In 1937, Italy took a large stele and set it up in Rome. In **2005** it returned to Ethiopia and stands today again in Aksum. The ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Persian founder of a religion, **Mani**, lived in the 3rd century. He named four great empires of his time: **Rome, Persia, Aksum and China**. This shows how well known and important Aksum was at the time. From the 7th century, the empire gradually lost power.

gewusst: According to an Ethiopian tradition, the biblical Ark of the Covenant is said to be kept in Aksum, but nobody may see it.
Ge'ez has its own script, from which the present-day script of Amharic developed.

teile.einleitung: The Theory of Forms is a core part of the philosophy of Plato. According to it, the things we see are only imperfect copies of eternal, unchanging Forms, or Ideas.
wichtigste: The Theory of Forms comes from the Greek philosopher Plato.
For Plato the unchanging Forms are true reality.
The things we see are only copies of the Forms.
For Plato, knowing is recollection, anamnesis.
The Form of the Good stands at the highest place.

abschnitte.text: **Plato** lived in **Athens** in the 5th and 4th centuries BC. He asked: What is really real? All the horses we see are different, and they change. Yet we recognise them all as a horse. So for Plato there is a **Form** of the horse, which is eternal and **unchanging**. The things we perceive with the senses are only imperfect **copies** of these Forms.
