How do we know the Forms if we never see them? Plato thinks that the **immortal soul** saw the Forms before birth. So learning is a **recollection**, in Greek **anamnesis**. In the dialogue “**Meno**”, Socrates shows this with an example. He asks a young slave, who has never learned mathematics, only questions. In this way the slave finds the solution to a geometry problem himself.

At the highest place for Plato stands the **Form of the Good**. In his work the “**Republic**” he compares it to the **sun**. Just as the sun makes things visible, the Form of the Good makes all other Forms knowable. In the famous **allegory of the cave**, people sit in a cave and see only shadows on the wall. They take the shadows for reality, until one of them goes outside and sees the sun.

gewusst: Plato's pupil Aristotle criticised the Theory of Forms and held that the universal is contained in things themselves.

teile.einleitung: Archimedes was a Greek mathematician and inventor. He lived about 2,200 years ago in Syracuse on the island of Sicily. He is regarded as one of the greatest thinkers of antiquity.
wichtigste: Archimedes lived about 2,200 years ago in Syracuse in Sicily.
He was a mathematician and inventor.
In the bath he noticed how the water rose, and is said to have cried “Eureka!”.
He was supposed to check for the king whether a crown was of pure gold.
With a lever he even wanted to move the Earth.
The Archimedes screw lifts water.
He showed that a sphere fills two thirds of the cylinder that encloses it.

abschnitte.text: Archimedes was born around 287 BC in **Syracuse**, a Greek city on **Sicily**. He was a **mathematician**, **physicist** and **inventor**. He was in contact with scholars in Alexandria in Egypt. He was well acquainted with the king of Syracuse. For him he solved many a difficult task.

The king wanted to know whether his **crown was of pure gold** or whether the goldsmith had mixed in silver. Archimedes was not allowed to damage the crown. According to the legend, he stepped into a full bathtub and saw how the **water rose**. Then the idea came to him: a body displaces as much water as the space it takes up itself. Delighted, he is said to have cried **“Eureka!”**, which means “I have found it!”. From this developed the **Archimedes principle** about buoyancy in water.

Archimedes studied how a **lever** works. With a long lever, you can move heavy loads with little force. He is said to have said: “Give me a firm point, and I will move the Earth.” Also well known is the **Archimedes screw**. It consists of a spiral in a tube. When you turn it, **water is lifted up**, for example to irrigate fields.

Archimedes calculated areas and solids very exactly. He found out that a **sphere** fills exactly **two thirds** of the cylinder that encloses it. He was so proud of this that he wished for a sphere and cylinder on his tomb. He determined the number **pi** surprisingly exactly. In his work **“The Sand Reckoner”**, he estimated how many grains of sand would fit into the whole universe. For this he invented a way of writing very large numbers.

In the war between Rome and Carthage, the Romans besieged Syracuse. Archimedes helped with war machines in the defence of the city. In **212 BC**, the Romans conquered Syracuse. In the process, Archimedes was killed by a soldier. According to tradition, he said beforehand: “Do not disturb my circles!”

gewusst: Archimedes screws are still used today, for example in sewage works.
The Roman orator Cicero found the overgrown tomb of Archimedes again by means of the sphere and cylinder.

teile.einleitung: The Colossus of Rhodes was a huge statue of the sun god Helios. It is one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, but stood for only a short time.
wichtigste: The Colossus showed Helios, the patron god of the island of Rhodes.
The statue was made of bronze and about 30 metres high.
It was paid for with the proceeds from siege engines left behind.
An earthquake made the Colossus collapse after about 60 years.
It was the wonder that stood for the shortest time.
That it stood astride the harbour is probably a legend.

abschnitte.text: **Rhodes** is a Greek island in the Mediterranean. It lies near the coast of present-day **Turkey**. In antiquity the city of Rhodes was a rich trading place with an important harbour. The patron god of the island was the sun god **Helios**. In his honour the inhabitants built the huge statue.

An enemy had **besieged** the city for a long time but could not capture it. When he withdrew, he left his **siege engines** behind. The inhabitants sold them and paid for the Colossus with the money. So war equipment became a monument of thanks. The building took many years.

The Colossus was about **30 metres** high, as high as a house with ten storeys. Its outer shell was made of cast **bronze**. Inside, **iron bars** and stones probably gave it support. It was built by the sculptor **Chares of Lindos**. For the time it was a technical masterpiece.

Only about **60 years** after its completion a strong **earthquake** brought the Colossus down. After that it lay for a long time as rubble on the ground. Travellers still came to marvel at the huge fragments. Of all the seven **wonders** the Colossus stood for the shortest time.

abschnitte.titel: What did it really look like?
abschnitte.text: In many pictures the Colossus stands with **legs apart** over the harbour entrance, and ships sail between them. That would hardly have been technically possible and is regarded as a **legend**. The statue probably stood on solid ground. How exactly it looked is not known, because no reliable depiction survives.

gewusst: The word “colossal” for something enormously large recalls such giant statues.
The Statue of Liberty in New York was called a “new Colossus” in a poem.

teile.einleitung: Cleisthenes was a politician in ancient Athens. With his reforms around 508/507 BC he reorganised the citizen body and so laid the foundation for Athenian democracy.
wichtigste: Cleisthenes came from the noble family of the Alcmaeonidae.
His reforms took place around 508/507 BC, after the overthrow of the tyrant Hippias.
He divided the citizens of Attica into ten new tribes.
The smallest political unit was the communities, the demes.
The new council, the Boule, had 500 members.

abschnitte.text: For a long time **tyrants**, that is, sole rulers, governed Athens. In 510 BC the tyrant **Hippias** was driven out. After that noble families quarrelled over power. Cleisthenes won the support of the people. Around **508/507 BC** he pushed through a great reorganisation.

Cleisthenes made the communities, the **demes**, the smallest political unit. Every citizen was entered in his deme and carried its name as an addition. Several demes formed a **trittys**. One trittys each from the city, from the coast and from the inland were combined into a **tribe**. In this way **ten tribes** arose, in which people from quite different areas came together. This weakened the old ties to the noble families.

Each tribe provided **50 councillors**, who were chosen by **lot**. In this way the council, the **Boule**, with **500** members arose. It prepared the decisions of the **Assembly**, in which all citizens could vote. At that time, however, only free men of Athens counted as citizens, not women, foreigners or slaves.

gewusst: Giving out offices by lot was meant to prevent only rich and well-known men from always being chosen.
The word “democracy” comes from “demos”, people, and “kratos”, rule.

teile.einleitung: The Wildkirchli consists of three caves below the Ebenalp in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden. It is famous for traces of the Neanderthals, for its cave chapel and for the hermits who lived here.
wichtigste: The Wildkirchli lies below the Ebenalp in Appenzell Innerrhoden.
It consists of three caves in the limestone, with a combined length of about 150 metres.
From 1904, the St Gallen researcher Emil Bächler dug here.
He found stone tools of Neanderthals and many animal bones.
From 1658 to 1853, hermits lived in the caves.
The chapel is dedicated to the Archangel Michael.

abschnitte.text: The **Wildkirchli** consists of **three caves** in the **limestone**. Together they are about 150 metres long, and a hiking trail leads through one of them. They lie below the **Ebenalp** in the canton of **Appenzell Innerrhoden**. Very close by, the well-known **Berggasthaus Aescher** clings to the rock face. It belongs to the Wildkirchli Foundation.

From **1904**, the St Gallen natural scientist **Emil Bächler** dug in the caves. He found **stone tools** and many **animal bones**, mainly of the cave bear. The worked stones are several tens of thousands of years old and come from **Neanderthals**. That was a sensation: until then it was believed that the people of the Old Stone Age had avoided the Alps.

In **1621**, the monk **Philipp Tanner** set up a chapel in honour of the **Archangel Michael**. But he left the place as early as 1624, and the chapel at first fell into oblivion. In the altar cave, **services** are still held to this day. The name Wildkirchli, “wild little church”, comes from the chapel in the wild rock face.

In **1658**, the priest **Paulus Ulmann** settled here as the first hermit. He developed the site into a **hermitage**. In 1679 he founded a **foundation** to secure its upkeep. After that, several hermits lived in the caves one after another and looked after the chapel. The last one left the Wildkirchli in **1853**.

gewusst: The Wildkirchli was the first place to prove traces of Old Stone Age people in the Alps.
The Berggasthaus Aescher became world famous because it stands so spectacularly on the rock face.

teile.einleitung: The Ides of March is 15 March. On this day in 44 BC Gaius Julius Caesar was murdered in Rome by senators. The date still stands today for a fateful event.
wichtigste: In the Roman calendar the Ides were the middle of the month, in March the 15th.
Caesar was killed at a meeting of the Senate on 15 March 44 BC.
The meeting took place in the Curia of Pompey.
According to Suetonius, more than 60 men took part in the conspiracy.
Caesar had shortly before become dictator for life.
The conspirators were defeated at Philippi in 42 BC.

abschnitte.text: The Romans divided their months differently from us. The **Ides** were the middle of the month. In March they fell on **15 March**. Originally this day was a festival. Through the murder of Caesar in **44 BC** it became world famous. To this day the “Ides of March” stands for a day on which disaster threatens.

**Gaius Julius Caesar** had great power after a civil war. At the beginning of 44 BC he became **dictator for life**, in Latin dictator perpetuo. Many **senators** feared that he wanted to rule like a **king**. For them that meant the end of the free **Republic**. According to the writer **Suetonius**, more than **60 men** conspired against him. Their leaders included **Brutus** and **Cassius**.

According to tradition, the seer **Spurinna** warned Caesar of a danger that would come no later than the Ides of March. His wife **Calpurnia**, after a bad dream, is said to have begged him not to go to the Senate. Caesar hesitated, but at the urging of one of the conspirators he went to the meeting after all. The poet **Shakespeare** later wrote: “Beware the Ides of March.”

The meeting of the Senate took place in the **Curia of Pompey**, a hall next to the Theatre of Pompey. There the conspirators attacked Caesar with **daggers** and killed him. He is said to have died at the foot of a statue of **Pompey**, his former opponent. Later his body was burned in the **Forum**. On this spot a temple was built for the deified Caesar, the Temple of **Divus Iulius**.

The conspirators wanted to save the Republic, but new **civil wars** followed. One of them, Brutus, had a **coin** struck with the inscription “**EID MAR**”. It shows two daggers and a **cap of liberty**, a sign of the supposed liberation of Rome. In **42 BC** Caesar's supporters defeated the army of the conspirators at **Philippi** in Macedonia. After that Caesar's heir **Octavian** became ever more powerful and later, as Augustus, the first emperor.

gewusst: After his death Caesar was officially declared a god by the Senate.
The month of July is named after Julius Caesar.

teile.einleitung: The Hittites were a people of ancient times with a large empire in Anatolia, present-day Turkey. Their capital was called Hattusa. Around 1200 BC their empire collapsed.
wichtigste: The Hittite Empire lay in the centre of Anatolia.
The capital Hattusa, with the Lion Gate, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Hittite is the oldest written Indo-European language.
Bedřich Hrozný deciphered the language in 1915.
The Hittites were feared for their chariots.
Their peace treaty with Egypt is among the oldest known peace treaties.

abschnitte.text: The empire of the Hittites lay in the centre of **Anatolia**, that is, in present-day **Turkey**. Later their influence reached as far as **Syria**. Around **1595 BC** King **Mursili I** marched as far as Mesopotamia and plundered **Babylon**. That ended the dynasty to which Hammurabi had once belonged. The Hittites were one of the great powers of their time, alongside Egypt and Babylon.

The capital was called **Hattusa**. Its ruins lie near the present-day village of **Boğazkale**. The city had mighty walls, temples and palaces. A landmark is the **Lion Gate**: two lions carved from stone stand there as guardians. Since 1986 Hattusa has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Thousands of **clay tablets** with cuneiform were also found there.

For a long time nobody could read the texts from Hattusa. In **1915** the Czech researcher **Bedřich Hrozný** deciphered the language. He recognised that Hittite belongs to the **Indo-European languages**. It is the oldest written language of this family. That makes it distantly related to **English**, Latin and Greek.

The Hittites were feared for their **chariots**. These were pulled by horses and carried a crew of three. Around 1274 BC Hittites and Egyptians fought in the **battle of Kadesh** in Syria. A few years later King **Hattusili III** and Pharaoh **Ramesses II** made a peace treaty. A copy of the clay tablet hangs in the **United Nations headquarters** in New York.

abschnitte.titel: A thousand gods and the end
abschnitte.text: The Hittites took gods from conquered and neighbouring peoples into their religion. That is why they themselves spoke of the “**land of a thousand gods**”. Around **1200 BC** several kingdoms in the eastern Mediterranean collapsed. The Hittite Empire also broke up, and Hattusa was abandoned. The reasons are not entirely clear.

gewusst: The Hittites were already mentioned in the Bible, long before their empire was rediscovered.
In the peace treaty between the Hittites and the Egyptians, both sides also promised each other help against enemies.

teile.einleitung: How did Rome, one of the most famous cities in the world, come into being? The Romans told an exciting myth about it, of the twins Romulus and Remus, who were suckled by a she-wolf. Archaeologists have also found real traces of the first settlements on the Tiber.
wichtigste: According to Roman tradition, Rome was founded in 753 BC.
According to the myth, the twins Romulus and Remus founded the city.
A she-wolf is said to have suckled the abandoned twins.
Rome lies on the River Tiber in central Italy.
According to tradition, Rome is built on seven hills.
The first settlement is said to have arisen on the Palatine.
At the beginning Rome was ruled by kings, the last of whom was Tarquinius Superbus.
The Etruscans strongly influenced early Rome.

abschnitte.text: According to the myth, **Romulus and Remus** were the sons of the god of war Mars and the king's daughter Rhea Silvia from the city of Alba Longa. A wicked uncle, King Amulius, had the babies put in a basket on the Tiber. The basket ran aground on the bank, and a **she-wolf** suckled the children. Later a shepherd named Faustulus found them and raised them with his wife.

As adults the brothers wanted to found a city at the place where they had been rescued. But they quarrelled over who should be king and where the city should stand. Romulus drew a boundary furrow on the **Palatine**, and Remus jumped mockingly over it. For this Romulus is said to have killed his brother. The new city was named **Roma** after him.

The Romans later worked out the founding year as **753 BC**. The founding day was taken to be 21 April, which is still celebrated in Rome today as the city's birthday. Many Romans even counted the years from the founding of the city, in Latin **ab urbe condita**. But the date is not an exact fact; it is a calculation from a later time.

Rome lies on the **Tiber**, about 25 kilometres from where it flows into the Mediterranean. At this spot the river was easy to cross, and the hills offered protection from enemies and floods. According to tradition Rome is built on **seven hills**, which include the Palatine, the Capitoline and the Aventine. On the Palatine archaeologists have found remains of simple **huts** of wood and clay dating from about the 8th century BC. From several small villages a city gradually grew.

At the beginning, according to tradition, Rome was ruled by seven **kings**, starting with Romulus. Some of them came from the **Etruscans**, a people from central Italy who strongly influenced Rome. From them the Romans learned, for example, a great deal about building, religion and crafts. The last king, **Tarquinius Superbus**, was regarded as a cruel ruler. After he was driven out around 509 BC, Rome became a republic.

The myth of Romulus and Remus is still a symbol of Rome today. A famous bronze figure, the **Capitoline Wolf**, shows the she-wolf with the two twins. The image of the she-wolf can be found in Rome on coins, coats of arms and even in the logo of a football club. The small settlement on the Tiber later became the capital of a huge empire, which also included present-day Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: An old story that often has a true core but contains a lot of invention.
One of the seven hills of Rome, on which the first settlement is said to have been.
A people in central Italy that was powerful there before the Romans.
A state without a king, in which elected people govern.
Latin for “since the founding of the city”, a Roman way of counting years.

gewusst: The word palace comes from the Palatine, because the emperors later built their palaces there.
The twins under the Capitoline Wolf were only added much later, in the time of the Renaissance.
Every year on 21 April Rome celebrates its birthday with parades in Roman costume.

teile.einleitung: The **stone axe** was the most important tool of the farmers of the New Stone Age. With it they felled trees and worked wood. The blade was of hard stone, the handle of wood.
wichtigste: With the stone axe, the farmers of the New Stone Age felled trees.
The blade was of hard stone, the handle of wood.
The blade was ground smooth and sharp on a stone.
When the blade was blunt, it was ground anew.
In Swiss pile dwellings, the sockets were often made of red deer antler.
The wood was needed for houses and fires.

abschnitte.text: The **blade** was of **hard stone**. First the stone was roughly shaped. Then it was **ground** for a long time on another stone, with sand and water. In this way the blade became **smooth and sharp**. If it became **blunt** during work, it was simply ground **anew**.

The **handle** was of **wood**. In the **pile dwellings** of Switzerland, the blade often sat in a **socket of red deer antler**. This socket was then fixed in the wooden handle. The antler cushioned the hard blows, so the blade or the handle broke less quickly.

In the **New Stone Age**, people settled down and became farmers. For fields, they had to clear forest. With the stone axe they **felled** trees. They needed the **wood** for **houses**, fences, tools and the **fire**. Experiments show that with a good stone axe, a tree can be felled surprisingly quickly.

At many Swiss lakes, remains of **pile-dwelling settlements** were found, for example on Lake Zurich, Lake Biel and Lake Neuchâtel. In the damp ground, wooden handles, antler sockets and blades were well preserved. So today we know exactly how a stone axe was built. The pile dwellings around the Alps are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: For the blades, people liked to choose especially tough rocks that do not splinter easily.
At the pile dwellings, not only blades were found, but also the workshops in which they were ground.

teile.einleitung: The Limes was the fortified frontier of the Roman Empire. Especially well known is the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes between the Rhine and the Danube, which is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: The Limes consisted of ramparts, ditches, palisades, watchtowers and forts.
The Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes ran between the Rhine and the Danube.
It was about 550 kilometres long.
Since 2005 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Around 260 AD the Romans gave up this Limes.
The fort of Saalburg near Bad Homburg was rebuilt and is now a museum.

abschnitte.titel: From a path to a frontier
abschnitte.text: The Latin word **“limes”** originally meant a **boundary path**. It meant a path or a cleared strip, for example between fields. Only later did the word refer to the **fortified imperial frontier**. This consisted of **ramparts**, **ditches**, **palisades** of wooden stakes, **watchtowers** and **forts**. The Limes was not meant to stop every attack, but it controlled who crossed the border.

abschnitte.titel: Between the Rhine and the Danube
abschnitte.text: The Rhine and the Danube already formed a natural border. But between them lay a gap. This was closed by the **Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes**. It was about **550 kilometres** long and ran through present-day **southern Germany**. That makes it one of the largest archaeological monuments in Europe. Since **2005** it has belonged to the World Heritage Site **“Frontiers of the Roman Empire”**, together with sites in Great Britain.

A **fort** was a fortified, usually rectangular camp with a wall, gates and towers. The soldiers who guarded the frontier lived there. The **Saalburg** fort in the Taunus near **Bad Homburg** was rebuilt around **1900** at the wish of Emperor **Wilhelm II**. Today it is a **museum** of the Roman period. There one can see vividly what a Roman fort looked like.

In the 3rd century the Roman Empire fell into a serious crisis. Around **260 AD** the Romans could no longer hold the area behind the Limes. The frontier was moved back to the **Rhine**, the **Iller** and the **Danube**. As a result present-day northern Switzerland again lay directly on the imperial frontier.

On the Rhine the Romans afterwards built new fortifications and **watchtowers**, of which remains survive to this day. Around 300 the fort **Castrum Rauracense** arose at **Kaiseraugst**. Many inhabitants of the area withdrew behind its strong walls. Later the fort was even the seat of a **bishop**.

gewusst: Hadrian's Wall in England is also part of the World Heritage Site “Frontiers of the Roman Empire”.
Along the Limes there were probably about 900 watchtowers within sight of one another.

teile.einleitung: Agriculture was the foundation of ancient Egypt. Every year the Nile flooded the fields and brought fertile mud that made good harvests possible.
wichtigste: The year had three seasons: flooding, sowing and harvest.
A nilometer was used to measure how high the water rose.
Farmers drew water from the Nile with the shaduf.
Cattle pulled the wooden plough.
Grain was cut with sickles and stored in granaries.
Farmers paid their dues with part of the harvest.

abschnitte.text: In Egypt it hardly ever rains. But every year the **Nile** rose over its banks and flooded the fields. When the water went down, fertile **mud** was left behind. On it the grain grew very well. With a **nilometer**, a staircase or shaft with markings, the water level was measured. From it people could see whether a good harvest was to be expected.

The Egyptian year had **three seasons**, each about four months long. First came the time of the **flood**. After that followed the time of **sowing**, when the fields were tilled. At the end came the time of **harvest**. So the whole calendar followed the river.

**Cattle** pulled the wooden **plough** across the fields. To bring water to higher fields, farmers used the **shaduf**. This is a long beam with a bucket at one end and a **counterweight** at the other. In this way water could be lifted easily. Canals distributed the water further.

The most important plants were grains such as **emmer** and **barley**. From them people made bread and beer. From **flax** they made linen cloth. From the palms they harvested sweet **dates**. The ripe grain was cut with **sickles**, which in earlier times often had blades of **flint**.

The harvested grain was stored in **granaries** of mud brick. There it stayed dry and safe for bad years. For a long time there was no coined money. So farmers handed over **part of the harvest** as dues to the pharaoh's state. Scribes counted and noted exactly what was delivered.

gewusst: Since the building of the Aswan High Dam in the 20th century, the yearly flooding of the Nile no longer happens.
The Greek Herodotus called Egypt a “gift of the Nile”.

teile.einleitung: Ancient grains are old kinds of cereal such as emmer and einkorn. They were already grown by the first farmers of the New Stone Age and are ancestors and relatives of our wheat today.
wichtigste: Cereals arose from wild grasses.
The grains sit in the ear at the top of the stalk.
Emmer and einkorn are old kinds of wheat.
In einkorn, each spikelet usually holds one grain, in emmer usually two.
That is why emmer is also called two-grain.
In both kinds, the husks have to be removed before milling.

abschnitte.text: All cereals are **grasses**. The first farmers gathered the grains of wild grasses and sowed the best ones again and again. In this way, over many generations, plants arose with larger grains that did not fall off by themselves so easily. This selection is called **breeding**. It was an important step in the **New Stone Age**.

At the top of the stalk grows the **ear**. It consists of many small **spikelets**, in which the grains ripen. In **einkorn**, each spikelet usually holds only one grain, hence its name. In **emmer** there are usually two grains, which is why it is also called **two-grain**. Both belong to **wheat**.

To get the grains out of the ears, you have to **thresh**. In this you beat the ears, and the grains fall out. In emmer and einkorn, however, the grain sits fast in a hard covering, the **husk**. This has to be removed first before the grains can be ground to flour on a grindstone. That was a lot of work.

For a long time, the old kinds were hardly grown any more, because modern wheat gives a bigger yield. Today emmer and einkorn are being planted more again, in Switzerland too. **Bread** or **pasta** is made from them. The plants are regarded as robust and cope with poor soils too.

gewusst: Spelt too, which is popular in Switzerland, is a husked cereal.
In the pile-dwelling settlements of Switzerland, charred grains of emmer and einkorn were found.

teile.einleitung: Greek theatre arose in ancient Athens and is the origin of our theatre today. The performances took place in the open air, in large banks of seats on a hillside.
wichtigste: The great theatre festivals in Athens were held in honour of **Dionysus**.
**Tragedy** is the serious kind of play, comedy the funny one.
The rows of seats were called the **theatron**, “place for watching”.
The stage building was called the **skene**, which is where our word “scene” comes from.
**Only men** were allowed to appear as actors.
The theatre of **Epidaurus** is famous for its acoustics.
**Sophocles** wrote the tragedy “Oedipus the King”.

abschnitte.text: The great theatre festivals in Athens were held in honour of the god **Dionysus**, the god of wine and festivals. The theatre was therefore also a religious event. Many citizens came together and watched plays for several days. The most important theatre stood on the slope of the Acropolis and was dedicated to Dionysus.

Greek theatres were built on a hillside. The rising rows of seats were called the **theatron**, which means “place for watching”. Below lay a round space, the **orchestra**, where the chorus sang and danced. Behind it stood the stage building, the **skene**. Our word **“scene”** comes from this word.

There were two main kinds. **Tragedy** deals with serious subjects, and the main character often falls into misfortune. A famous example is **“Oedipus the King”** by **Sophocles**. In **comedy** people laughed at politicians, neighbours and everyday life. **Only men** were allowed to appear as actors, and they played the female roles too, wearing **masks**.

The theatre of **Epidaurus** in Greece was built in the 4th century BC. It is famous for its **excellent acoustics**. Even in the top rows you can still hear quiet words from the orchestra. The theatre is very well preserved and is still used for performances today.

The Romans took over the idea of the theatre from the Greeks. They built theatres in the area of present-day Switzerland too. In **Augusta Raurica** near Basel there is a large Roman theatre. Concerts and performances are held there again in summer today.

gewusst: The word “theatre” comes directly from the Greek “theatron”.
With different masks, one actor could play several roles in the same play.

teile.einleitung: Weaving means joining threads crosswise into a fabric. In the New Stone Age, people learned to spin and to weave, and the pile dwellers in Switzerland left behind surprisingly well-preserved fabrics.
wichtigste: Before weaving, clothes were made mainly from fur and leather.
Threads are first twisted from fibres, which is called spinning.
People spun with a spindle, a turning stick.
On the loom, weights of clay held the lengthwise threads taut.
The lengthwise threads are called the warp, the crosswise thread the weft.
From flax, linen is woven, and from lime bast, cords were plaited.

abschnitte.text: The hunters and gatherers of the Old Stone Age sewed their clothes mainly from **fur** and **leather**. With the **New Stone Age**, people settled down. They grew **flax** and used fibres from plants. Later the **sheep** with its dense fleece also supplied **wool**, which could be spun and woven.

Before you can weave, you need **threads**. For this, fibres are twisted into a long thread, which is called **spinning**. The simple tool for it is the **spindle**, a stick that turns. A small ring of clay, the **spindle whorl**, makes it heavier and helps it turn evenly.

On the **loom**, threads are joined crosswise. The lengthwise threads are called the **warp**, and the crosswise thread that goes to and fro is called the **weft**. On the **warp-weighted loom**, the warp threads hung straight down. Weights of **clay** or stone held them taut. Such loom weights are often found in excavations.

The pile dwellers also used **bast**. This is a tough layer under the bark of trees, especially the **lime tree**. From it, cords, mats and fabrics were plaited. The most important woven fabric, however, was **linen**, which is made from the fibres of flax.

Fabrics normally rot quickly. In the **pile-dwelling settlements** of Switzerland, however, many textiles were preserved. They lay in the **damp ground** on the lakeshores. There oxygen is lacking, and wood and fabrics decay much more slowly. So today we can still see how people wove thousands of years ago.

gewusst: Spindle whorls of clay are among the most common finds from the New Stone Age.
Ötzi too wore clothing of fur and leather and a cape of grass.

teile.einleitung: Aristotle was one of the most important philosophers of ancient Greece. He lived in the 4th century BC and researched almost all fields of knowledge of his time. His thinking shaped Europe for almost 2,000 years.
wichtigste: Aristotle was born in 384 BC in Stagira.
He is regarded as the founder of logic, the study of correct reasoning.
He developed the syllogism, a form of argument made of two premises and a conclusion.
For him, virtue was the right mean, for example courage between cowardice and recklessness.
He called man a “zoon politikon”, a being of the community.
He described hundreds of animal species and is regarded as the founder of zoology.
In his picture of the world, the Earth stood at the centre of the universe.

abschnitte.text: Aristotle was born in **384 BC** in **Stagira** in the north of Greece. At about 17 years old he went to Athens. There he studied for about 20 years at the Academy of the philosopher **Plato**. Later he was the teacher of the young **Alexander**, who became known as Alexander the Great. In Athens he founded his own school, the **Lyceum**. He died in 322 BC.

While teaching, Aristotle is said to have liked to **walk about** in a colonnade. His pupils were therefore called **Peripatetics**, “those who walk about”. The Greek word for the covered walk was peripatos. The school collected books and research results on many subjects. In this way a kind of early research institute arose.

Aristotle is regarded as the founder of **logic**. That is the study of how to reason correctly. He developed the **syllogism**: from two statements, the premises, a third follows. An example: all humans are mortal. Socrates is a human. So Socrates is mortal. This way of thinking was still taught in schools many centuries later.

For Aristotle, a **virtue** often lay in the **right mean** between two faults. **Courage**, for example, lies between **cowardice** and **recklessness**. In his work **“Politics”**, he described man as a **“zoon politikon”**. This means a being that lives in community with others. He also compared different forms of state with one another.

Aristotle observed and described **hundreds of animal species** and arranged them in groups. That is why he is regarded as the founder of **zoology**, the study of animals. In Aristotle's picture of the world, the **Earth** stood at the **centre** of the universe. Besides earth, water, air and fire, he assumed a fifth element: the **aether**, of which the heavens were supposed to consist. This picture of the world held until modern times.

gewusst: In the Middle Ages, Aristotle was often called simply “the Philosopher”, and everyone knew who was meant.
The word “quintessence” means “the fifth being” and recalls the fifth element, the aether.

teile.einleitung: The Old Kingdom is an early period of ancient Egypt, from about 2700 to 2200 BC. In this time the first great pyramids arose. That is why it is also called the Age of the Pyramids.
wichtigste: The capital of Egypt in the Old Kingdom was Memphis.
Imhotep is regarded as the architect of the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara.
King Sneferu had the Bent Pyramid built at Dahshur.
The Great Pyramid at Giza arose under the 4th Dynasty.
The 5th Dynasty built sun temples for the god Ra.
The oldest Pyramid Texts stand in the pyramid of Unas.
The Old Kingdom was followed by the First Intermediate Period.

abschnitte.text: In the Old Kingdom, Egypt was a united country with a strong king, the **pharaoh**. He was regarded as a god on earth. The capital was **Memphis**, near present-day Cairo. Many **officials** administered the land, collected dues and organised great building projects. History is divided into **dynasties**, that is, ruling families.

In the 3rd Dynasty, King **Djoser** had a **step pyramid** built at **Saqqara**. It is regarded as the oldest great stone building in the world. The architect is thought to be **Imhotep**, a high official. He was later even worshipped as a god of wisdom and healing. Before that, tombs had mostly been built as flat structures, so-called **mastabas**.

King **Sneferu** tried out new shapes. At **Dahshur** he had the **Bent Pyramid** built, whose sides change their slope in the middle. After that came the Red Pyramid, a true pyramid with smooth sides. His son **Khufu** (Cheops) built the huge pyramid of **Giza** in the **4th Dynasty**. Later the pyramids of Khafre and Menkaure followed there, as well as the Great Sphinx.

The kings of the **5th Dynasty** worshipped the sun god **Ra** in particular. They built him their own **sun temples**. Their pyramids were smaller than those of Giza. In the pyramid of King **Unas** stand the oldest known **Pyramid Texts**. These are spells in hieroglyphs that were meant to help the king in the afterlife.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Old Kingdom
abschnitte.text: In the 6th Dynasty, the princes in the provinces became ever more powerful. The power of the king declined. Around 2200 BC the empire fell apart into several parts. This unsettled time is called the **First Intermediate Period**. Only in the Middle Kingdom was Egypt united again.

gewusst: At about 146 metres high, the Great Pyramid was the tallest structure in the world for over 3,800 years.
It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still stands today.

teile.einleitung: **Svante Pääbo** is a Swedish researcher. He studies the genetic material of people who lived long ago, for example the Neanderthals. In 2022 he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this.
wichtigste: Svante Pääbo comes from Sweden.
In 2022 he received the Nobel Prize for his discoveries concerning the genomes of extinct forms of humans.
He is regarded as a co-founder of palaeogenetics.
In 1985 he detected ancient human DNA in an Egyptian mummy.
In 1997 his team sequenced mitochondrial DNA of a Neanderthal.
In 2010 it published the first draft of the Neanderthal genome.
His father Sune Bergström also received a Nobel Prize.

abschnitte.text: **Palaeogenetics** studies **ancient DNA** from bones, teeth or mummies. Svante Pääbo is regarded as one of its most important co-founders. **DNA** is the genetic material in which the blueprints of a living thing are stored. After death it slowly breaks down into small pieces. Pääbo developed methods to read these fragments all the same.

abschnitte.titel: From the mummy to the Neanderthal
abschnitte.text: In a paper published in **1985**, Pääbo detected DNA in an **Egyptian mummy**. In **1997**, his team succeeded in sequencing **mitochondrial DNA** of a Neanderthal. In the same year he became founding director of a department at the **Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology** in Leipzig. In **2010**, his team published the first draft of the whole **Neanderthal genome**.

A great difficulty is **contamination** by modern human DNA. Even a flake of skin from a researcher can spoil a sample. Pääbo therefore introduced very **strict laboratory methods**: clean rooms, protective clothing and many checks. Only in this way can you be sure that you are really measuring the ancient DNA.

abschnitte.titel: A Nobel Prize in the family
abschnitte.text: In **2022**, Pääbo received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine**. It honoured his discoveries concerning the genomes of extinct forms of humans and the evolution of humankind. His father, **Sune Bergström**, had also received this prize, in 1982. Among other things, Pääbo's research showed that many people today carry a little Neanderthal genetic material in them.

gewusst: With ancient DNA from a small finger bone from a cave in Siberia, Pääbo's team discovered a previously unknown form of human, the Denisovans.
In many people outside Africa, a small part of the genetic material comes from Neanderthals.

teile.einleitung: The Gracchan reforms were laws passed by the brothers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus in the 2nd century BC. They were meant to provide poor Roman citizens with land and bread, and they set off fierce power struggles.
wichtigste: The core of the land law was to **distribute state land to landless citizens**.
An individual was allowed to use at most **500** iugera of state land as a basic amount.
**A commission of three men** was to distribute the land.
Tiberius had his fellow official Octavius **removed from office by the people's assembly**.
**Scipio Nasica** led the senators who beat Tiberius to death in 133 BC.
Gaius provided **cheaper grain for citizens in Rome**.
In 121 BC the **Senatus consultum ultimum** was applied for the first time.

abschnitte.text: Rome owned a lot of **state land** that it had conquered in wars. Rich families used large parts of it and had it farmed by slaves. Many small farmers, on the other hand, lost their farms and moved to Rome in poverty. Because only citizens with property became soldiers, the army also lacked men. This is where the reforms began.

In 133 BC the tribune **Tiberius Gracchus** proposed a land law. Its core was to **distribute state land to landless citizens**. An individual was allowed to keep at most **500 iugera** as a basic amount, which is about 125 hectares. What lay above that was to be distributed. For this, **a commission of three men** was set up.

The tribune **Marcus Octavius** vetoed the law. Tiberius **had him removed from office by the people's assembly**. This broke with old rules and outraged many senators. When Tiberius stood for election again, violence broke out. Senators led by **Scipio Nasica** beat him to death along with many followers. The land commission, however, carried on working.

From 123 BC **Gaius Gracchus** was tribune of the people. His **grain law** brought **cheaper grain for citizens in Rome**. He had roads built, planned new colonies and strengthened the equestrians in the courts. He also proposed giving the allies in Italy more rights. Many of these plans met strong resistance in the Senate.

In 121 BC the Senate passed an emergency decree, the **Senatus consultum ultimum**. With it the consuls were to do everything to protect the state. It was applied for the first time then, against Gaius and his followers. Gaius and many followers were killed in the process. The reforms showed that political disputes in Rome were more and more often decided by violence.

gewusst: An iugerum was roughly the area that a team of oxen could plough in one day.
The commission of three men at first consisted of Tiberius, his brother Gaius and Gaius's father-in-law Appius Claudius.

teile.einleitung: The marathon is a long-distance race over 42.195 kilometres. Its name recalls the Greek place Marathon and a famous legend from antiquity.
wichtigste: A marathon is exactly 42.195 kilometres long.
The name comes from the place Marathon north-east of Athens.
There in 490 BC a famous battle took place.
According to the legend a messenger ran to Athens to report the victory.
The runner of the legend is usually called Pheidippides.
A half marathon is about 21.1 kilometres long.

abschnitte.text: **Marathon** is a place in **Greece**, north-east of **Athens**. In **490 BC** the Athenians fought there against an army of **Persians**. The Athenians won the battle. That is about 2,500 years ago. The distance from Marathon to Athens is about **40 kilometres**.

According to the legend a messenger ran from Marathon to Athens to announce the **victory**. After that he is said to have collapsed exhausted. The runner is usually called **Pheidippides**. Whether he really ran this distance is not certain. For the historian **Herodotus** tells of a different run: Pheidippides is said to have run to **Sparta** before the battle to fetch help.

At the first modern **Olympic Games** in 1896 in Athens there was a marathon for the first time. It recalled the old legend. Since **1921** the distance has been exactly **42.195 kilometres**. Today there are marathons in many cities of the world with thousands of participants. In Switzerland too there are several, for example a race up into the Jungfrau region.

A **half marathon** is half as long as a marathon, that is, about **21.1 kilometres**. It is very popular with many runners. Any race that is even longer than a marathon is called an **ultramarathon**. Some ultramarathons cover over 100 kilometres. For such distances one needs a lot of training and endurance.

gewusst: The first Olympic marathon in 1896 was won by a Greek, Spyridon Louis.
The present-day length of 42.195 kilometres was first run at the 1908 Olympic Games in London.

teile.einleitung: Ashoka was an emperor of the Maurya Empire in India in the 3rd century BC. After a bloody war he turned away from violence. He promoted Buddhism and proclaimed his teachings in inscriptions throughout the empire.
wichtigste: Ashoka ruled the Maurya Empire in India in the 3rd century BC.
After the Kalinga War he rejected violence.
He called his principles Dhamma and had them carved into rocks and pillars.
A wheel with 24 spokes, which goes back to him, stands in the middle of the Indian flag.
He sent his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka to spread Buddhism.
James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837 and made the edicts readable.

abschnitte.text: Ashoka was a grandson of Chandragupta, the founder of the **Maurya Empire**. He ruled from about 268 to 232 BC. His empire covered almost the whole of India. The capital was **Pataliputra**, present-day Patna. In his inscriptions he mostly called himself **Devanampiya Piyadasi**. That means roughly “Beloved of the Gods, the one of kindly gaze”.

Ashoka conquered the region of **Kalinga** on the east coast of India. This **Kalinga War** claimed very many victims. Ashoka later regretted the suffering he had caused. He turned to **Buddhism** and rejected violence. He now wanted to rule with kindness and justice.

Ashoka had his rules and teachings **carved into rocks and pillars**. These inscriptions are called **edicts**. He demanded respect for all living beings, honesty and tolerance towards other religions. He called these principles **Dhamma**. Most of the edicts are written in the **Brahmi script**. At **Kandahar** in present-day Afghanistan, an inscription in **Greek and Aramaic** was found in 1958.

According to the tradition of the Theravada Buddhists, the **third Buddhist council** took place at Pataliputra under Ashoka. A council is a great assembly of monks. Ashoka sent envoys to many countries. He sent his son **Mahinda** to **Sri Lanka**. There Buddhism is still the most important religion today.

For a long time, nobody could read the old inscriptions. Only in **1837** did the Briton **James Prinsep** decipher the Brahmi script. In this way Ashoka became known again. Today the **lion capital** of one of his pillars is the state emblem of India. The **wheel with 24 spokes**, the Ashoka Chakra, stands in the middle of the **Indian flag**.

gewusst: Ashoka had trees planted and wells dug along roads so that travellers found shade and water.
His edicts are among the oldest readable written records of India.

teile.einleitung: Hadrian's Wall is a long Roman border wall in the north of England. Emperor Hadrian had it built from AD 122 across the country, from coast to coast.
wichtigste: Hadrian's Wall is a wall about 117 kilometres long.
It stands in the north of present-day England.
Building began in AD 122 on the orders of Emperor Hadrian.
It protected and controlled the northern border of the Roman Empire.
Roman soldiers guarded it from forts, milecastles and turrets.
Later the Romans built the Antonine Wall further north.

abschnitte.text: Hadrian's Wall runs from the **west coast** to the **east coast** of Britain, roughly from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth. It is about **117 kilometres** long, which is about 80 Roman miles. A large part was built of stone, and in the west at first also of turf blocks. In front of the wall lay a ditch, and behind it ran another ditch with banks, the **vallum**.

Emperor Hadrian visited Britain in **122** and ordered the building. The wall was meant to secure the **border** of the Roman Empire. In the north lived tribes that the Romans never conquered permanently, such as the **Caledonians** in present-day Scotland. But the wall was not only a barrier. The Romans also controlled here who went in or out with goods, and could charge customs duties.

About every Roman mile stood a small guard post, a **milecastle**. A small group of soldiers lived in it, and a gate allowed controlled passage to the north. Between two milecastles stood two **watchtowers** each. In addition there were larger **forts** for hundreds of soldiers. Quite close by lies the camp of Vindolanda, where many wooden writing tablets were found.

Under Emperor **Antoninus Pius**, Hadrian's successor, the Romans advanced further north. From about 142 they built the **Antonine Wall** in Scotland, a rampart of earth and turf. It was shorter, but was given up again after about 20 years. After that Hadrian's Wall once more became the most important border. The Romans held it until about the year 400.

Many stones of the wall were later used for houses, churches and roads. Even so, long stretches survive to this day. Since 1987 Hadrian's Wall has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, today together with the Antonine Wall and the Limes in Germany as “Frontiers of the Roman Empire”. A walking path runs along the whole wall; on foot it takes several days.

gewusst: At Vindolanda a birthday invitation was found that one woman wrote to a friend. It is regarded as one of the oldest known texts in Latin written by a woman's own hand.
The wall does not lie on today's border with Scotland, but entirely within England.

teile.einleitung: Heinrich Schliemann was a German merchant and excavator in the 19th century. He firmly believed in the myths of Homer and searched for the city of Troy.
wichtigste: Schliemann was born in 1822 in Mecklenburg in Germany.
He became very rich as a merchant.
He paid for excavations with his money.
He dug for Troy on the hill of Hisarlik in present-day Turkey.
In 1873 he found a hoard of gold that he called “Priam's Treasure”.
At Mycenae he found the so-called “Mask of Agamemnon”.

abschnitte.text: Heinrich Schliemann was born in **1822** in **Mecklenburg**. His family had little money. He worked as a merchant and became very rich through **trading**, among other places in Russia. He learned many **languages**, including ancient Greek. With his fortune he could later devote himself entirely to the search for ancient cities.

Schliemann loved the works of **Homer**, especially the **Iliad** about the Trojan War. He was convinced that Troy had really existed. From 1871 he dug on the hill of **Hisarlik** in present-day **Turkey**. There he found the remains of several cities that had been built one on top of the other. Today Hisarlik is regarded as the site of Troy.

In **1873** Schliemann found a large **hoard of gold** with jewellery and vessels. He called it “**Priam's Treasure**”, after the king of Troy in the myth. Later it turned out that the treasure is much **older** than the time in which the Trojan War is supposed to have taken place. Schliemann took the treasure out of the country. After the Second World War it went to Moscow, where it is today.

At **Mycenae** in Greece Schliemann dug up **royal graves**. There he found several masks of gold. One of them he called the “**Mask of Agamemnon**”, after the legendary king of Mycenae. This mask too is older than the time in which Agamemnon is supposed to have lived. It is now in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

Schliemann made **archaeology** known to many people. He showed that real places can lie behind old myths. But his methods are **criticised** today. He dug very fast and deep and in doing so destroyed layers that would have revealed a great deal. Schliemann died in **1890** in Naples.

gewusst: Schliemann claimed that as a child he had already decided to find Troy. Many researchers think this is a nice story that he invented later.
At Troy, nine major layers of settlement from different periods are distinguished.

teile.einleitung: The Diadochi were the generals of Alexander the Great who fought over his empire after his death in 323 BC. The Greek word means “successors”. Their struggles gave rise to several large kingdoms.
wichtigste: Alexander the Great died in 323 BC without leaving an adult heir.
His generals, the **Diadochi**, fought for power for decades.
**Ptolemy I** founded a dynasty that ruled Egypt until 30 BC.
The **Seleucid Empire** at times covered most of the former Persian Empire.
Antigonus Monophthalmus fell in 301 BC at the battle of **Ipsus**.
The **Antigonids** ruled Macedonia from about 276 BC.

abschnitte.titel: A quarrel over a world empire
abschnitte.text: Alexander the Great had conquered an empire stretching from Greece to India. When he died in 323 BC, there was no adult successor. His generals first divided the territories among themselves, but soon fell out. In the **Wars of the Diadochi** they fought each other for many years. In the end the empire had broken up into several kingdoms.

The general **Ptolemy I** secured Egypt for himself. He founded the dynasty of the **Ptolemies**, which ruled there until 30 BC. The last queen of this family was the famous **Cleopatra VII**. Under the Ptolemies the capital **Alexandria** became a centre of science, with a great library.

**Seleucus I** won the largest territory. His **Seleucid Empire** at times covered most of the former Persian Empire. Around 300 BC he founded the city of **Antioch** on the River **Orontes**, which later became the capital. In 281 BC Seleucus defeated his rival **Lysimachus** at the battle of **Corupedium**, and Lysimachus fell in it.

The powerful **Antigonus Monophthalmus** wanted to win back the whole empire. But his opponents joined forces, and he fell in 301 BC at the battle of **Ipsus**. His descendants, the **Antigonids**, ruled **Macedonia** permanently from about 276 BC. In Asia Minor the **Attalid** family made the city of **Pergamon** into an important kingdom.

The time after Alexander is called the **Hellenistic age**. In the kingdoms of the Diadochi, the Greek language and culture spread far to the east. New cities arose, and trade and science flourished. Little by little, however, the kingdoms were conquered by the **Romans**. With Egypt in 30 BC, the last of them fell.

gewusst: The nickname “Monophthalmus” means “the one-eyed”.
The word “Diadochi” comes from the Greek word for “successors”.

teile.einleitung: A felucca is a traditional wooden sailing boat. The feluccas on the Nile in Egypt are especially well known, and they are still sailing there today.
wichtigste: A felucca is **a wooden sailing boat**.
Its sail is **triangular**.
Many feluccas can be seen today **on the Nile**, for example in Aswan.
In Egypt the wind mostly blows **from the north**.
Even in ancient Egypt, people used the wind and the current of the Nile for sailing boats.

abschnitte.titel: A boat with a triangular sail
abschnitte.text: The **felucca** is a small **wooden sailing boat**. It has a mast with a large, **triangular** sail that hangs from a long slanting pole. Such sails are called **lateen sails**. Feluccas have no engine and need only the wind. They are found on the Nile, but also on the coasts of the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

The Nile flows from south to north into the Mediterranean. In Egypt, however, the wind mostly blows **from the north**. That is handy: going south you sail with the wind against the current. Going north you simply let the current carry you. The ancient Egyptians already used this advantage with their sailing boats.

Today many feluccas can be seen **on the Nile**, especially in **Aswan** and Luxor. In the past they mainly carried goods and people. Today many tourists sail on them to enjoy the river at sunset. So the felucca has become a symbol of the Nile landscape.

gewusst: In the writing of the ancient Egyptians, the sign for “travelling south” showed a boat with a sail.

teile.einleitung: Augusta Raurica was a Roman city on the Rhine, very close to Basel. Its ruins lie in the present-day municipalities of Augst and Kaiseraugst and are among the most important Roman sites in Switzerland. Anyone who walks through the theatre or the temple remains here can easily imagine life almost 2,000 years ago.
wichtigste: Augusta Raurica lies about ten kilometres east of Basel.
The ruins are in Augst in the canton of Basel-Landschaft and Kaiseraugst in the canton of Aargau.
Around 44 BC Lucius Munatius Plancus founded the Roman colony.
The city is named after the Celtic people called the Rauraci.
At its peak about 10,000 to 20,000 people lived here.
The Roman theatre is still used for performances today.
In 1961 and 1962 a great silver treasure was discovered.

abschnitte.text: Augusta Raurica lies on the south bank of the **Rhine**, about ten kilometres east of Basel. Important routes crossed here, and the Rhine served as a waterway for goods. The name joins the emperor **Augustus** with the Celtic people of the **Rauraci**, who lived in this area. Today the ruins lie in the municipalities of Augst and Kaiseraugst.

Around 44 BC the Roman general **Lucius Munatius Plancus** founded a colony here. His tomb inscription still survives in Gaeta in Italy. The city was only properly built up a few decades later, under Emperor Augustus. In the 2nd century AD it enjoyed its **golden age** with about 10,000 to 20,000 inhabitants. There was a forum with temples, baths, workshops, houses and a water pipe.

The most important building is the Roman **theatre**, one of the best preserved north of the Alps. It had room for about 10,000 spectators. After a long **restoration** it is used again today for concerts and plays. There was also an amphitheatre on the edge of the city, where animal hunts and fights took place.

In 1961 and 1962, while a gym was being built in Kaiseraugst, a great **silver treasure** was found. It consists of about 270 pieces, including splendid plates, bowls, spoons and coins. It was probably buried around 350 AD in a troubled time and never collected. The treasure is among the most important finds from late Roman times and can be seen in the **Roman Museum** in Augst.

In the 3rd century AD the city was weakened by unrest and attacks from Germanic groups. Around 300 AD the Romans built a **fortress** right on the Rhine, the Castrum Rauracense in Kaiseraugst. It was meant to protect the empire's **border** on the Rhine. People continued to live inside its walls, and later there was even a bishop here.

Augusta Raurica is now a large **open-air museum**. You can visit a rebuilt Roman house, walk through an underground sewer and look at temple remains. In the animal park live old breeds of farm animals, like those the Romans knew. Every summer the **Roman Festival** takes place, where performers show Roman life.

begriffe.erklaerung: A settlement newly founded by Romans, with Roman citizens.
A Celtic people who lived in the area around Basel.
A fortified Roman camp or fortress.
A museum outdoors where you can visit buildings and ruins.

gewusst: The silver treasure of Kaiseraugst was not recognised at first, because the pieces were mistaken for old scrap metal during building work.
Only a small part of the ancient city has been excavated so far; much of it still lies under fields and houses.
The excavations at Augusta Raurica are among the oldest archaeological research in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Maurya Empire was the first great empire to cover almost the whole of India. It was founded around 320 BC by Chandragupta Maurya and lasted until about 185 BC.
wichtigste: Chandragupta Maurya founded the empire around 320 BC.
The capital was Pataliputra, present-day Patna on the Ganges.
The adviser Kautilya is said to have written the textbook “Arthashastra”.
The Greek Megasthenes described the court of the Mauryas.
The best-known ruler was Ashoka, a grandson of Chandragupta.
The lion capital from this period is today the national emblem of India.

abschnitte.text: Around **320 BC** **Chandragupta Maurya** overthrew the **Nanda dynasty**. He created the first great empire to cover almost the whole of India. The capital was **Pataliputra** on the **Ganges**, on the site of present-day **Patna**. It was then one of the largest cities in the world. According to the tradition of the **Jains**, Chandragupta abdicated at the end of his life and lived as an ascetic following the rules of **Jainism**.

An important adviser of Chandragupta was **Kautilya**, also called **Chanakya**. He is regarded as the author of the **Arthashastra**. This textbook on statecraft describes how a king should manage his realm, his finances and his spies. It is one of the most important sources on thinking in ancient India.

In the west ruled **Seleucus I**, a successor of Alexander the Great. After a war he gave up around **303 BC** territories in present-day Afghanistan and Pakistan. In return he received **500 war elephants**. His envoy **Megasthenes** lived at the court of Chandragupta and wrote the work **“Indica”**. It survives only in quotations by later authors.

After Chandragupta his son **Bindusara** ruled from about 297 to 273 BC. He extended the empire to the south. After him his son **Ashoka** prevailed over his brothers. Ashoka promoted **Buddhism** and had inscriptions put up on rocks and pillars. One of these pillars bore the famous **lion capital** with four lions sitting back to back. India chose it in **1950** as its **national emblem**.

After Ashoka the empire grew weaker. Around **185 BC** the last king, **Brihadratha**, was overthrown and killed at a military review by his general **Pushyamitra Shunga**. Pushyamitra then founded the **Shunga dynasty**. With that the rule of the Mauryas ended.

gewusst: The wheel from the lion capital, the Ashoka Chakra, can be seen today in the middle of the Indian flag.
Pataliputra was surrounded by a long wooden palisade, as Megasthenes reported.

teile.einleitung: Darius I was one of the most important kings of the ancient Persian Empire. He ruled from 522 to 486 BC and reorganised his huge empire with provinces, roads and a uniform currency.
wichtigste: Darius I ruled the Persian Empire from 522 to 486 BC.
He came to power after overthrowing the supposed usurper Gaumata together with six conspirators.
He divided the empire into provinces called **satrapies**.
He introduced the gold coin called the **daric**.
His trilingual **Behistun Inscription** helped to decipher cuneiform.
In 490 BC a Persian army was defeated by the Athenians at **Marathon**.

abschnitte.text: Darius came from the family of the **Achaemenids**. After the death of King Cambyses, Darius claimed that a magus named **Gaumata** had pretended to be Cambyses' brother and seized the throne. Together with six conspirators, Darius killed him in 522 BC and became king himself. Afterwards he had to put down several uprisings throughout the empire. Later he had his own version of events carved into a rock.

The Persian Empire stretched from Egypt to India. Darius divided it into provinces called **satrapies**. Each was run by a governor, the **satrap**, and had to pay taxes regularly. The Greek historian **Herodotus** lists twenty such tax districts. So that the satraps did not become too powerful, inspectors travelled through the empire, whom people called the **eyes and ears of the king**.

Darius introduced the gold coin called the **daric**, which was made of almost pure gold and showed a king with a bow. A long **Royal Road** linked the city of Susa with Sardis in Asia Minor, so messengers could travel quickly. In Egypt Darius had a **canal from the Nile to the Red Sea** completed. He also began building the splendid royal city of **Persepolis**.

At **Behistun** in present-day Iran, Darius had a huge inscription carved into a rock face. It tells of his rise to power in three languages: **Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian**. Because the same story could be compared in three languages, researchers in the 19th century managed to decipher **cuneiform**. The inscription is therefore very valuable for the study of history.

Around 500 BC Greek cities in Asia Minor rose up against the Persians. The Persians put down this **Ionian Revolt** and in 494 BC destroyed the city of **Miletus**. Because Athens had supported the rebels, Darius sent an army to Greece. In 490 BC the Athenians defeated this army on the plain of **Marathon**. Darius died in 486 BC, and his son **Xerxes** succeeded him.

gewusst: The marathon race takes its name from the battle of Marathon.
In the 19th century the Englishman Henry Rawlinson climbed up the rock face at Behistun to copy the inscription.

teile.einleitung: Many towns in Switzerland already had a name in Roman times. From these Latin or Celtic names the present-day place names arose over the centuries.
wichtigste: Vitudurum became Winterthur, Salodurum became Solothurn.
Curia became Chur, Basilia became Basel.
Octodurus is present-day Martigny in the Valais.
Aquae Helveticae is Baden, Arbor Felix is Arbon.
Noviodunum became Nyon, Eburodunum became Yverdon-les-Bains.
Tenedo is the present-day place Bad Zurzach.

abschnitte.text: About 2,000 years ago the area of present-day Switzerland belonged to the **Roman Empire**. **Celts**, for example the Helvetii, had lived here before. So many places had **Celtic** names that were taken over by the Romans and written in Latin. Other names are truly **Latin**. Over time the pronunciation changed, and so the present-day names arose.

Many names end in **-durum** or **-dunum**. These are Celtic word parts. **Vitudurum** lay in the district of **Oberwinterthur** and became **Winterthur**. **Salodurum** on the Aare became **Solothurn**. **Noviodunum** on Lake Geneva became **Nyon**, where the Romans founded a colony. **Eburodunum** at the southern end of Lake Neuchâtel is today called **Yverdon-les-Bains**.

Some names describe the place. **Aquae Helveticae** means “waters of the Helvetii”. This refers to the warm springs of **Baden**, in which the Romans already bathed. **Arbor Felix** on Lake Constance means “lucky tree”. From it came **Arbon**.

**Curia** was a Roman place in Raetia, and today **Chur** is the capital of Graubünden. **Basilia** lay on the Rhine on the **Münsterhügel**, and from it came **Basel**. **Octodurus** in the Valais lay on the way to the Great St Bernard. Today it is called **Martigny**, and a Roman **amphitheatre** still stands there. **Tenedo** on the Rhine had an important river crossing and is today called **Bad Zurzach**.

gewusst: Zurich also has a Roman name: the settlement was called Turicum.
Avenches was called Aventicum by the Romans and was the main town of the Helvetii.

teile.einleitung: Icarus is a figure from Greek legend. With wings of feathers and wax he escaped from the island of Crete with his father Daedalus. Because he flew too close to the sun, he fell into the sea.
wichtigste: Icarus was the son of the clever inventor Daedalus.
King Minos held the two of them on Crete.
Daedalus built wings of feathers and wax.
He warned Icarus: do not fly too high and not too low.
Icarus flew too close to the sun and the wax melted.
He fell into the sea, which is now called the Icarian Sea.

abschnitte.text: **Daedalus** was a very skilful inventor and builder from Athens. He worked for King **Minos** on the island of **Crete**. According to the legend, he built the **Labyrinth** there, in which the monster the Minotaur lived. Later Minos held Daedalus and his son **Icarus** on the island. Because the king had all the ships guarded, they could not escape across the sea.

Daedalus had an idea: if they could not escape over the water, then they would go through the **air**. He gathered **bird feathers** and stuck them together with **wax** into large wings. One pair for himself and one for Icarus. Then the two practised flying. Soon they could rise into the air like birds.

Before the flight Daedalus warned his son: “**Not too high and not too low!**” Too high up, the **sun** was too hot and could melt the wax. Too low down, the **spray** of the sea would make the feathers wet and heavy. Then one could no longer fly. So Icarus was always to stay in the middle and follow his father.

At first all went well. But Icarus enjoyed flying so much that he climbed **higher** and higher. He came too close to the sun. The heat made the **wax melt**, and the feathers came loose. Icarus fell into the **sea**. Daedalus flew on sadly and, according to the legend, reached the island of Sicily.

A part of the sea in Greece is named after him, the **Icarian Sea**. The island of **Ikaria** also bears his name. The story is often told as a warning: anyone who is overconfident and ignores advice can fail. The Roman poet **Ovid** made the legend especially well known. Many painters, poets and musicians took it up later.

gewusst: The dream of flying like Icarus accompanied people for over 2,000 years, until the first aeroplanes were built.
A famous painting shows a peaceful landscape in which all that can be seen of the falling Icarus is his legs in the water.

teile.einleitung: The Roman Forum was the great square in the centre of ancient Rome. Here the Romans met to shop, pray, celebrate and make speeches, and here politics was made.
wichtigste: The Roman Forum was **the great square in Rome**.
It lies between the **Capitoline and Palatine** hills.
People went there to **shop and make speeches**.
Many **temples** stood on the Forum.
The Senate met in the **Curia**.
The famous road **Via Sacra** led across the Forum.
Today the Forum is **a field of ruins**.

abschnitte.text: The **Roman Forum** lies in a hollow between the **Capitoline and Palatine** hills. In early times this valley was marshy. The Romans drained it with a large sewer, the **Cloaca Maxima**. After that the square became the centre of the city. Over the centuries the Romans kept building new buildings here.

On the Forum people went to **shop and make speeches**. From a speakers' platform, the **Rostra**, politicians spoke to the people. The Senate met in the **Curia**. In large halls, the **basilicas**, court cases were held and business was done. Anyone who wanted to achieve something in Rome had to be seen on the Forum.

On the Forum stood many **temples** for the Roman gods. In the round **Temple of Vesta**, priestesses called **Vestal Virgins** kept **a sacred fire**. It was never allowed to go out, because it stood for the welfare of the city. A very old spot is the **Lapis Niger**, a pavement of black marble. Beneath it one of the oldest Latin inscriptions was found.

The **Via Sacra**, the “sacred road”, led across the Forum. On it victorious generals marched in a solemn **triumphal procession** to the Capitol. A **triumphal arch** is **a large gateway built to celebrate** a victory. On the Forum the arch of Emperor **Titus** and the arch of **Septimius Severus** still stand.

After the end of the Roman Empire the buildings fell into ruin. Stones were used for new houses, and the square was covered with earth. Only since the 19th century has the Forum been excavated more thoroughly. Today it is **a field of ruins** that very many people visit every year. Roman cities in Switzerland, such as **Augusta Raurica**, also had a forum of their own.

gewusst: The word “forum” originally means “square” or “market”.
The Rostra platform was named after ships' beaks, which were fixed there as signs of victory.

teile.einleitung: The Lighthouse of Alexandria stood on the island of Pharos in front of the harbour of the Egyptian city of Alexandria. It was over 100 metres high and is one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
wichtigste: The lighthouse stood on the small island of Pharos.
Alexandria was founded in 331 BC by Alexander the Great.
A fire at the top of the tower showed ships the way.
The tower was probably over 100 metres high.
Several earthquakes destroyed it in the Middle Ages.
Its stones were later used to build a fortress.

abschnitte.text: **Alexandria** is a large port city in **Egypt** on the Mediterranean. It was founded in **331 BC** by **Alexander the Great**, after whom it is named. After his death the **Ptolemies** ruled there. Alexandria became one of the most important cities of antiquity, known for trade and learning.

The coast in front of Alexandria is flat and dangerous for ships. So a huge tower was built on the island of **Pharos**. At the top a **fire** burned that could be seen far out over the sea. In this way ships also found their way safely into the harbour at night. The tower was probably **over 100 metres** high and was among the tallest buildings of its time.

The tower was so famous that its name became a word. In French a lighthouse is called **“phare”**, in Italian **“faro”**. Both words come from **Pharos**. That is why the Lighthouse of Alexandria is often simply called “the Pharos”.

In the **Middle Ages** several **earthquakes** badly damaged the tower. In the end only ruins remained. A sultan had the **Citadel of Qaitbay** built on the same spot. For this, stones of the old tower were also used. The fortress still stands today at the harbour of Alexandria.

gewusst: Divers have found huge blocks of stone and statues in the harbour of Alexandria that probably belonged to the lighthouse.
The lighthouse stood for well over 1,000 years, much longer than most of the other wonders.

teile.einleitung: The Marian reforms were a series of changes in the army of the Roman Republic around 107 BC. They made the army more effective, but also greatly changed the politics of Rome.
wichtigste: Gaius Marius was consul seven times in all.
From 107 BC he also took propertyless citizens into the army in large numbers.
The soldiers received their equipment from the state.
They carried their own baggage and were therefore called “Marius's mules”.
The eagle became the standard of every legion.
Afterwards the soldiers felt loyal above all to their general.

abschnitte.text: **Gaius Marius** came from Arpinum and was a so-called **homo novus**, a “new man”: before him no one in his family had been consul. He was **consul seven times** in all, and from 104 to 100 BC even every year. This went against the usual rules of the **Republic**. From 107 BC he fought a war against the Numidian king **Jugurtha** in North Africa and ended it successfully.

In the past only citizens with **landed property** were allowed to serve in the legion. They had to pay for their weapons themselves. But there were fewer and fewer such farmers. So in 107 BC Marius also recruited **propertyless citizens**, in Latin **capite censi**. They received their **equipment from the state**. In this way an army of professional soldiers who served for a long time gradually came into being.

Marius had the soldiers **carry** their weapons, tools and provisions **themselves**. The long baggage train with wagons became smaller, and the army became more mobile. So the legionaries were mockingly called “**Marius's mules**”. According to Pliny the Elder, in 104 BC Marius made the **eagle**, in Latin **aquila**, the only standard of every legion. To lose it in battle was seen as the greatest disgrace.

The peoples of the **Cimbri** and **Teutones** were then moving through Europe and inflicted heavy defeats on Rome. At times the Celtic tribe of the **Tigurini** from the area of present-day Switzerland also moved with them. With the new army Marius defeated the Teutones in 102 BC at **Aix-en-Provence** in southern France. In 101 BC he defeated the Cimbri at **Vercellae** in northern Italy.

The soldiers without property expected **booty** and **land** from their general for the time after their service. So they often felt more loyal to him than to the state. This is called **military clientelism**. Powerful generals could in this way also use their armies in politics, as Sulla and Caesar later did. Many historians see in this one reason for the **civil wars** that finally ended the Republic.

gewusst: Many researchers now think that not all the innovations came from Marius at once, but developed over a longer time.
Marius was married to an aunt of Julius Caesar.

teile.einleitung: Lousonna was a Roman settlement on the shore of Lake Geneva. From it the city of Lausanne later developed.
wichtigste: Lousonna is the Roman name of Lausanne.
The settlement lay directly on Lake Geneva and had a harbour.
The ruins lie in the present-day district of Vidy.
In Vidy the International Olympic Committee now has its seat.
Goods were often transported across the lake by ship.

abschnitte.titel: A Roman settlement on the lake
abschnitte.text: **Lousonna** was a settlement from the **Roman period** on the shore of **Lake Geneva**. From it the city of **Lausanne** later developed. The ruins lie in the present-day district of **Vidy**. Excavators found there remains of houses, streets, a marketplace and temples. In the **Roman Museum** of Vidy many finds can be seen.

Lousonna had a **harbour** on the lake. On water heavy goods made good progress, much more easily than on the roads. An **inscription** of **boatmen** shows that there was lively shipping on the lake. The settlement lay on an important route between the Rhône valley and the Swiss Plateau. So it was a good place for traders and craftsmen.

Where Lousonna lay, the headquarters of the **International Olympic Committee** now stands. Beneath and beside it still lie remains of the Roman settlement. Because of the Committee Lausanne also calls itself the **“Olympic Capital”**. So in Vidy antiquity and the present meet.

gewusst: The ruins of Lousonna lie partly in a park on the lake, where one can stroll about freely.
The name Lousonna is probably of Celtic origin.

teile.einleitung: The Edict of Milan of 313 AD was an agreement between the Roman emperors Constantine and Licinius. It granted all people in the empire, including Christians, the free practice of their religion.
wichtigste: The agreement was made at the beginning of 313 AD in Milan.
The emperors Constantine and Licinius took part.
It granted religious freedom to all, including Christians.
Confiscated church property was to be returned.
The text has come down to us in Lactantius and Eusebius.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of **313 AD** the emperors **Constantine** and **Licinius** met in **Milan**. The occasion was the wedding of Licinius to Constantine's half-sister **Constantia**. Constantine then ruled the west, Licinius a part of the east. At the meeting they also agreed on religious policy. The agreement is often called the **“Edict of Toleration of Milan”**.

Every person in the empire was to be allowed to practise the **religion** he wanted. With this **Christianity** was permitted, but **not yet the state religion**. Meeting places and property that had been taken from the Christians were to be **returned without payment**. Anyone who had bought such property could demand **compensation** from the state.

Already in **311** Emperor **Galerius**, shortly before his death, had issued an edict of toleration. With it the persecution of Christians in the east ended. The Edict of Milan went clearly further two years later. Its text does not survive as a law in its own right. The Christian author **Lactantius**, in his work on the deaths of the persecutors, reproduces a letter of Licinius, and a Greek version is found in **Eusebius**.

gewusst: There is no actual “Edict of Milan” as a legal text, so experts prefer to speak of an agreement.
Only over 60 years later, under Emperor Theodosius, did Christianity become the state religion.
