teile.einleitung: Hammurabi I was a king of Babylon in Mesopotamia. He is famous for one of the oldest known collections of laws, the Code of Hammurabi.
wichtigste: Hammurabi ruled from about 1792 to 1750 BC, so about 3,800 years ago.
He was king of Babylon and made the city the centre of a large empire.
His laws stand on a stone pillar more than two metres high, a stele.
The stele is made of dark, almost black rock.
The roughly 282 laws are written in cuneiform.
The stele was found around 1901 in Susa in present-day Iran.

abschnitte.text: Hammurabi was the sixth king of the first dynasty of **Babylon**. Babylon lay on the River Euphrates in present-day **Iraq**. At the beginning his kingdom was small. But through wars and alliances he gained control of large parts of **Mesopotamia**, the land between the Euphrates and the Tigris. He also had canals built and temples renewed.

The collection of laws is called the **Code of Hammurabi**. “Code” comes from a Latin word for a collection. Researchers count about **282 laws**. They regulate, for example, trade, rent, work, family, inheritance and punishments. Often the principle of retaliation applies: anyone who harms another should suffer the same. This is called “**an eye for an eye**”. But the punishments also depended on whether someone was free, dependent or a slave.

The laws are carved into a **stele more than two metres high** made of hard, dark rock. Everything is written in **cuneiform**, a script of wedge-shaped signs. At the top of the stele you can see a picture: King Hammurabi stands before the **sun god Shamash**. Shamash was also the god of justice. The picture was meant to show that the laws are just and willed by the gods.

The stele was found around **1901** by French researchers in the ancient city of **Susa**. Susa lies in present-day **Iran**. How did it get there? A king from the neighbouring land of Elam had taken it away from Mesopotamia as **war booty** long after Hammurabi's time. Today the stele stands in the **Louvre** in Paris.

gewusst: At the end of the stele there is a long text in which Hammurabi curses anyone who changes or destroys his laws.
Part of the inscription was ground away, probably by the conqueror from Elam. The missing passages are partly known from copies on clay tablets.

teile.einleitung: In the Roman Republic two consuls led the state, advised by the Senate. Fixed rules were meant to prevent one man from gaining too much power.
wichtigste: Two consuls were elected every year.
Annuity means: an office lasted only one year.
Collegiality means: an office was always held by at least two equal persons.
The consuls were elected in the Centuriate Assembly.
The consuls held the imperium, the highest power of command.
Decisions of the Senate were formally only advice but were mostly followed.
In emergencies a dictator could be appointed for six months at most.

abschnitte.titel: Two consuls instead of a king
abschnitte.text: After the kings were expelled, Rome became a **republic**. At its head now stood two **consuls**. They held the **imperium**, the highest military and civil power of command. With it they could lead armies, give judgement and impose punishments. In Rome the year was even named after the two consuls.

Two principles were meant to prevent abuse of power. **Annuity** comes from the Latin **annus**, year: every office lasted only one year. **Collegiality** means that an office was always held by at least two **equal** persons. They could check and block each other. Switzerland still knows a similar collegial principle today in the **Federal Council**.

abschnitte.titel: The election in the Centuriate Assembly
abschnitte.text: The consuls were elected in a popular assembly, the **Centuriate Assembly** (comitia centuriata). It was organised by **property classes**. Rich citizens had clearly more weight in it than poor ones. So the consuls mostly came from respected and wealthy families.

In the **Senate** sat mainly former office holders. At the very top of the senate list stood the **princeps senatus**, usually a respected former censor. He was often allowed to give his opinion first. A decision of the Senate, a **senatus consultum**, was formally only **advice** to the office holders. But because of the high standing, the **auctoritas**, of the Senate, it was mostly followed.

In a serious emergency a **dictator** could be appointed. He received sole power of command, but for **six months** at most. After his year in office a consul's power was often extended. As a **proconsul** he then led an army or governed a **province**. In this way Rome could administer its large empire.

gewusst: The abbreviation SPQR means “the Senate and People of Rome” and can still be seen on manhole covers in Rome today.
The Swiss Federal President is also in office for only a year, like the Roman consuls.

teile.einleitung: Hatshepsut was a woman who ruled as pharaoh in ancient Egypt. She reigned for about 20 years in the 15th century BC and is famous for her terraced temple and an expedition to Punt.
wichtigste: Hatshepsut ruled from about 1479 to 1458 BC.
She belonged to the 18th dynasty at the start of the New Kingdom.
She was married to the pharaoh Thutmose II.
She had herself shown wearing the artificial royal beard.
Her mortuary temple lies at Deir el-Bahari near Luxor.
After her death many of her images and names were erased.

abschnitte.text: Hatshepsut was the daughter of Pharaoh Thutmose I. She married her half-brother **Thutmose II**. When he died, the heir to the throne, **Thutmose III**, was still a child. Hatshepsut first took over the government for him. After a few years she had herself crowned **pharaoh**. Women on the pharaoh's throne were very rare.

At ceremonies a pharaoh wore special signs, for example an **artificial beard**. Hatshepsut had herself shown on many statues with this beard and in royal dress. In this way she made clear that she had the full role of a king. Thutmose III remained **co-ruler** during this time. Her reign is regarded as a rather peaceful time with great **building projects**.

Her famous **mortuary temple** lies in a rocky bowl at **Deir el-Bahari** on the west bank at **Luxor**. It rises in several **terraces** towards the steep cliffs. Her close confidant **Senenmut**, a high official, is regarded as the architect. The temple is decorated with many coloured **reliefs**, that is, pictures worked out of the stone.

Hatshepsut sent ships to the distant land of **Punt**. Where exactly Punt lay is not certain; it is thought to have been on the coast of the Red Sea in East Africa. The expedition brought back **frankincense**, **myrrh**, **ebony** and exotic animals. Even incense trees are said to have been brought along. The reliefs in her temple show this journey in detail.

Some time after Hatshepsut's death many of her **statues were smashed** and her name was chiselled out of inscriptions. The reasons are **disputed**. Many researchers suspect that Thutmose III wanted to secure the succession for his own family. Thutmose III then ruled alone and became a great **general**. Only modern Egyptologists pieced the story of the female pharaoh back together.

gewusst: Her name means roughly “the foremost of noble women”.
Many smashed statues of Hatshepsut were put back together from fragments in the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: The Greek alphabet is one of the oldest alphabetic scripts in the world. It has 24 letters, from alpha to omega, and is still used today in Greece and in mathematics and science.
wichtigste: The Greek alphabet has **24** letters.
The first is called alpha, the last **omega**.
The Greeks also wrote **the vowels** with letters of their own.
Today Greek is written **from left to right**.
The number 3.14 is called **pi**, like the Greek letter.
The capital **delta** looks like a triangle.
**Rho** looks like a P, but is pronounced like “R”.

abschnitte.text: The Greeks took over their script around the 8th century BC from the **Phoenicians**. The Phoenician script had signs only for consonants. The Greeks also wrote **the vowels**, that is A, E, I, O, U, with letters of their own. That made reading much easier. The word **alphabet** comes from the first two letters: alpha and beta.

The Greek alphabet has **24 letters**. It begins with **alpha** and ends with **omega**. Each letter has a capital and a small form. Some look like our letters, but have a different sound. **Rho** looks like a P, but is pronounced like “R”. The small **omega** looks a bit like a w, and **lambda** corresponds to our “L”.

Today Greek is written **from left to right**, like English. In early times this was not yet fixed. Sometimes the lines ran alternately to the right and to the left. This way of writing is called **boustrophedon**, which means roughly “as the ox ploughs”. The ox turns at the end of the field and ploughs back in the opposite direction.

Many Greek letters are used today in mathematics and science. The number 3.14 is called **pi**. The capital **delta** looks like a triangle and often stands for a change. The capital omega is the symbol for the unit ohm, used for electrical resistance. The Latin alphabet in which we write also comes from the Greek one, by way of the Etruscans.

gewusst: The phrase “the alpha and omega” comes from alpha and omega, the first and last Greek letters.
The Cyrillic script, in which Russian for example is written, was also developed from the Greek alphabet.

teile.einleitung: Achilles is a hero of the Greek legends. He was the strongest fighter of the Greeks in the Trojan War. His most famous story is told in the Iliad.
wichtigste: Achilles is the main figure of the Iliad, one of the oldest works of European poetry.
His mother was the sea nymph Thetis.
She dipped him as a baby into the river of the underworld, the Styx, and only the heel stayed dry.
He fought in the Trojan War on the side of the Greeks.
He defeated the Trojan hero Hector.
Paris hit him with an arrow in the heel.
The Achilles tendon in the foot is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Achilles was the son of King **Peleus** and the sea nymph **Thetis**. A legend tells that Thetis dipped him as a baby into the river of the underworld, the **Styx**. The water made him almost invulnerable. But she held him by the **heel**, and this spot stayed dry. Achilles was brought up by the wise **centaur Chiron**, a creature half human, half horse. From him he learned hunting, fighting and the art of healing.

The Greeks marched against the city of **Troy** to bring back the abducted Helen. Achilles led his warriors and was regarded as the best fighter. The **Iliad**, which is attributed to the poet **Homer**, tells of the **wrath of Achilles**. After a quarrel with the commander Agamemnon, he refused for a time to fight. Without him, the Greeks fell into great trouble.

His best friend was **Patroclus**. He went into battle in the armour of Achilles and was killed by the Trojan **Hector**. Full of grief, Achilles returned to the war and defeated Hector. Later Hector's father, King Priam, came to him in secret. He asked for the body of his son, and Achilles gave it up. With this scene the Iliad almost ends.

According to the legend, the Trojan prince **Paris** hit Achilles with an arrow exactly in the heel. The god Apollo is said to have helped him. Achilles died of this wound. His death is not told in the Iliad, but in other legends. To this day he is a symbol of a strong hero with a single weakness.

The strong tendon above the heel is called the **Achilles tendon**. It joins the calf muscles to the heel bone. An **Achilles heel** is a weak spot at which someone is easily attacked. In this way the ancient hero lives on in many languages.

gewusst: The Achilles tendon is the strongest tendon in the human body.
The story of the river Styx is not in Homer, but comes from later tales.

teile.einleitung: The Acropolis is a rocky hill in the middle of Athens. On it stand famous temples from the 5th century BC, above all the Parthenon. It is one of the best-known structures of antiquity.
wichtigste: The Acropolis is the citadel hill of Athens with temples for the goddess Athena.
You enter it through a large gatehouse, the Propylaea.
The Parthenon was built by the architects Ictinus and Callicrates.
The sculptor Phidias led the sculptural decoration.
At the Erechtheion, figures of young women carry the roof.
In 1687, the explosion of a gunpowder store destroyed large parts of the Parthenon.
Since 1987, the Acropolis has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: The word **Acropolis** means “upper city”. Many Greek cities had one, but that of Athens is the most famous. After the Persian Wars, the destroyed buildings were rebuilt. Under the statesman **Pericles**, magnificent temples of marble arose in the 5th century BC. You enter the hill through the **Propylaea**, a large gatehouse with columns.

The **Parthenon** is the largest temple on the Acropolis. It was dedicated to the goddess **Athena**, the protector goddess of the city. It was built by the architects **Ictinus** and **Callicrates**. The sculptor **Phidias** led the sculptural decoration and created a huge statue of Athena in gold and ivory. A long **frieze** shows the procession of the **Panathenaea**, the most important festival of Athens.

Beside the entrance stands the small **Temple of Athena Nike**, dedicated to the goddess of victory. At the **Erechtheion**, instead of columns, six figures of young women carry the roof of a porch. They are called **caryatids**. On the south slope lies the **Theatre of Dionysus**, where the Athenians performed plays. Very close by also stands the Odeon of Herodes Atticus.

In the Middle Ages, the Parthenon was converted into a **Christian church**. Under the Ottomans it later served as a mosque. In **1687**, Venetian troops bombarded the Acropolis. The Ottomans stored gunpowder in the Parthenon, and a mighty **explosion** occurred. Since then, the temple has been missing a large part of its roof and walls.

Since **1987**, the Acropolis has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Experts have been restoring the buildings with great care for decades. Many original figures stand today in the Acropolis Museum at the foot of the hill. Some of the sculptures are in the British Museum in London. Greece would like these pieces back, and Britain has so far kept them.

gewusst: The Parthenon has almost no straight lines: columns and floor are slightly curved so that it looks straight from afar.
The caryatids at the Erechtheion are copies today, and the originals stand protected in the museum.

teile.einleitung: Augustus was the first emperor of the Roman Empire. Before he became emperor he was called Octavian and was the great-nephew and adopted son of Julius Caesar. Under his rule a long period of peace began, and the month of August still bears his name.
wichtigste: Augustus was the first Roman emperor.
Before his rule he was called Octavian.
He was the great-nephew and adopted son of Julius Caesar.
In 31 BC he defeated Antony and Cleopatra in the naval battle of Actium.
The honorary name Augustus means roughly “the revered one”.
Under him a long period of peace began in the empire.
The month of August and the city of Augusta Raurica are named after him.

abschnitte.text: Augustus was born in Rome in 63 BC as **Gaius Octavius**. His grandmother was a sister of **Julius Caesar**. Caesar liked the young man and named him in his will as adopted son and heir. After Caesar's murder in 44 BC, the 18-year-old called himself Gaius Julius Caesar; for this period he is now called **Octavian**.

At first Octavian fought together with Mark **Antony** against Caesar's murderers. Later the two became rivals, because Antony allied himself with the Egyptian queen **Cleopatra**. In 31 BC Octavian defeated them both in the naval battle of **Actium** in Greece. A year later Antony and Cleopatra took their own lives, and Egypt became Roman.

In 27 BC the Senate gave Octavian the honorary name **Augustus**, which means roughly “the revered one”. Officially he called himself only Princeps, the first citizen, and acted as if the Republic still existed. In reality, however, he held all the important power over the army and the state. This new form of rule is called the **Principate**, and Augustus is regarded as the first Roman emperor. He ruled until his death in AD 14.

After many civil wars, a long period of peace began under Augustus, the **Pax Augusta**. In Rome he had many temples and buildings put up, and he boasted that he had found a city of brick and left one of marble. A famous monument is the **Altar of Peace**, the Ara Pacis. According to the Bible, **Jesus** was born in the time of Emperor Augustus.

Under Augustus his stepsons Drusus and Tiberius conquered the **Alps** in 15 BC. As a result the area of present-day Switzerland also became fully part of the Roman Empire. The Roman city of **Augusta Raurica** near Basel bears his name. Cities such as Augsburg in Germany and Aosta in Italy are also named after him.

In 8 BC the month of Sextilis was renamed **August** in honour of the emperor. After his death Augustus was worshipped as a god in Rome. His account of his deeds, the Res Gestae, survives on a temple wall in Ankara. His successor was his stepson **Tiberius**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ruler over a large empire; the word comes from Caesar.
The form of rule of Augustus, in which one man governed as the first citizen.
The long period of peace that began under Emperor Augustus.
A son who was legally taken into a family.

gewusst: The famous marble statue Augustus of Prima Porta was originally painted in bright colours.
Augustus was rather weak in health, but still lived to be 75.
Because he ruled for so long, many Romans knew no other ruler when he died.

teile.einleitung: The hypocaust was an underfloor heating system of the Romans. Warm air from a furnace flowed under the floor and through the walls and so heated rooms from below.
wichtigste: A hypocaust heated rooms from below.
The word means roughly “heated from below”.
Wood was burned in a furnace outside the room.
The floor stood on small brick pillars.
Hollow wall tiles led the warm air upwards.
They were found mainly in baths and the villas of wealthy people.

abschnitte.text: The word **hypocaust** comes from Greek. “**Hypo**” means under, and “**kaiein**” means to burn or to heat. So it means something that is heated from below. **Wood** was burned in a **furnace** outside the room. The hot air then flowed under the floor and warmed it.

The floor did not lie directly on the earth. It stood on many small **pillars of brick**. They are also called pilae. Between them was a hollow space through which the **warm air** flowed. Then the air passed up through **hollow wall tiles** and out again. In this way the **walls** became warm too, and the room was heated evenly.

Such a heating system was **expensive** and needed a lot of wood. It was built mainly in **baths**, the large public bathhouses. There were warm rooms and pools of hot water there. **Wealthy people** also had it installed in their villas. Remains of hypocausts are found in many areas of the old Roman Empire, including **Switzerland**, for example in **Augusta Raurica** near Basel.

The fire had to burn for a long time and be fed with wood constantly. This hard and hot work was mostly done by **slaves**. It took a long time for a room to become properly warm. But the warmth also stayed in the floor and walls for a long time. Whole **forests** were cut down for the many heating systems and baths.

gewusst: Modern underfloor heating works in a similar way, except that today warm water usually flows in pipes under the floor.
The Romans called the furnace in which the fire burned the “praefurnium”.

teile.einleitung: The Delian League was an alliance of many Greek cities under the leadership of Athens. It was founded after the Persian Wars so that the cities could protect themselves together against the Persians. Over time Athens became more and more powerful within it.
wichtigste: The Delian League was founded in 478/477 BC.
The shared treasury was first kept on the island of Delos.
Aristides, called “the Just”, set the first contributions.
The yearly payments of the allies were called phoros.
Around 470 BC Naxos was the first island to try to leave, and it was conquered.
In 454 BC Athens had the treasury moved to its own city.
Around 449 BC Athens is said to have made the disputed Peace of Callias with Persia.

abschnitte.text: After the Persian Wars the Greeks feared new attacks from Persia. So in **478/477 BC** many cities and islands founded an alliance. **Athens**, which had a strong fleet, took the lead. The alliance is called the **Delian League** because it was based on the island of Delos, and also the **Athenian League** because Athens lies in the region of **Attica**.

The shared **treasury** was first kept on the holy island of **Delos**. Every city had to provide ships or pay money. The yearly payments were called **phoros**. The first contributions were set by the Athenian **Aristides**. Because he was thought to be especially honest, he was called **“the Just”**. Most members preferred to pay money rather than build ships themselves.

Over time Athens decided more and more on its own. Around **470 BC** the island of **Naxos** wanted to be the first to **leave** the league. Athens did not allow this and **conquered** the island. In **454 BC** Athens moved the league's treasury to its own city. Many see this as the beginning of Athenian rule over the allies.

Around **449 BC** Athens is said to have made the **Peace of Callias** with Persia. Whether this treaty really existed is **disputed** among researchers. Later Athens fell into a long war with **Sparta**, the Peloponnesian War. Athens lost it in 404 BC, and the league broke up.

gewusst: Many researchers believe that part of the league's money also went into the magnificent buildings on the Acropolis.
In the 4th century BC Athens founded a second league.

teile.einleitung: The Hanging Gardens of Semiramis are among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. They are said to have stood in Babylon. Whether they really existed is still not known for certain.
wichtigste: The Hanging Gardens are counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
According to the accounts they were gardens on high terraces.
They needed a great deal of water in the dry region.
They are named after the legendary queen Semiramis.
No certain remains have been found to this day.
Some researchers suspect the gardens were in Nineveh rather than Babylon.

abschnitte.text: According to old accounts the Hanging Gardens were **gardens on high terraces**. The plants grew on steps one above the other, like a green mountain. From below it looked as if the gardens were **hanging**. That is where their name comes from. They are among the **Seven Wonders** of the Ancient World, together with the Pyramids of Giza and the Lighthouse of Pharos.

In the region it rained little, and it was hot and **dry**. So the gardens needed **a great deal of water**. It had to be laboriously carried up from the river. Researchers suspect **water-lifting devices**, for example water wheels or water screws. They were turned by people or animals, because there was no electricity then.

Greek stories linked the gardens with the queen **Semiramis**. But she is above all a **legendary figure**. Another legend tells that a king built the gardens for **his wife**. She came from a land of mountains and forests and **missed her green homeland**. The Babylonian priest **Berossus** was the first, around 290 BC, to write that King **Nebuchadnezzar II** built the gardens. His work survives only in quotations by later authors.

In Babylon **no certain remains** of the gardens have been found to this day. It is also striking that the historian **Herodotus**, around 450 BC, described the walls and temples of Babylon in detail but did not mention the gardens. So researchers argue about whether they really existed. The researcher Stephanie Dalley suspects that they stood in **Nineveh**, a city of the **Assyrians** on the Tigris.

gewusst: Babylon lay in present-day Iraq, south of Baghdad.
Of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, only the Pyramids of Giza still stand today.

teile.einleitung: Babylonia was an ancient kingdom in Mesopotamia, in the area of present-day Iraq. Its capital Babylon on the Euphrates was one of the largest and most famous cities in the world for many centuries. It gave us one of the oldest collections of laws and important discoveries about stars and numbers.
wichtigste: The city of Babylon lay on the River Euphrates in present-day Iraq.
Around 1750 BC King Hammurabi had a famous collection of laws written on a stone pillar.
Many of the punishments in it follow the principle of an eye for an eye.
Under Nebuchadnezzar II, Babylon enjoyed a golden age in the 6th century BC.
The blue Ishtar Gate was rebuilt in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin.
The Hanging Gardens, one of the seven wonders of the world, are said to have stood in Babylon.
In 539 BC the Persian king Cyrus II conquered the city.

abschnitte.text: Babylonia lay in the south of **Mesopotamia**, the land between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris. The capital **Babylon** was on the Euphrates, about 85 kilometres south of present-day Baghdad. People watered their fields with canals and grew barley and date palms. Because there was hardly any stone or wood, almost everything was built from **mud bricks**.

King **Hammurabi** ruled in the 18th century BC and made Babylon the centre of a large empire. Around 1750 BC he had laws written in cuneiform on a stone pillar more than two metres high, the **Code of Hammurabi**. It deals with trade, family, wages and punishments. Many punishments follow the principle of **an eye for an eye**: anyone who harmed someone was to suffer the same. The stele was found in 1901 in Susa in Iran and now stands in the Louvre in Paris.

In the 6th century BC Babylon enjoyed a great golden age under King **Nebuchadnezzar II**. He had mighty city walls, palaces and the magnificent **Ishtar Gate** built, with blue glazed bricks and pictures of lions, bulls and dragons. A copy using original bricks was rebuilt in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. In the city there was also a huge stepped temple, a **ziggurat**, which people link with the Tower of Babel in the Bible.

In 587/586 BC Nebuchadnezzar conquered **Jerusalem**, and many Jews were taken away to Babylon. This time is called the **Babylonian Exile**. In 539 BC the Persian king Cyrus II conquered Babylon, and the Jews were allowed to go home. Later Alexander the Great died here. After that the city gradually lost its importance and fell into ruin.

The Babylonians watched the sky very carefully and wrote down the movements of the Moon and planets on clay tablets. They could even predict lunar eclipses. In **mathematics** they calculated with a number system based on the number 60. That is why an hour has 60 minutes and a circle has 360 degrees. Since 2019 their ruins have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

begriffe.erklaerung: The land between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris, in present-day Iraq.
One of the oldest known collections of laws in the world.
A tall stepped temple made of mud bricks in Mesopotamia.
A life away from your homeland, into which you were forced.

gewusst: The German archaeologist Robert Koldewey dug up Babylon from 1899 and found the bricks of the Ishtar Gate.
Whether the Hanging Gardens of Babylon really existed is still uncertain, because no traces of them have been found.
When we read a clock today, we are still using an idea of the Babylonians.

teile.einleitung: Ancient Greece was a culture that flourished around the Mediterranean about 2,500 years ago. From the ancient Greeks come the theatre, the Olympic Games, democracy and many ideas of science. Much of this shapes our lives to this day.
wichtigste: Greece lies on the Mediterranean and has over a thousand islands.
The Greeks lived in many independent city states, and such a city was called a polis.
The poet Homer told of the Trojan War and of the wanderings of Odysseus.
The first letters of the Greek alphabet are called alpha and beta.
The Greeks invented the theatre, in which actors wore masks.
Greek temples are surrounded by columns.
At the oracle of Delphi, the Greeks consulted the gods about the future.

abschnitte.text: Greece lies in the south-east of Europe on the **Mediterranean**. The land is very mountainous and has well over a thousand islands. Because the mountains made travel over land hard, the Greeks often went by ship. They founded **colonies** on many coasts, for example Massalia, present-day Marseille. In the dry soil, mainly **olive trees**, vines and grain grew.

There was no single Greek country, but many small city states. Such a city with its surrounding land was called a **polis**. The best known were **Athens** and Sparta. In Athens, the first democracy arose around 508 BC, whereas Sparta was known for its strict upbringing and its warriors. Together, the Greeks defeated the Persians in the 5th century BC.

The Greeks invented the **theatre** with tragedies and comedies. The actors, all men, wore **masks** so that their role could be recognised even from the back row. The theatres were built in a semicircle into a hillside and had surprisingly good acoustics. From 776 BC, the **Olympic Games** in honour of Zeus took place at Olympia every four years.

The poet **Homer** is said to have composed the Iliad about the Trojan War and the Odyssey about the wanderings of Odysseus. In it, the Greeks get into the city of Troy with a wooden horse. Famous **philosophers** such as Socrates, Plato and Aristotle thought about justice, nature and the good life. Mathematicians such as Pythagoras and Euclid were Greeks too. Our word alphabet comes from the first Greek letters **alpha** and beta.

The Greeks worshipped many gods, who were supposed to live on Mount Olympus. For them they built **temples** that were surrounded by columns. There are three kinds of column: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian. To learn the future, people travelled to the **oracle of Delphi**, where a priestess, the Pythia, proclaimed answers of the god Apollo.

The Greeks stored oil, wine and grain in clay jars, the **amphorae**. Many of these vessels are painted with pictures from legends and everyday life. From them we know a great deal today about life at that time. Merchants brought Greek goods as far as areas north of the Alps.

begriffe.erklaerung: A Greek city state, that is, a city with its own surrounding land and its own government.
A large clay jar with two handles for oil, wine or grain.
A place where people asked the gods for advice about the future.
Thinking about great questions, for example what is just and true.

gewusst: Words such as democracy, theatre, mathematics and telephone come from Greek.
At the ancient Olympic Games, the athletes competed naked.
In the tomb of a Celtic prince at Vix in France, a huge Greek bronze vessel was found that weighs over 200 kilograms.

teile.einleitung: The woolly rhinoceros lived in the Ice Age in the cold steppes of Europe and Asia. With its thick coat and two horns, it was well adapted to the cold.
wichtigste: The woolly rhinoceros had a long, woolly coat against the cold.
It carried two horns of keratin on its nose.
It was a plant eater and grazed on grasses and herbs.
It lived in the cold mammoth steppe from Europe to Asia.
In the frozen ground of Siberia, animals were found with skin and hair.
Stone Age people painted woolly rhinoceroses on cave walls.

abschnitte.titel: A rhinoceros in a fur coat
abschnitte.text: The **woolly rhinoceros** had long, **woolly fur**. In this way it endured the icy cold of the Ice Age. At the front of the nose sat a long **horn**, and behind it grew a smaller second horn. The horns consisted of **keratin**, the same substance as hair and fingernails. That is why they were only rarely preserved.

The woolly rhinoceros lived in the cold steppes from **Europe to Asia**, and there were none in America. This landscape is called the **mammoth steppe**: cold, dry and almost without trees. As a **plant eater**, it grazed on **grasses and herbs**. It usually carried its head **low, pointing down**, much like today's white rhinoceros. The shape of its skull shows this.

abschnitte.titel: As if in a deep freezer
abschnitte.text: In **Siberia**, the ground is frozen all year round. There some woolly rhinoceroses were preserved almost as if in a deep freezer, with **skin and hair**. A special find was made in **1929** at **Starunia**, today in Ukraine. There **earth wax** and **salt water** protected an animal from decay, so that even skin and soft parts were preserved.

The people of the Stone Age knew the woolly rhinoceros. In caves in **France**, for example in the **Chauvet Cave**, there are old **paintings** of woolly rhinoceroses. The pictures show how important these animals were to the hunters. At the end of the last Ice Age, the woolly rhinoceros died out.

gewusst: In Switzerland too, bones of woolly rhinoceroses have been found.
The woolly rhinoceros lived at the same time as the mammoth and the cave bear.

teile.einleitung: Livestock farming means that people keep, feed and breed animals in order to get meat, milk, wool or working power. It began in the New Stone Age, when people settled down. Together with arable farming, it changed human life for ever.
wichtigste: Over many generations, wild animals became domestic animals, which is called domestication.
The dog was the first domestic animal, and already lived with hunters and gatherers.
Goats and sheep are among the first farm animals in the Near East.
Domestic cattle descend from the aurochs, domestic pigs from the wild boar.
The last known aurochs died in the year 1627.
With livestock farming, meat was available more reliably than from hunting.
The farmers of the New Stone Age in central Europe did not yet keep chickens.

abschnitte.text: About 11,000 years ago, people in the **Near East** began to keep animals. This region with fertile soils is called the Fertile Crescent, and lies roughly in present-day Turkey, Syria, Iraq and Iran. Among the first **farm animals** were goats and sheep, and cattle and pigs soon followed. People caught young wild animals, tamed them and let the calmest animals have young.

abschnitte.titel: From wild animal to domestic animal
abschnitte.text: When people select and breed animals over many generations, the animals change. This long process is called **domestication**. Domestic animals are often smaller and tamer than their wild ancestors. The **dog** descends from the wolf and already accompanied hunters and gatherers long before there were farmers. Domestic cattle descend from the mighty **aurochs**, the pig from the wild boar.

The animals supplied meat, milk, fur, leather, wool and bones for tools. Because the animals were always close by, food was available far more **reliably** than from hunting. Towards the end of the New Stone Age, farmers harnessed cattle to **ploughs** and carts. In this way they could work larger fields and transport heavy loads. The animals' dung was valuable too, because it fertilised the fields.

Arable and livestock farming came to the area of present-day Switzerland about 7,500 years ago. The farmers often lived in **pile-dwelling settlements** on lakes and kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. In winter they fed the animals with leaves and twigs, because there was not yet hay in large quantities. Chickens only came to central Europe much later, in the Iron Age. From early livestock farming, the typical **alpine farming** of Switzerland developed much later.

The **aurochs** was a gigantic wild bovine with long horns curving forwards. A bull could be almost as tall at the shoulder as a grown person. Because people hunted it and cleared its forests, it became ever rarer. The last known aurochs, a cow, died in **1627** in a forest in Poland.

Through arable and livestock farming, more people could be fed, and villages grew larger. This great change is called the **Neolithic Revolution**. However, animals also passed diseases on to humans, and the work was hard. To this day, almost all our farm animals descend from animals that were tamed in the New Stone Age.

begriffe.erklaerung: When people turn wild animals into domestic animals over many generations.
An animal that people keep because it supplies food, wool or working power.
An extinct, very large wild bovine, the ancestor of our cows.
The change from hunting and gathering to arable and livestock farming in the New Stone Age.

gewusst: Many people could at first not digest milk well as adults, and that only changed little by little with dairy farming.
The Heck cattle is an attempt of the 20th century to breed, from domestic cattle, an animal that looks like an aurochs.
The dog was already living with humans when there were no farmers yet.

teile.einleitung: Pottery is the making of vessels from clay. Since the New Stone Age, people in Europe have shaped pots, bowls and jugs and fired them hard in the fire.
wichtigste: Clay vessels are made from clay, a soft, mouldable earth.
In the fire or a kiln, the clay becomes hard.
In Europe, people began to make a lot of pottery in the New Stone Age.
The first pots were shaped by hand from coils of clay.
Linear Pottery is named after the patterns on its pots.
Of the pile dwellers in Switzerland, potsherds are often preserved.

abschnitte.text: **Clay** is a soft, damp earth that can be shaped well. If a vessel is only left to dry, it becomes soft again in water. Only through **firing** in the fire or in a **kiln** does the clay become hard as stone. People who make clay vessels are called **potters**.

In the **New Stone Age**, people settled down. They grew grain and kept animals. Now they needed vessels for **cooking** and **storing**. In pots you could cook porridge and store grain or water. Hunters, who often moved on, could hardly have taken heavy pots with them.

The first pots were made entirely **by hand**. Clay was rolled into long sausages, the **coils**. These were laid on top of one another in a circle and smoothed over. The **potter's wheel**, which turns, only came to central Europe much later. Many pots were decorated with patterns before firing.

The first farming culture of central Europe is called **Linear Pottery**. It existed from about 5500 to 4900 BC. Its name comes from the band-shaped lines that were incised into the vessels. Researchers often name such cultures after their pottery, because potsherds are found so often.

Fired clay breaks easily, but the **potsherds** do not rot. In the lakes of Switzerland, many potsherds from pots of the **pile dwellers** were found. Archaeologists put them back together like a jigsaw puzzle. From the shape and pattern they recognise from which period a vessel comes.

gewusst: Potsherds are among the most common finds in archaeological excavations.
Some pots of the pile dwellers still contained charred food remains.

teile.einleitung: The ancient Egyptians believed in a great many gods, who watched over the sun, the Nile, death and almost every area of life. Many of these gods were shown with animal heads, for example with the head of a falcon, a cat or a jackal. We know their stories and pictures from temples, tombs and papyrus scrolls.
wichtigste: The ancient Egyptians worshipped a great many gods.
The sun god Ra was one of the most important gods.
Osiris ruled over the realm of the dead and is often shown with green skin.
Isis was the wife of Osiris and a powerful goddess of magic.
Horus had a falcon's head, and Bastet was shown as a cat.
Thoth, with the head of an ibis, was the god of scribes.
After death, a person's heart was weighed against a feather.

abschnitte.text: According to Egyptian belief, the sun god **Ra** travelled across the sky every day in a barque. At night he journeyed through the underworld and fought there against the serpent Apophis. Later he was joined with the god Amun of Thebes to form **Amun-Ra**. The sacred **scarab**, a dung beetle, was a sign of the rising sun. Just as the beetle rolls its ball of dung, a god was supposed to roll the sun across the sky.

A famous legend tells of **Osiris**, who ruled Egypt as a good king. His jealous brother **Seth**, the god of the desert, of storms and of disorder, killed him. The goddess of magic **Isis**, the wife of Osiris, found his body and brought him back to life. Osiris then became ruler of the realm of the dead, which is why he is often shown with green skin, the colour of new growth. Their son Horus later defeated Seth and became the protector god of the pharaohs.

Many gods had a human body and an animal head. **Horus** wears a falcon's head, and the god of the dead Anubis the head of a jackal. **Thoth**, with the head of an ibis, was the god of scribes, of wisdom and of the moon. The goddess **Bastet** was shown as a cat and protected home and family. The lion-headed Sekhmet was regarded as wild and dangerous, but could also heal diseases.

The goddess **Hathor** is often shown with cow's horns and a sun disc. She was the goddess of love, music and joy. The goddess **Maat** stood for truth and order, and her sign was an ostrich feather. The Egyptians believed that the pharaoh had to make sure that this order in the world was preserved.

The Egyptians believed in a life after death. At the **judgement of the dead**, the heart of the deceased was laid on a scale and weighed against the feather of Maat. Anubis operated the scale, and Thoth wrote down the result. If the heart was as light as the feather, the dead person was allowed to pass on into the afterlife. Spells that were meant to help with this were written in the so-called **Book of the Dead**.

For their gods, the Egyptians built huge **temples**, such as the temple of Karnak near Luxor. In the innermost room stood a statue of the god, which only priests were allowed to enter. Every day the statue was washed, dressed and provided with food. Some animals were regarded as sacred, and many cats, ibises and falcons were even buried as **mummies**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The test after death in which a person's heart was weighed.
A sacred beetle that was a sign of the sun for the Egyptians.
The goddess of truth and order, whose sign is a feather.
A collection of magic spells that was put into the tomb with the deceased.

gewusst: The pharaoh Akhenaten tried to have almost only a single sun god, Aten, worshipped, but after his death people returned to the old gods.
In the city of Bubastis, where Bastet was worshipped, cemeteries with many cat mummies were found.
The well-known Udjat eye, also called the Eye of Horus, was a popular protective amulet in Egypt.

teile.einleitung: **Stonehenge** is a famous stone monument in England. It consists of a circle of huge stones and is about 5,000 years old. To this day, researchers wonder how the people of the Stone Age were able to build it.
wichtigste: Stonehenge stands in England.
It is a circle of huge stones and about 5,000 years old.
The largest stones are called sarsen stones and weigh about 25 tonnes.
The smaller bluestones came from Wales.
Lintels lie across two standing stones.
Especially many people come at the summer solstice.
Stonehenge is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Stonehenge stands in southern England, in the county of Wiltshire. It was not built all at once, but in several phases. At the beginning, about **5,000 years ago**, there was a round ditch with a bank. Later the large stones were set up. In total, the work lasted many centuries.

The large stones are called **sarsen stones**. They are made of sandstone and weigh about **25 tonnes**, as much as several elephants. They come from the nearer surroundings. The smaller **bluestones**, by contrast, came from **Wales**, over 200 kilometres away. How people transported them so far is still being researched.

On every two standing stones lies a **lintel** across the top. So that it does not slide off, the stones were joined with **tenons and holes**, just as is done in wooden buildings. The lintels are also slightly curved so that together they form a ring. This shows how skilful the builders were.

Stonehenge is aligned with the sun. At the **summer solstice**, the sun rises in a line with the entrance. Then especially many people come to see it. Since 1986, Stonehenge has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. What exactly it was used for is not certain: perhaps as a place for festivals, for burials or as a calendar.

gewusst: In the area around Stonehenge there are many more Stone Age monuments and burial mounds.
Stonehenge also fits the sun at the winter solstice: then it sets in the opposite direction.

teile.einleitung: Athena is one of the most important goddesses in Greek myths. She was the goddess of wisdom and the protector of the city of Athens. The Romans worshipped her under the name Minerva.
wichtigste: Athena was the goddess of wisdom.
Her bird is the owl.
According to the myth, she was born from the head of Zeus.
According to the myth, the city of Athens is named after her.
She gave the people of Athens an olive tree.
In pictures she usually carries a spear, a helmet and a shield.
The Romans called her Minerva.

abschnitte.text: Athena was the goddess of **wisdom** and clever plans. She also protected **crafts**, especially weaving. In war she stood for careful thinking, not for wild fighting. In pictures and statues she usually carries a **spear**, a **helmet** and a shield. Many heroes of the myths, such as Odysseus, received her help.

Her birth is especially astonishing. Zeus, the father of the gods, had terrible headaches. The god of the forge then split open his head. Out jumped Athena, already grown up and in full armour. That is why the myth says that Athena was born **from the head of Zeus**.

Athena and the sea god **Poseidon** both wanted to become the protector of a city. Each brought a gift. Poseidon made a spring of salt water gush forth. Athena gave an **olive tree**, which provides wood, fruit and oil. The people found her gift more useful. So the city was named **Athens** after her.

Athena's bird is the **owl**. It is thought to be wise because it can see in the dark. In Athens the owl was stamped on coins. Even today the Greek 1 euro coin shows an owl copied from an old design. The owl is still a symbol of wisdom and knowledge.

One myth tells of the weaver **Arachne**. She boasted that she could weave better than the goddess. A contest followed, and Athena became angry. She turned Arachne into a **spider**, who has been weaving ever since. The **Romans** called Athena **Minerva**. Her greatest temple was the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens.

gewusst: In science, spiders and their relatives are called arachnids, after the weaver Arachne.
The saying “to carry owls to Athens” means to do something unnecessary, because there are already enough of them there.

teile.einleitung: Athens is one of the most famous cities of antiquity and today the capital of Greece. Here, about 2,500 years ago, democracy arose, and on the citadel hill of the Acropolis the temple of the Parthenon still stands today. The city is named after the goddess Athena.
wichtigste: Athens is the capital of Greece and is named after the goddess Athena.
On the citadel hill of the Acropolis stands the great temple of the Parthenon.
The politician Pericles had the Parthenon built.
In ancient Athens, democracy arose, the rule of the people.
Only adult men with citizenship were allowed to vote.
The owl was the symbol of the city.
The marketplace was called the Agora, the harbour is called Piraeus.

abschnitte.text: According to a legend, the goddess **Athena** and the sea god Poseidon quarrelled over who should become the protector god of the city. Poseidon made a spring gush from the rock, but its water was salty. Athena gave the city an **olive tree**, and the inhabitants decided in her favour. Her sacred animal, the **owl**, became the symbol of the city and was to be seen on the silver coins of Athens.

In the middle of Athens rises the citadel hill of the **Acropolis**. On it, the politician **Pericles** had the **Parthenon** built between 447 and 432 BC, a temple of white marble for Athena. Inside stood a statue of the goddess about twelve metres tall, made of gold and ivory. The sculptor Phidias led the work on the sculptures. The Acropolis is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Around 508 BC, Athens introduced a new form of government, **democracy**. The word means rule of the people. In the **Assembly**, however, only adult men with citizenship were allowed to vote, so no women, no slaves and no foreigners. Anyone who seemed too powerful could be banished from the city for ten years. For this, the citizens scratched his name on potsherds, the **ostraka**.

The marketplace in ancient Athens was called the **Agora**. There people traded, debated and made politics, and the philosopher Socrates spoke with people here. The harbour of Athens is **Piraeus**, about ten kilometres from the old town. In antiquity, long walls joined the city and the harbour so that Athens could be supplied in war. With its large fleet, Athens was an important sea power.

Today Athens is the **capital** and largest city of Greece. In the region around Athens, Attica, about 3.8 million people lived in 2021. In 1896, the first **modern Olympic Games** took place here, and again in 2004. In the modern Acropolis Museum, you can see many original figures from the Parthenon up close.

begriffe.erklaerung: The citadel hill of Athens with its famous temples.
A form of rule in which the people have a say.
The marketplace and meeting place in ancient Athens.
A vote with potsherds to banish a citizen for ten years.

gewusst: On the Greek 1 euro coin, the same owl is shown as on the old silver coins of Athens.
In the course of time, the Parthenon served as a temple, church, mosque and powder store, and in 1687 it was badly damaged in an explosion.
Because the Mediterranean knew so many owl coins, people said in antiquity “to carry owls to Athens” for something superfluous.

teile.einleitung: The Venus of Willendorf is a small female figure from the Old Stone Age. It was found in Austria in 1908 and is about 29,500 years old.
wichtigste: The figure was found in 1908 at Willendorf in the Wachau on the Danube.
It is about 29,500 years old and belongs to the Gravettian.
The excavation was led by Josef Szombathy, and it was found by the worker Johann Veran.
Traces of red ochre are preserved on the figure.
Instead of a face, the head carries rows all round, like curls.
According to a 2022 study, the stone probably comes from the area of Lake Garda.

abschnitte.text: **Willendorf** lies in the **Wachau**, a valley on the **Danube** in Austria. In August 1908, the figure came to light during excavations. The excavation was led by **Josef Szombathy** of the **Natural History Museum Vienna**. It was discovered by the worker **Johann Veran**. Today it is on display in the Natural History Museum in Vienna.

The figure is only about 11 centimetres tall and fits in one hand. It shows a plump woman. The **face** is not worked out. Instead, the whole head is covered with **rows** that look like locks of hair or a cap. Traces of **red ochre** show that it was once painted red.

The figure comes from the **Old Stone Age** and is about **29,500 years** old. It belongs to the **Gravettian** culture. From this period, many similar female figures are known all over Europe. What they were used for is not known for certain. Perhaps they were lucky charms or figures connected with people's beliefs.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the stone come from?
abschnitte.text: The figure is carved from **oolite**, a kind of limestone made of tiny little spheres. For a long time it was believed that the stone came from Moravia. High-resolution studies in 2022, however, pointed to **northern Italy**, probably the area around **Lake Garda**. This shows that people at that time travelled long distances.

The **Venus of Dolní Věstonice** from the Czech Republic is about 30,000 years old. It is made of **fired clay** and is among the oldest objects of this material. Clearly older still is the **Venus of Hohle Fels** from Germany, found in 2008. It is made of mammoth ivory and is at least 35,000 years old.

gewusst: The Venus of Willendorf is one of the best-known works of art of the Stone Age.
The name “Venus” was only given to it by researchers, after the Roman goddess.

teile.einleitung: Marcus Aurelius was emperor of Rome from 161 to 180 AD. He is regarded as a wise and just ruler and is often called the “philosopher emperor” because of his thoughts on life.
wichtigste: Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 AD.
He is often called the “philosopher emperor”.
He wrote down his thoughts in Greek in the “Meditations”.
On the Danube he fought a long war against the Marcomanni and other tribes.
A famous bronze equestrian statue shows him on a horse.
After him his son Commodus became emperor.

abschnitte.text: Marcus Aurelius was emperor of the **Roman Empire** from **161 to 180 AD**. Already as a young man he learned a great deal about languages, law and **philosophy**. He was regarded as dutiful and just. So he is often called the **“philosopher emperor”**. Many count him among the good emperors of Rome.

Marcus Aurelius wrote down his thoughts on life in a book for himself. It is called the **“Meditations”**. Although he was a Roman, he wrote in **Greek**, the language of scholars. In it he thinks about duty, calm and the right way to deal with other people. He followed the teaching of the **Stoa**, which stresses composure and reason. The book is still read all over the world today.

Although Marcus Aurelius would rather have been thinking, he had to wage a lot of war. On the **Danube** he fought against the **Marcomanni** and other Germanic tribes. He spent many years there in the field camp. He is said to have written part of his Meditations there. In Rome the **Column of Marcus Aurelius** with its pictures recalls these wars.

A large **bronze statue** shows Marcus Aurelius **on a horse**. Many bronze statues were later melted down so that the metal could be reused. This one survived because people believed it showed the Christian emperor **Constantine**. The original now stands in the museum on the **Capitoline Hill** in Rome, and a copy stands in the square in front.

Marcus Aurelius died in **180**. After that his son **Commodus** became emperor. Commodus was quite different from his father and took little interest in government. Many historians see in the death of Marcus Aurelius the end of a good time for the empire.

gewusst: The equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius is one of the few large bronze statues from ancient Rome that survive to this day.
Marcus Aurelius is shown on the Italian 50-cent euro coin, as an equestrian figure.

teile.einleitung: Velociraptor was a small, nimble predatory dinosaur of the Cretaceous. Its name means “swift predator”, and its fossils come from Mongolia and China.
wichtigste: Velociraptor was about as big as a turkey, around 2 metres long.
It ran on two legs and could not fly.
It was a meat eater and hunted smaller animals.
On its second toe it carried a large sickle claw.
Its fossils were found in Mongolia and in China.
A famous fossil shows it in combat with a Protoceratops.

abschnitte.text: In films, Velociraptor often looks as big as a human. In reality it was about as big as a **turkey**. It was around **2 metres long**, a large part of which was the long **tail**. The tail helped it keep its balance when running fast.

The name comes from Latin: **velox** means swift, **raptor** means predator. Velociraptor ran on its **two hind legs**. Its arms were too short for real wings, so it could not fly. It was a **meat eater** and hunted smaller animals.

On the **second toe** of each foot it carried a large, curved **claw**. It looked like a sickle and is therefore called the **sickle claw**. When running, it held it up so that it did not wear down. Experts suspect that it used it for holding on to prey.

The fossils of Velociraptor come from **Mongolia** and from **China**. A particularly famous fossil shows a Velociraptor and a **Protoceratops**, a plant eater with a neck frill, fighting each other. Both were buried together, perhaps by a collapsing sand dune, and so became fossilised.

gewusst: On a forearm bone of a Velociraptor, attachment points for feathers were found, so it was feathered.
The fossil of the fight with the Protoceratops was discovered in 1971 in the Gobi Desert.

teile.einleitung: The ancient Greeks believed in many gods, who lived like a great family on Mount Olympus. These gods looked like humans, but had superhuman powers and lived for ever. They could love, quarrel and be jealous, just like humans.
wichtigste: Zeus was the king of the Greek gods and hurled lightning bolts.
The most important gods lived on Mount Olympus.
Hera was the wife of Zeus.
Poseidon ruled the sea with his trident.
Hades was the ruler of the underworld.
According to the myth, Athena was born from the head of Zeus.
Hermes was the messenger of the gods, with winged shoes.

abschnitte.text: The twelve most important gods are called the **Olympians**, because they were said to live on **Olympus**. At about 2,900 metres, Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece. The gods ate **ambrosia** there and drank nectar, which made them immortal. The Greeks believed that the gods interfered in the lives of humans. So they made sacrifices to them and asked for help.

**Zeus** was the king of the gods and lord of the sky and weather. When he was angry he hurled lightning bolts. His sacred animal was the eagle. His wife **Hera** was the goddess of marriage and family. Because Zeus was often unfaithful to her, she was jealous in many myths.

**Poseidon** was the god of the sea and carried a **trident**. When he struck the ground with it, earthquakes and storms were said to arise. His brother **Hades** ruled the underworld, the realm of the dead. There the three-headed dog Cerberus guarded the entrance. Hades was not evil, but strict, because anyone who had once entered his realm was not allowed to go back.

**Athena** was the goddess of wisdom and clever fighting; according to the myth she sprang in full armour from the head of Zeus. **Aphrodite** was the goddess of love and beauty, and her son Eros shot arrows of love. **Artemis** was the goddess of hunting and wild animals and carried a bow and arrows. Her twin brother Apollo was the god of light, music and prophecy.

**Hermes** was the messenger of the gods, and with wings on his shoes and helmet he was especially fast. He was also the god of traders, travellers and thieves. **Ares** was the wild god of war and was not especially popular with the other gods. Other Olympians included Hephaestus, the god of smiths, Demeter, the goddess of the harvest, and Dionysus, the god of wine.

The **Romans** took over many Greek gods, but gave them names of their own. So Zeus became the god Jupiter, Hera became Juno and Poseidon became Neptune. Aphrodite was called Venus by the Romans, Ares was called Mars and Hermes was Mercury. The **planets** of our solar system are named after these Roman names.

begriffe.erklaerung: The highest mountain in Greece, where the gods were said to live.
The twelve most important Greek gods.
The realm of the dead in Greek myth.
The food of the gods, which made them immortal.

gewusst: The sports brand Nike is named after the Greek goddess of victory, Nike.
The planet Mercury is the fastest planet and takes its name from the swift messenger of the gods.
The Olympic Games at Olympia were held in honour of Zeus.

teile.einleitung: **Trilobites** were prehistoric animals that lived in the sea. They had a hard shell and belong to the arthropods. They existed long before the dinosaurs, and today we know them only as fossils.
wichtigste: Trilobites lived in the sea.
Their body is divided lengthwise into three parts.
A hard shell protected their body.
Many could roll up when in danger.
Many had compound eyes.
They belong to the arthropods.
The first trilobites appeared in the Cambrian.

abschnitte.text: The name **trilobite** means roughly “three lobes”. For the body is divided **lengthwise into three parts**: a raised middle part and two flatter side parts. From front to back there are also the head, the trunk with many segments and the tail shield.

A **hard shell** protected the body. Many trilobites could **roll up** when in danger, like a woodlouse. The shell did not grow with the animal. When a trilobite became bigger, it **moulted**: it slipped out of the old shell, and a new one formed. That is why empty pieces of shell are often found as fossils.

Many trilobites had **compound eyes**, which consist of many small single eyes. The lenses were made of calcite, a mineral. That is why they were preserved as fossils. Trilobites are among the first animals with well-developed eyes.

Trilobites belong to the **arthropods**, like insects, spiders and crustaceans today. The first appeared in the **Cambrian**, more than 500 million years ago. So they lived **much earlier** than the dinosaurs. There were thousands of different species. At the end of the Permian, about 250 million years ago, the last died out.

gewusst: Trilobites existed for almost 300 million years, much longer than the dinosaurs.
Some trilobites were only a few millimetres small, others over half a metre long.

teile.einleitung: The Gracchi were two brothers in ancient Rome who wanted to help poor citizens with new laws. Both met fierce resistance and died violently.
wichtigste: The brothers were called **Tiberius and Gaius** Gracchus.
Their mother **Cornelia** was seen as a model Roman woman.
Tiberius was tribune of the people in **133 BC**.
He wanted to **distribute state land to poor citizens**.
Nobody was to hold more than **500** iugera of state land, without a supplement for sons.
Tiberius **was beaten to death by senators and their followers**.
Gaius gave citizens **grain at a reduced price**.

abschnitte.text: Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus came from a distinguished Roman family. Their mother **Cornelia** was the daughter of the famous general Scipio Africanus. After the early death of her husband she brought up her children herself and gave them a good education. The Romans regarded her as a **model Roman woman**. It is said that she called her sons her jewels.

Many Roman farmers had lost their land, while rich families owned large estates. **Tiberius Gracchus** became tribune of the people in **133 BC**. With his **land law** he wanted to **distribute state land to poor citizens**. Nobody was to be allowed to use more than **500 iugera** of state land, with a supplement for sons. One iugerum was about a quarter of a hectare.

Many senators were against the law, because they themselves used a lot of state land. When Tiberius wanted to be elected tribune again, unrest broke out. Tiberius **was beaten to death by senators and their followers**, and many of his supporters with him. It was the first time in a long while that a political dispute in Rome ended so bloodily.

Ten years later his younger brother **Gaius Gracchus** became tribune of the people. He passed many laws. One **grain law** provided that citizens in Rome could buy **grain at a reduced price**. Gaius too got into fierce conflict with the Senate. In 121 BC he was killed in fighting in Rome.

The Gracchi pushed through their policies by way of the **people's assembly**, not the Senate. Politicians who proceeded in this way were later called **populares**. Their opponents, who defended the power of the Senate, were called **optimates**. The conflict between these two camps shaped the last hundred years of the Roman Republic.

gewusst: A tribune of the people could block decisions of other officials with an objection, the veto.
The Romans called the people's assembly through which the Gracchi passed their laws the “concilium plebis”.

teile.einleitung: Akhenaten was an Egyptian pharaoh in the 14th century BC. He changed the religion of Egypt greatly, because he placed the sun god Aten above all other gods.
wichtigste: Akhenaten came to the throne under the name **Amenhotep IV**.
He placed the god **Aten, the sun disc**, above all other gods.
He had the new capital **Akhetaten** built, today called Amarna.
He ruled for **about 17 years**.
His wife was **Nefertiti**.
According to DNA tests, **Tutankhamun** is thought to be his son.

abschnitte.text: Akhenaten came to the throne as **Amenhotep IV**. Soon he placed the god **Aten**, the **sun disc**, above all other gods. The old gods such as Amun lost importance, and their temples received less money. The pharaoh gave himself the new name **Akhenaten**, which means roughly “he who is useful to Aten”. This change was unique in the history of Egypt.

For his god Akhenaten had a new capital built in the middle of Egypt: **Akhetaten**, “Horizon of the Aten”. The place is now called **Amarna**, which is why we speak of the **Amarna period**. There temples were built without roofs, so that the sun could shine in. After Akhenaten's death the city was soon abandoned.

In this time a new style of art arose, **Amarna art**. The royal family was shown far more lively and natural than before. Aten was shown as a **sun disc with rays ending in hands**. The painted bust of Queen **Nefertiti** is famous. The German archaeologist **Ludwig Borchardt** found it in 1912 during excavations at Amarna, and today it stands in Berlin.

At Amarna hundreds of clay tablets were found, the **Amarna letters**. They are letters between the pharaoh and other rulers, most of them in **cuneiform**. The **Great Hymn to the Aten**, a song of praise to the sun, also comes from Akhenaten's time. It is often compared with **Psalm 104** from the Bible, because both praise creation in a similar way.

Akhenaten ruled for **about 17 years**. After his death Egypt returned to the old gods. His son **Tutankhamun**, as DNA tests show, gave Amun first place again. Later pharaohs had Akhenaten's name struck from many lists. Only modern research has made him known again.

gewusst: Tutankhamun was first called Tutankhaten, so his name still contained the god Aten.
The Amarna letters show that rulers at that time already exchanged gifts and messages busily.

teile.einleitung: Gaius Julius Caesar was one of the most famous Romans of all. He was a successful general and politician, conquered Gaul and finally became the most powerful man in Rome. His name lives on to this day in the month of July and in the word Kaiser.
wichtigste: Julius Caesar was above all a general and politician in ancient Rome.
From 58 to 51 BC he conquered Gaul, where France mainly lies today.
He defeated the Helvetii, who wanted to move from present-day Switzerland into Gaul.
He wrote an account of his campaigns, De bello Gallico.
He had a close relationship with the Egyptian queen Cleopatra.
He introduced a new calendar, the Julian calendar.
In 44 BC he was murdered, and Brutus was among the killers.
The month of July and the word Kaiser come from his name.

abschnitte.text: Caesar was born in Rome in **100 BC**. His family belonged to the old nobility but was not especially rich. He made a career as a politician and held various offices, for example he became **consul**, the highest office of the Republic. To become more powerful, he allied himself with the politicians Pompey and Crassus.

From 58 to 51 BC Caesar waged war in **Gaul**, the area of present-day France, Belgium and parts of Switzerland. Right at the start, in 58 BC, he defeated the **Helvetii** near Bibracte as they tried to move west from the Swiss Plateau. After that they had to return to their homeland. In 52 BC he defeated the Gallic leader **Vercingetorix** at Alesia. About these wars Caesar himself wrote the book **De bello Gallico**, which is still read in Latin lessons today.

The Senate in Rome feared Caesar's power and demanded that he give up his army. In 49 BC he instead crossed the border river **Rubicon** with his soldiers and so began a civil war. He is said to have remarked that the die was cast. Caesar defeated his former ally Pompey and finally became **dictator for life**.

In the civil war Caesar also came to Egypt. There he met the young queen **Cleopatra** and helped her to stay in power. The two had a son together, who was called Caesarion. After a quick victory in Asia Minor in 47 BC, Caesar wrote the famous sentence **“Veni, vidi, vici”**, which means: I came, I saw, I conquered.

Many senators were afraid that Caesar wanted to become king and abolish the Republic. On 15 March 44 BC, the **Ides of March**, he was murdered with daggers by a group of conspirators at a meeting of the Senate. Among them was **Brutus**, whom Caesar had regarded as a friend. After his death there was civil war again, until his adopted son Octavian became the first emperor as Augustus.

In 46 BC Caesar introduced a new calendar with 365 days and a leap day every four years, the **Julian calendar**. Our calendar today is an improved version of it. The month of **July** is named after him because he was born in that month. From his name came the titles of ruler **Kaiser** in German and Tsar in Russian.

begriffe.erklaerung: A leader who commands a whole army in war.
That is what the Romans called the land of the Gauls, roughly present-day France.
In ancient Rome, a man who was allowed to decide almost alone in times of emergency.
The assembly of the most important politicians in ancient Rome.
A Celtic people who lived in the area of present-day Switzerland.

gewusst: Caesar was never emperor, although the word Kaiser comes from his name.
The Latin name Helvetia for Switzerland recalls the Helvetii, whom Caesar defeated.
The expression “to cross the Rubicon” still means taking a step that cannot be undone.

teile.einleitung: The denarius was the most important silver coin in ancient Rome. People used it to pay throughout the Roman Empire, including in the area of present-day Switzerland.
wichtigste: The denarius was a **Roman silver coin**.
The Latin word “denarius” means **containing ten**.
One denarius was worth **4 sestertii**.
The Roman gold coin was called the **aureus**.
On many coins the **emperor's head** could be seen.
Very many Roman coins were found in **Augusta Raurica**.
The currency **dinar** takes its name from the denarius.

abschnitte.text: The Romans introduced the **denarius** in the 3rd century BC. It was made of **silver** and was about as big as a modern 10 centime coin. The name comes from the Latin word “denarius”, which means **containing ten**. Originally a denarius was worth ten small bronze coins called **asses**. For centuries the denarius remained Rome's most important coin.

abschnitte.titel: How much was a denarius worth?
abschnitte.text: The Romans had several coins. One denarius was worth **4 sestertii**, the sestertius being a smaller coin. Worth even more was the gold coin, the **aureus**, which was worth 25 denarii. For a long time a denarius was roughly the daily wage of an ordinary worker. Later the emperors put less and less silver into the coins, so the denarius lost value.

On the front of many coins the **emperor's head** could be seen, with his name around it. That way people throughout the empire knew who was ruling. On the back there were often gods, temples or victories. Coins were therefore also a kind of advertising for the emperor. Today they help researchers to date finds.

In the area of present-day Switzerland too, people paid with Roman money. In **Augusta Raurica** at Augst and Kaiseraugst, near Basel, archaeologists have found a great many Roman coins. A famous silver treasure was also discovered there. You can see such finds in the museum at Augusta Raurica.

gewusst: The currency **dinar**, which exists today for example in Serbia and Jordan, takes its name from the denarius.
In Britain the symbol for the old penny was a “d”, the abbreviation for denarius.

teile.einleitung: The Julio-Claudian dynasty was the first imperial family of Rome. It included Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero. It ruled from 27 BC to 68 AD.
wichtigste: The dynasty begins with Augustus, the first Roman emperor.
He was followed in 14 AD by his stepson Tiberius.
Caligula was murdered by Praetorians in 41 AD.
Under Claudius the conquest of Britain began in 43 AD.
Under Nero a large part of Rome burned in 64 AD.
After Nero's death the Year of the Four Emperors followed in 69 AD.

abschnitte.text: The name of the dynasty comes from two families: the **Julii**, to whom Caesar and Augustus belonged, and the **Claudii**. **Augustus** became the first emperor in 27 BC. In his time, in **9 AD**, Germanic tribes under **Arminius** destroyed three legions in the **Battle of the Teutoburg Forest**. Augustus afterwards gave up the conquest of Germania as far as the Elbe. Under Augustus the Alps and the area of present-day Switzerland also came under Roman rule.

In **14 AD** **Tiberius** followed Augustus. He was his stepson and adopted son and ruled until 37 AD. From 26 AD he withdrew to the island of **Capri** and ruled from there. In Rome during this time his Praetorian prefect **Sejanus** gained great influence. The **Praetorians** were the emperor's bodyguard.

After Tiberius, **Caligula** became emperor. In January **41 AD** he was murdered by officers of the **Praetorian Guard**. The Guard then proclaimed his uncle **Claudius** emperor. In **43 AD** Claudius had troops land in **Britain** and travelled there briefly himself. From this came the province of **Britannia**.

The last emperor of the dynasty was **Nero**. In **64 AD** the **Great Fire of Rome** raged and destroyed large parts of the city. Nero put the blame on the **Christians** and had many of them persecuted. After the fire he had a huge palace built for himself, the Golden House. In 68 he lost the support of the army and the Senate and died.

abschnitte.titel: The Year of the Four Emperors
abschnitte.text: With Nero's death the Julio-Claudian dynasty ended. The **Year of the Four Emperors, 69 AD**, followed. In this year **Galba**, **Otho**, **Vitellius** and **Vespasian** fought one after another for power. Vespasian prevailed. He founded the **Flavian dynasty**, which later had the Colosseum built.

gewusst: The month of August is named after Emperor Augustus.
Claudius himself wrote history books, among other things about the Etruscans, but they are lost.

teile.einleitung: The Assyrian Empire existed in various phases over more than a thousand years. It began as a trading power and later became one of the largest empires of the ancient Near East. Its traces are found in reliefs, inscriptions and in the Bible.
wichtigste: In the 19th century BC, the city of Kanesh in Anatolia was the centre of Old Assyrian long-distance trade.
In 853 BC, Shalmaneser III fought at Qarqar against a coalition of kings.
The Black Obelisk shows the Israelite king Jehu before Shalmaneser III.
The kingdom of Urartu on Lake Van was a main rival of Assyria.
In 701 BC, Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem without taking the city.
Aramaic became the common language of the empire.
A last Assyrian rump state held out until 609 BC at Harran.

abschnitte.text: In the **Old Assyrian period**, Ashur was above all a trading city. In the 19th century BC, merchants travelled with donkey caravans as far as Anatolia, in present-day Turkey. The centre of this long-distance trade was the city of **Kanesh**. Mainly tin and textiles were traded. Thousands of clay tablets with letters and accounts of the merchants have been found there.

In the 9th century BC, King **Shalmaneser III** extended the power of Assyria to the west. In **853 BC** he fought at **Qarqar** in Syria against a **coalition** of Syrian and Israelite kings. A coalition is an alliance of several partners. The **Black Obelisk** is a monument from his time. It shows the Israelite king **Jehu** bowing before Shalmaneser.

In the north, on **Lake Van**, lay the kingdom of **Urartu**. In the 9th and 8th centuries BC, it was a main rival of Assyria. Later Assyria became a great power. In **701 BC**, King **Sennacherib** besieged the city of **Jerusalem**. But he did not take it, and the king there, Hezekiah, stayed in power. Assyrian inscriptions and the Bible report on this.

Many peoples lived in the empire. Besides Akkadian, **Aramaic** established itself as the **common language**, that is, a language in which everyone could communicate. The art of the Assyrians is famous. The reliefs from the North Palace of **Ashurbanipal** in **Nineveh** show the **royal lion hunt**. Hunting lions was seen as a sign that the king protects his subjects.

At the end of the 7th century BC, the empire was attacked by Babylonians and Medes. In 612 BC the capital Nineveh fell. A last **rump state**, that is, a small remnant of the empire, still held out at **Harran**. In **609 BC** it too fell. After that the Neo-Babylonian Empire took over supremacy.

gewusst: The Black Obelisk and the lion hunt reliefs are today in the British Museum in London.
The merchants' letters from Kanesh are among the oldest surviving business letters in the world.

teile.einleitung: Pandora's box is a well-known myth from ancient Greece. It tells how misfortune came into the world. The poet Hesiod wrote it down almost 2,700 years ago.
wichtigste: According to the myth, Pandora was the first woman.
Zeus sent her to humans with a jar.
He wanted to punish people because they had received fire.
Pandora was not allowed to open the jar.
When she did so anyway, all the evils of the world came out.
Only hope stayed behind.
In the oldest version the box was a large jar.

abschnitte.text: The Titan **Prometheus** had stolen **fire** from the gods and brought it to humans. The father of the gods, **Zeus**, was very angry about this. He wanted to **punish** humankind for it. Prometheus himself was chained to a rock as a punishment. For humans, Zeus thought up something different.

Zeus had **Pandora** created. According to the myth she was the **first woman**. The gods gave her many gifts, such as beauty and skill. Her name therefore means roughly “the one given all gifts”. Zeus sent her to humans with a **jar**. She must on no account **open** it.

Pandora was curious and opened the jar anyway. Out flew **all the evils of the world**: sickness, toil, worries and suffering. Before that, people had lived without these plagues. Pandora quickly shut the lid again. Only **hope** stayed behind in the jar. Some people read it this way: whatever happens, humans still have hope.

In the oldest version, by **Hesiod**, the container is a **large jar**, called a pithos in Greek. Only much later, in the 16th century, did it become a **box**. A scholar had translated the word inaccurately. Since then people have spoken of Pandora's box, although originally a jar was meant.

Today people say **“to open Pandora's box”**. They mean doing something that **causes a lot of trouble** which cannot be undone. You often hear the expression in newspapers, for example about dangerous decisions. So the old myth lives on in our language.

gewusst: The scholar who turned the jar into a box was Erasmus of Rotterdam, who also lived in Basel for a long time.
