A moon of the planet Saturn is called Pandora.

teile.einleitung: The gold bust of Marcus Aurelius is one of the most famous Roman finds in Switzerland. It was discovered in 1939 in Avenches, the old Aventicum, in the canton of Vaud.
wichtigste: The bust shows the Roman emperor **Marcus Aurelius**.
It is made mainly **of gold**.
It was found in **1939** in Avenches.
It lay **in an old sewer**.
It weighs **about 1.6 kg**.
The original is now kept **in a bank vault**.
Marcus Aurelius ruled **in the 2nd century AD**.

abschnitte.text: A **bust** is **a figure of the head and shoulders** of a person. The Romans set up busts of their emperors in many places. That way people throughout the empire could see who was ruling. Most busts were made of stone or bronze. A bust **made of gold** like the one from Avenches is very rare.

In **1939** archaeologists were digging in **Avenches** in the canton of Vaud. In Roman times **Aventicum**, the capital of the Helvetii, lay there. Near a temple they found the bust **in an old sewer**. Why it lay there is not known for certain. Perhaps someone had hidden it in troubled times.

The bust is made mainly **of gold** and weighs **about 1.6 kg**. It was beaten from a sheet of gold, that is, hammered into shape by hand. You can recognise the emperor by his curly hair and beard. Because it is so valuable, the original is now kept **in a bank vault**. In the Roman Museum in Avenches you can see an exact copy.

**Marcus Aurelius** ruled the Roman Empire **in the 2nd century AD**, from 161 to 180. He was not only an emperor but also a philosopher. He wrote down his thoughts in a book called the **“Meditations”**. It is about duty, calmness and a good life. During his reign he often had to fight on the borders of the empire.

gewusst: The gold bust is one of only a very few surviving gold portraits of emperors.
In Rome there is a famous bronze equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius.

teile.einleitung: The Ishtar Gate was a magnificent city gate of Babylon. It was built around 575 BC under King Nebuchadnezzar II and is decorated with bright blue glazed bricks.
wichtigste: The Ishtar Gate was a main gate in the city wall of Babylon.
It was built around 575 BC under Nebuchadnezzar II.
It is named after the goddess Ishtar.
The bricks are blue and covered with a glaze.
On the gate one sees bulls and dragons.
The Processional Way with pictures of lions led through the gate.

abschnitte.text: The Ishtar Gate was one of the main gates in the wall of **Babylon** in **Mesopotamia**. Babylon lay in present-day Iraq. Through this gate one entered the inner city from the **north**. King **Nebuchadnezzar II** had it built around **575 BC**. He made Babylon magnificent with walls, palaces and temples. The Ishtar Gate was the most beautiful gate of his city.

The bricks of the gate shine in a strong **blue**. They were covered with a **glaze**, a glass-like layer, and then fired. That is why they still gleam today. On the blue ground one sees pale and golden-yellow **animals**. The gate is named after **Ishtar**, an important goddess of Mesopotamia. She was the goddess of love and war.

On the gate one sees **bulls** and dragon-like **mythical creatures**. The bull was the animal of the weather god **Adad**. The dragon with a snake's head, called a mušḫuššu, belonged to **Marduk**, the chief god of Babylon. The animals stand in rows one above another. They were meant to show that the gods protected the city.

The **Processional Way** led through the gate. On it, at great festivals, **processions** moved in honour of the gods. The walls along the street were decorated with many **lions** made of coloured bricks. The lion was the animal of the goddess Ishtar. Anyone walking along this street was meant to feel the power of the king and the gods.

From **1899** a team from **Germany** excavated Babylon. The archaeologist **Robert Koldewey** led the work for many years. Thousands of pieces of the coloured bricks were found. They were taken to **Berlin** and put together there. In the **Pergamon Museum** the front part of the gate and parts of the Processional Way were rebuilt.

gewusst: The gate in the Berlin museum is only the smaller front part. The whole gate was much bigger and would not have fitted there.
In Babylon itself a reconstruction of the gate stands today for visitors.

teile.einleitung: Writing is one of the most important inventions of humankind. With it you can record knowledge, laws and stories so that they can still be read centuries later. One of the first scripts arose more than 5,000 years ago in Mesopotamia.
wichtigste: One of the first scripts in the world arose around 3300 BC in Mesopotamia.
The first signs were used mainly for bookkeeping and administration.
A pictogram shows an object as a simplified picture.
Writing arose independently in Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica.
In the early advanced civilisations, usually only a few trained scribes could read and write.
With writing, history begins for researchers; before that we speak of prehistory.
Our alphabet goes back through the Greeks and Romans to the Phoenicians.

abschnitte.text: In the first cities of **Mesopotamia** many people lived together, and temples managed large stores of supplies. To record how much grain, how many sheep or how much beer someone had handed over, people drew signs on **clay tablets**. The oldest such tablets come from the city of Uruk and are about 5,300 years old. So writing was first used for **bookkeeping** and administration; only later did people also write letters, laws and stories.

The first written signs were **pictograms**, that is, simplified pictures, such as a picture of an ear of grain for grain. Over time the signs became simpler and more abstract. Some soon stood no longer just for a thing, but for a **sound**. That made it possible to write names and words that cannot be drawn. In Mesopotamia this developed into cuneiform, in Egypt into hieroglyphs.

Writing was not invented just once. Scripts arose independently of each other in **Mesopotamia**, in **Egypt**, in **China** and in **Mesoamerica**. Chinese writing is more than 3,000 years old and is still used today in a developed form. In Mesoamerica the Maya, for example, wrote with picture signs.

Writing is one of the typical features of an **advanced civilisation**. Others include cities with administration, division of labour, rulers and great buildings. But only a few people could read and write, usually trained **scribes** who studied for many years. For historical research, writing is an important dividing line: what happened before is called **prehistory**, and after it history begins.

Around 1000 BC the **Phoenicians**, a trading people on the coast of present-day Lebanon, used a script with only about 22 letters. Each letter stood for a sound, which made learning much easier. The Greeks took over this **alphabet** and added signs for vowels. From the Greeks the script passed to the Etruscans and Romans, and from the Latin alphabet arose our script today.

When the first great pyramids were being built in Egypt, farmers in the area of present-day Switzerland lived in **pile-dwelling settlements** by the lakes. They did not yet know writing. Only the Celts occasionally used Greek letters. With the Romans, Latin script came to our country, and many inscriptions on stones survive to this day.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simple picture sign that shows an object.
A fixed series of letters that stand for individual sounds.
A culture with cities, writing, administration and division of labour.
The long time in human history before there were written sources.

gewusst: The word alphabet is made up of alpha and beta, the first two Greek letters.
We still use pictograms today, for example on toilet doors or road signs.
Some of the oldest written records in the world are not poems, but lists of supplies.

teile.einleitung: An amphora is a large vessel with two handles. In antiquity, Greeks and Romans used it above all to store and transport wine and olive oil. Many amphorae have survived to this day.
wichtigste: An amphora is a large vessel with two handles.
Amphorae were mostly made of clay.
Potters made them on the potter's wheel.
The Greeks often transported wine and olive oil in them.
Transport amphorae often had a point at the bottom so that they could be stuck in sand.
Many painted Greek vases are black and reddish brown.
Winners at the Panathenaic festival in Athens received amphorae full of olive oil.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from Greek and means roughly “carried on both sides”. For an amphora has **two handles**, one on each side. It has a bulging body and a narrow neck. It was made of **clay** that was fired in a kiln. This was done by **potters** in workshops of their own.

Amphorae were something like the crates and bottles of antiquity. In them people transported mainly **wine** and **olive oil**, but also grain or fish sauce. Many transport amphorae had a **point** at the bottom. In this way they could be stuck in **sand** or stacked tightly against one another in a ship. Divers still find old shipwrecks full of amphorae in the Mediterranean today.

Some amphorae were purely everyday vessels, others real works of art. Greek potters and painters decorated them with pictures of gods, heroes and scenes of everyday life. Typical colours are **black** and **reddish brown**. In the older **black-figure** painting, the figures are black on a reddish ground. In the later **red-figure** painting, it is the other way round.

In Athens, people celebrated the festival of the **Panathenaea** in honour of the goddess Athena. There were also sporting contests. The winners received **amphorae full of olive oil** as a prize. These prize amphorae showed the goddess Athena on one side and the sport on the other. Olive oil was very valuable at that time.

For archaeologists, amphorae and their sherds are very important. Shape and stamps often reveal where a vessel comes from and how old it is. In this way, old trade routes can be traced. In Roman settlements in Switzerland too, for example at **Augusta Raurica**, many amphora sherds have been found. They show that wine and oil from the south came across the Alps.

gewusst: In Rome there is a hill, Monte Testaccio, that consists almost entirely of millions of broken amphorae.
The Greek vessel called an amphora gave its name to a unit of measure: the Romans called a measure of capacity of about 26 litres an “amphora”.

teile.einleitung: Gladiators were fighters in ancient Rome who competed against each other in front of spectators in large arenas. For centuries their fights were one of the most popular forms of entertainment in the Roman Empire. The name comes from the Latin word gladius, which means sword.
wichtigste: Gladiators fought in front of an audience in an amphitheatre.
The word gladiator comes from the Latin word for sword.
Slaves and prisoners were often made into gladiators.
They were trained in gladiator schools, which belonged to a lanista.
The largest amphitheatre in Rome is the Colosseum, with room for about 50,000 people.
The gladiator Spartacus led a great slave revolt.
A Roman amphitheatre still stands in Avenches today.

abschnitte.text: The first gladiator fights took place in the 3rd century BC at the funerals of distinguished Romans. Later they became great **games** with which emperors and rich politicians thrilled the people. Many gladiators were **slaves**, prisoners of war or convicted criminals. But there were also free men who volunteered because they hoped for fame and money. Rarely, even women fought.

Gladiators lived and trained in a **gladiator school**. Their owner was called a **lanista**; he trained the fighters and hired them out to organisers. The gladiators received good food and medical care, because they were valuable. Not every fight ended in death; often a loser was allowed to live on if he had fought bravely. Anyone who survived many fights could receive a wooden sword as a sign of freedom.

There were many kinds of gladiator with different **equipment**. The **retiarius**, the net fighter, fought almost without armour, with a net and a trident. His frequent opponent was the secutor, with helmet, shield and sword. The murmillo wore a large helmet with a fish symbol. Usually two different types fought each other so that the fight stayed exciting.

The largest amphitheatre in Rome is the **Colosseum**, which was opened in AD 80. It had room for about 50,000 spectators, who had to sit according to their rank. Beneath the arena there were passages and lifts used to bring animals and scenery up. In the **animal hunts** some fighters also had to face wild animals such as lions, bears or leopards.

The most famous gladiator is **Spartacus**. He came from Thrace and in 73 BC escaped with other gladiators from a school in Capua. Many slaves joined them, and a great **slave revolt** arose. Only after about two years was the army of Spartacus defeated by Roman troops.

There were amphitheatres in the area of present-day Switzerland too. In **Avenches** in the canton of Vaud, the Roman Aventicum, a large amphitheatre still stands, where concerts and operas are held today. Smaller arenas existed, for example, at Vindonissa near Windisch and in Augusta Raurica. During the 5th century AD the gladiator fights came to an end, partly because the Christians rejected them.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sand-covered fighting area in the middle of an amphitheatre.
A round or oval building with rows of seats around an arena.
The owner of a gladiator school.
A gladiator who fought with a net and a trident.

gewusst: The word arena comes from the Latin word for sand, with which the fighting area was strewn.
Famous gladiators were real stars; their names were scribbled on house walls.
Whether a thumb pointing down really was the sign for death is disputed among experts.

teile.einleitung: In **spinning**, short fibres are twisted into a long thread. Even in the Stone Age, people spun threads, for example from the fibres of the flax plant. From these threads, cords, nets and fabrics could be made.
wichtigste: In spinning, fibres are twisted into a thread.
Flax is an important plant for fibres.
In retting, flax stalks are left to rot in the dew or in water.
The hackle is used to clean and align the fibres.
In a cave in Georgia, flax fibres over 30,000 years old were found.

abschnitte.text: The fibres sit in the stalk of the flax plant. First the stalks are left lying in the dew on the meadow or in water. In this process, the parts that hold the fibres together **rot**. This step is called **retting**. After that, the woody parts are broken off and the fibres are pulled through the **hackle**, a tool with many sharp teeth like a comb. In this way the fibres become clean and lie neatly ordered.

For spinning, you took a bundle of fibres and drew out a few of them. With a **spindle**, a stick with a heavy ring, they were twisted. Through the twisting, the fibres hold together and become a firm **thread**. The rings of clay or stone, the **spindle whorls**, are often found in excavations, including in the pile-dwelling settlements of Switzerland.

In a cave in **Georgia**, flax fibres were found that are over **30,000 years** old. Some of them were even dyed. This shows that people were already working with fibres in the Old Stone Age. Later, in the New Stone Age, farmers grew flax in their fields and wove fabrics from it.

gewusst: To this day, linen is made from flax, a cool and strong fabric.

teile.einleitung: A **torc** is a neck ring that was worn above all by the Celts. It is open at the front and often made of gold, silver or bronze. In Switzerland, the **Erstfeld gold treasure** in the canton of Uri is a famous find with such neck rings.
wichtigste: A torc is a neck ring that is open at the front.
Among the Celts, important people wore it.
In 1962, building workers at Erstfeld in the canton of Uri found a gold treasure.
The treasure includes 4 neck rings.
One neck ring weighs about 125 grams.
The treasure is today in the Swiss National Museum in Zurich.
The statue “The Dying Gaul” shows a Celt with a torc.

abschnitte.text: A **torc** is a stiff **neck ring**. It is **open at the front**, and the two ends are often thickened and beautifully decorated. It was put on by bending it slightly apart. The name comes from the Latin word for “to twist”, because many rings are made of twisted metal rods.

Among the **Celts**, **important people** wore a torc, such as leaders and warriors. It showed rank and standing. Gods too were shown with a torc. The famous statue **“The Dying Gaul”** shows a wounded Celt wearing a torc around his neck. It stands today in Rome.

In **1962**, **building workers** at **Erstfeld** in the canton of **Uri** found a treasure of gold. It lay under a large stone on the hillside. The treasure includes **4 neck rings** and some arm rings. One neck ring weighs about **125 grams**. The rings are decorated with fine figures of people and animals. It is thought that the treasure was hidden or given as a gift to a deity.

Today you can see the Erstfeld gold treasure in the **Swiss National Museum in Zurich**. It is among the most beautiful goldwork of the Celts. The find site lies on the way to the Gotthard. This shows that people were already using this Alpine route over 2,000 years ago.

gewusst: The Erstfeld gold treasure is about 2,300 years old.
The Romans took over the torc and awarded it as a distinction to brave soldiers.

teile.einleitung: The Maya were careful observers of the sky and had several calendars at once. A solar year, a sacred calendar and a long count of days meshed like cogwheels.
wichtigste: The Maya solar year is called the Haab and had 365 days.
It consisted of 18 months of 20 days each, that is 360 days, and 5 extra days.
The five extra days were regarded as unlucky days.
The sacred calendar is called the Tzolkin and had 260 days.
After 52 years both calendars fell on the same day again, which is the Calendar Round.
The Maya observed Venus especially closely.

abschnitte.text: The Maya solar year is called the **Haab**. It had **365 days**, almost as many as our year. It was divided into **18 months** of **20 days** each. 18 times 20 makes 360 days. At the end of the year there were also **five extra days**. These days belonged to no month and were regarded as **unlucky days**. Many people were especially careful on them.

Besides the solar year there was the sacred calendar **Tzolkin** with **260 days**. It arises when one combines 13 numbers with 20 day names, since 13 times 20 is 260. Each day thus had a number and a name. With this calendar the priests determined **festivals and rituals** and good days for important events. Counting in twenties fits the number system of the Maya.

The Haab and the Tzolkin ran side by side at the same time, like two cogwheels of different sizes. Only after **52 years** did both calendars fall on the same starting day again. This period is called the **Calendar Round**. For the Maya the end of a Calendar Round was an important moment. To record longer periods they also used the **Long Count**, which counts the days since a starting date in large units.

The Maya observed the sky very closely. Especially important to them was **Venus**, which shines brightly in the morning or evening sky. They calculated its course astonishingly accurately and wrote the results down in **books** made of bark paper. One of the few surviving Maya books, the **Dresden Codex**, contains such Venus tables and tables of eclipses. It is today in Dresden.

On **21 December 2012** a great period of the Long Count ended. Some people therefore believed that the world would end on that day. But **nothing special** happened. For the Maya the end of a period simply meant that a new one began, just as with us a new year begins after 31 December. Researchers had already explained beforehand that the Maya had not predicted an end of the world.

gewusst: The Calendar Round of 52 years comprises 18,980 days.
Only very few of the Maya books survive, and one of them is in Dresden.
Some Maya in Guatemala still count the days of the 260-day calendar today.

teile.einleitung: In ancient Egypt cats were useful helpers and much-loved animals. They were even linked with a goddess and often mummified after death.
wichtigste: Cats hunted the mice and rats that ate the grain.
They also kept poisonous snakes away from the houses.
The cat goddess was called Bastet, and her most important temple stood in Bubastis.
The Egyptian word for cat sounded roughly like “miu”.
Many thousands of cat mummies have been found.
Our house cats descend from the African wildcat.

abschnitte.text: The Egyptians lived from farming and stored a lot of grain in **granaries**. Mice and rats liked to feast there too. Cats hunted these animals and so protected the stores. That is why they were very popular with **farmers**. Cats also hunted poisonous **snakes** and made the house safer.

abschnitte.titel: Where the house cat comes from
abschnitte.text: Our house cats descend from the **African wildcat**. This wildcat lives in Africa and Arabia. Because there were many mice near people, the cats came ever closer. In time they became tame and lived together with people. The Egyptians called the cat roughly **“miu”**, which sounds like a miaow.

The cat was the sacred animal of the goddess **Bastet**. Bastet was often shown as a woman with a cat's head or as a sitting cat. Her most important temple stood in the city of **Bubastis** in the Nile Delta. There great festivals were held in her honour. Many people wore small cat figures as lucky charms.

When a cat died, the family mourned. The Greek historian **Herodotus** reported that the family then **shaved off their eyebrows**. Many cats were embalmed like people and wrapped in cloths. Researchers found many thousands of such **cat mummies**. Some were laid down in temples as an offering for the goddess.

gewusst: The Egyptian word “miu” for cat is an imitation of the sound, just like our “miaow”.
There are coffins and figures of bronze that were made specially for cat mummies.

teile.einleitung: A **spear-thrower** is a throwing stick with which you can throw a spear much further and harder. It acts like an extension of the arm. People of the late Old Stone Age used it for hunting.
wichtigste: A spear-thrower makes the spear fly further.
It has a hook at one end for the spear.
It makes the arm longer when throwing.
You no longer had to get so close to the animal, which was safer.
Many spear-throwers were made of reindeer antler and decorated with animals.
The oldest in Europe date from the late Old Stone Age.
It is also called an atlatl, and in Australia a woomera.

abschnitte.text: The spear-thrower is a stick with a **hook** at one end. The rear end of the spear is laid in this hook. When throwing, you hold the thrower fast at the other end. It **lengthens the arm** like a lever. As a result the spear gets more momentum and **flies further**.

With the spear-thrower you could hit from a greater distance. Hunters **did not have to get so close** to dangerous or shy animals. That made hunting **safer** and more successful. Animals hunted included reindeer and wild horses.

The oldest known spear-throwers in Europe date from the **late Old Stone Age**. Many were carved from **reindeer antler**. Some are real works of art: **animals** are carved on them, such as horses, ibexes or birds. Such pieces were found mainly in France.

Spear-throwers existed on several continents. In America it is known by the name **atlatl**, a word from the language of the Aztecs. The Aboriginal people of Australia call their spear-thrower a **woomera**. In Europe it was later largely replaced by the **bow and arrow**.

gewusst: With a spear-thrower, a practised thrower can throw a spear much further than with the hand alone.
Today there are competitions in which people throw at targets with the atlatl.

teile.einleitung: The Mausoleum of Halicarnassus was the magnificent tomb of King Mausolus. It is one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and gave its name to all great tomb buildings.
wichtigste: The Mausoleum was the tomb of King Mausolus, who died in 353 BC.
His wife Artemisia had it finished.
It was about 45 metres high.
Halicarnassus is the present-day city of Bodrum in Turkey.
Knights later used its stones for a castle.
Many figures are today in the British Museum in London.

abschnitte.text: **Mausolus** ruled over the region of **Caria** on the coast of Asia Minor. His capital was **Halicarnassus**. Today the city is called **Bodrum** and lies in **Turkey**. Mausolus died in **353 BC**. His wife **Artemisia** mourned him greatly and saw to it that his tomb continued to be built.

The **Mausoleum** was a magnificent **tomb** in which the dead king lay. It was about **45 metres** high. On a high base stood columns, and above them a stepped pyramid. At the very top stood a **chariot with four horses** of stone. Famous Greek **sculptors** decorated the building with statues and reliefs. That is why it was counted among the **Seven Wonders**.

The tomb of Mausolus was so famous that magnificent tomb buildings are today called a **mausoleum**. So the word comes directly from the name of the king. All over the world there are mausoleums for rulers and famous people. A well-known example is the Taj Mahal in India.

In the **Middle Ages** the Mausoleum was badly damaged by earthquakes. The **Knights of St John**, a knightly order, later built a **castle** in Bodrum. For this they took stones from the ruined tomb. In the **19th century** researchers took statues and reliefs to England. They are now displayed in the **British Museum** in London.

gewusst: In the walls of the castle of the Knights of St John in Bodrum one can still recognise stones from the Mausoleum today.
The Mausoleum stood much longer than the Colossus of Rhodes, namely well over 1,000 years.

teile.einleitung: Homer is the most famous poet of ancient Greece. The two great epics, the Iliad and the Odyssey, are attributed to him. But almost nothing is known for certain about his life.
wichtigste: Homer composed in an old form of Greek.
His works arose about 2,700 years ago.
The Iliad tells of the war over Troy, the Odyssey of the wanderings of Odysseus.
The stories were first passed on by telling and singing.
The Iliad and the Odyssey each have 24 books.
His birthplace is not known for certain.

abschnitte.text: Experts think that Homer's works arose in the **8th or 7th century BC**, so about **2,700 years ago**. Several places claimed that Homer came from there, for example **Smyrna** and the island of **Chios**. It is not known for certain. Even in ancient times Homer was imagined as a **blind singer**. Some researchers even ask whether he existed as a single person at all.

The stories were first passed on **orally**. **Singers** recited the long poems by heart and often accompanied themselves on a stringed instrument. Only later were they **written down**. The verses follow a fixed rhythm, the **hexameter**. Repeated phrases such as “rosy-fingered Dawn” helped with remembering.

The title “**Iliad**” means poem about **Ilion**, another name for **Troy**. The Iliad tells of a few weeks in the **Trojan War**. At its centre stand the hero **Achilles** and his anger. The Iliad has more than **15,000 lines of verse**. Anyone who wanted to recite it all needed many hours.

The **Odyssey** tells of **Odysseus**, who after the war wanders for ten years on his way home. On the way he meets giants, sorceresses and monsters until at last he returns to **Ithaca**. Because he wandered for so long, any long, wearisome journey is now called an **odyssey**. Both works begin with a plea to the **Muse**, a goddess of poetry.

Scholars in **Alexandria** divided the Iliad and the Odyssey into **24 books** each. This matches the number of letters in the **Greek alphabet**. Homer's works were very important to the Greeks, and children learned to read with them. To this day they are read in many schools and translated into many languages.

gewusst: The Iliad does not tell of the wooden horse at all. Only the Odyssey mentions it briefly.
The Iliad and the Odyssey are among the oldest surviving works of European literature.

teile.einleitung: The Indus Civilisation was one of the first great advanced civilisations in the world. It lay on the river Indus in present-day Pakistan and in north-western India and flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BC.
wichtigste: The Indus Civilisation flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BC.
After the site of Harappa it is also called the Harappan Civilisation.
Large cities were Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro.
Its script has still not been deciphered.
Typical finds are small soapstone seals with animals.
Standardised stone weights show regulated trade.

abschnitte.text: The people of the Indus Civilisation built large cities such as **Harappa** and **Mohenjo-Daro**. Harappa was the first city to be excavated, so people also speak of the **Harappan Civilisation**. The streets were often laid out at **right angles**. Many houses were built of fired **bricks**. There were wells and **drains**, which was very advanced for that time.

The great cities flourished from about **2600 to 1900 BC**. So the Indus Civilisation was about the same age as the **Old Kingdom** in Egypt and the cities of **Mesopotamia**. Its territory was larger than that of these two civilisations. It carried on **trade** with Mesopotamia. Cuneiform texts name a distant trading land, **Meluhha**, which is usually identified with the Indus Valley.

Typical finds are small, square **soapstone seals**. They show animals, often a **unicorn-like bull**, and written signs. Merchants probably pressed them into clay to mark goods. Thousands of short inscriptions in the **Indus script** are known. But so far nobody has deciphered it. To this day it is a great **mystery**.

In many places **cube-shaped weights** of stone were found. Over a wide area they follow the same steps, first in doublings, then at larger values in tens. This points to a standardised **system of weights** and regulated trade over long distances. At **Lothal** in present-day Gujarat there is a large basin built of brick. Many researchers see in it a **dock** for ships, others a water tank.

From about **1900 BC** the great cities were gradually abandoned. Why is not entirely clear. **Climate change** is discussed in particular: the **monsoon rains** weakened, and rivers shifted or dried up. But the people did not vanish. They carried on living in smaller villages.

gewusst: In Mohenjo-Daro there is a large water tank of brick that is called the “Great Bath”.
The ruins of Mohenjo-Daro are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: In ancient Greece there was no compulsory schooling as there is today. In Athens, parents who could afford it sent their sons to teachers. They learned reading, writing, music and sport.
wichtigste: Boys in Athens started school at about 7 years old.
A servant, the paedagogus, went with them to school.
The pupils often wrote on wax tablets with a stylus.
Many learned to play the lyre.
Young Greeks did sport in the gymnasium.
Most girls learned spinning and weaving at home.
The Greek word that “school” comes from meant “free time”.

abschnitte.text: In **Athens** boys started school at **about 7 years old**. The parents paid the teachers themselves. So mainly children from well-off families could learn. A servant, often a slave, went with them on the way. He was called a **paedagogus**, which means “boy leader”. He looked after the boy and made sure he behaved well.

For writing, the pupils used **wax tablets**. These were small wooden boards with a layer of wax. Letters were scratched into it with a pointed **stylus**. With the flat end you could smooth them out again. The pupils also learned long passages from the works of **Homer** by heart. They also practised arithmetic.

A separate teacher taught the boys music. Many learned to play the **lyre**, a stringed instrument, and to sing along. Sport was just as important. In the **gymnasium** young Greeks practised running, jumping, wrestling, and throwing the discus and the javelin. A healthy body was thought to be just as important as a lively mind.

Most **girls** in Athens did not go to school. They learned **at home** from their mothers. This included **spinning**, **weaving** and running a household. Some also learned a little reading and writing. In **Sparta** it was different: girls did sport there too, and the boys were brought up strictly by the state.

Our word **“school”** comes from the Greek word **“schole”**. It originally meant **“free time”** or leisure. For the Greeks, learning was something you did in your free time, when you did not have to work. The word **gymnasium** also comes from Greek. In Switzerland a Gymnasium is now a school that leads to the Matura, the school-leaving exam.

gewusst: Older pupils in Athens could later continue learning with philosophers such as Plato at the Academy.
The word “pedagogy”, for the study of teaching, comes from the companion on the way to school.

teile.einleitung: The Maya built large cities with pyramids, palaces and plazas in Central America. Their buildings still stand today in Mexico, Guatemala and the neighbouring countries and show how much the Maya knew about mathematics and the sky.
wichtigste: The Maya lived in present-day Mexico, in Guatemala and in neighbouring countries, that is, in Central America.
Their pyramids are stepped pyramids with steep stairways.
On top of the pyramids there was often a small temple for ceremonies.
Chichén Itzá in Mexico is one of the most famous Maya cities.
Beside the pyramids lay courts for a ball game with a heavy rubber ball.
Many Maya cities were overgrown by the rainforest.

abschnitte.text: The pyramids of the Maya are **stepped pyramids**: they consist of several large steps lying one above another. A steep stairway leads right to the top. There often stood a small **temple**, in which priests held ceremonies for the gods. Unlike in Egypt, the pyramids were therefore above all stages for religious festivals. Some pyramids were built over older ones, like one bowl over another.

abschnitte.titel: Chichén Itzá and the shadow serpent
abschnitte.text: In **Chichén Itzá** on the Yucatán Peninsula stands the great pyramid of Kukulcán, which is also called El Castillo. It has four stairways with 91 steps each and one more step at the top, **365** in all, as many as the year has days. In spring and autumn the sun in the afternoon casts shadows on the edge of the stairway. Then it looks as if a **serpent** is crawling down the pyramid. At the foot of the stairway stone serpent heads can be seen.

Beside pyramids and palaces the Maya built **ball courts**. These were long, narrow fields with high walls on both sides. The game was played with a heavy **rubber ball** that one was not allowed to touch with the hands but, for example, hit with the hip. On some walls stone rings hang high up. The ball game was not only sport but also had a religious meaning.

Many Maya cities lie in the tropical **rainforest**, for example **Tikal** in Guatemala or Palenque in Mexico. After the inhabitants had left many cities, trees and plants grew over the buildings. Some pyramids then looked like wooded hills. Even today researchers discover new ruins in the jungle, often with laser measurements from aircraft that map the ground through the leaf canopy.

The Maya built with **limestone**, which was plentiful in their region. They had no metal tools for building, no draught animals and did not use the wheel for loads. Even so they raised huge buildings. The walls were plastered with stucco and often painted in colour, frequently in red. For roofs and rooms they used a **corbel vault**: the stones project further and further from both sides until they almost meet at the top.

gewusst: The steps of the pyramid of Chichén Itzá add up to 365, as many as the days of a year.
The shadow serpent appears around the equinox in March and in September.
Many Maya ruins are today UNESCO World Heritage Sites, including Chichén Itzá and Tikal.

teile.einleitung: Hieroglyphs are the written characters of ancient Egypt. They look like little pictures of birds, eyes, snakes or tools, but stand for words and sounds. For over 3,000 years, the Egyptians wrote with them, after which nobody could read them any more, until they were deciphered in 1822.
wichtigste: The Greek word hieroglyphs means sacred carvings.
Hieroglyphs can stand for words, for sounds or as determinatives.
Names of pharaohs are written in an oval frame, the cartouche.
For everyday texts on papyrus, scribes used a simplified script, Hieratic.
The Rosetta Stone helped with the decipherment.
Jean-François Champollion deciphered the hieroglyphs in 1822.
Hieroglyphs could be written from right to left, from left to right or from top to bottom.

abschnitte.text: The first hieroglyphs arose around 3200 BC in Egypt. The name comes from Greek and means **sacred carvings**, because they were seen above all in temples and tombs. In the classical period there were about 700 different signs, later many more. The last known inscription in hieroglyphs dates from AD 394 and comes from the island of **Philae**. After that, the script fell into oblivion.

Hieroglyphs are not a pure picture script. Some signs stand for a whole word, others for one or several **sounds**. Vowels such as a, e or i were usually not written, only the consonants. At the end of a word there was often a **determinative**, which shows which group the word belongs to, such as a little man for persons. The reading direction can be seen from the animals and people, because they face the beginning of the line.

Only a few people could read and write, above all the trained **scribes**. They learned for many years in scribal schools. For letters, lists and contracts on **papyrus**, they used a faster cursive script, **Hieratic**. Later still, a further shorthand arose, Demotic. They wrote with rushes and with black and red ink.

In 1799, French soldiers found a black block of stone near the town of Rosetta in the Nile delta. On the **Rosetta Stone**, the same text is written in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. Because scholars could read Greek, they had in it a key to the unknown script. Today the stone is on display in the **British Museum** in London, where it is among the most visited exhibits.

The Frenchman **Jean-François Champollion** compared the names in the **cartouches** with the Greek names Ptolemy and Cleopatra. In this way he found out which signs stand for which sounds. In 1822 he presented his decipherment. He recognised that the script mixes picture signs and sound signs. Since then, experts, the Egyptologists, have been able to read the inscriptions again.

begriffe.erklaerung: An oval frame in which the names of the pharaohs were written.
A sign at the end of a word that shows which group a word belongs to.
A simplified cursive script of the Egyptian scribes for everyday use.
The science that deals with ancient Egypt.

gewusst: Champollion is said to have fainted from excitement after his discovery.
The Rosetta Stone contains a decree of priests in honour of King Ptolemy V.
The sign for the number one million shows a man raising his arms in amazement.

teile.einleitung: The Kingdom of Israel was the northern kingdom of the Israelites in the ancient Near East. According to the Bible it arose after the death of King Solomon and lasted until its conquest by the Assyrians in 722 BC.
wichtigste: According to the Bible the kingdom split after Solomon's death into Israel and Judah.
Israel was the northern kingdom, Judah the southern kingdom.
According to the Bible, ten of the twelve tribes belonged to the northern kingdom.
The capital was Samaria, founded by King Omri.
In 722 BC the Assyrian Empire conquered the northern kingdom.

abschnitte.text: According to the **Bible**, King **Solomon** ruled over all the tribes of Israel. After his death the northern tribes refused to recognise his son as king. So around **926 BC** two kingdoms arose: the **northern kingdom of Israel** and the **southern kingdom of Judah**. According to the Bible, **ten** of the twelve tribes belonged to the northern kingdom. The northern kingdom was larger and more fertile than Judah.

In the **9th century BC** King **Omri** founded the city of **Samaria** as the new capital. It remained so until the end of the northern kingdom. Omri is also mentioned in an inscription outside the Bible, on the **Mesha Stele** from the land of Moab. Excavations in Samaria show remains of a large palace.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the northern kingdom
abschnitte.text: In the 8th century BC the **Assyrian Empire** in present-day Iraq became very powerful. In **722 BC** it conquered Samaria. Part of the population was **deported**, and the area became a province of the conquerors. Because these tribes then disappeared from history, people speak of the **“lost tribes”**.

gewusst: Many legends still surround the “lost ten tribes”.
The name Samaria lives on in the word “Samaritan”, known from a parable in the New Testament.

teile.einleitung: The Han dynasty ruled China from 206 BC to AD 220. In this time China became a strong state with officials, trade along the Silk Road and important inventions.
wichtigste: The Han ruled for more than 400 years, at about the same time as the Roman Empire.
The founder was Liu Bang, who is called Emperor Gaozu.
The capital was first Chang'an, later Luoyang.
Emperor Wu made Confucianism the basis of the state.
Wang Mang interrupted their rule, which is why we speak of the Western and Eastern Han.
The largest ethnic group in China is still called the Han Chinese today.

abschnitte.text: After the rapid collapse of the **Qin empire**, several leaders fought for power. **Liu Bang**, who came from a humble background, won out. As emperor he is called **Gaozu**. The capital of the **Western Han** was **Chang'an**, present-day Xi'an. The **Eastern Han** later ruled from **Luoyang**.

**Emperor Wu**, also called Han Wudi, ruled for more than 50 years. He made the teaching of **Confucius** the basis of the state. He founded an academy where future **officials** studied the Confucian writings. Confucianism then shaped China for about 2,000 years. To pay for his campaigns, Emperor Wu put **salt and iron** under a state **monopoly**: only the state was allowed to produce and sell them.

Under the Han the envoy **Zhang Qian** travelled far to the west. After that trade routes arose that were later called the **Silk Road**. The scholar **Sima Qian** wrote the “Records of the Grand Historian”, a model for all later history books in China. **Zhang Heng** invented a **seismoscope** with eight dragons in the year 132. **Paper** was also developed and improved in the Han period.

In AD 9 the official **Wang Mang** seized power and founded the Xin dynasty. After his fall in AD 23 the Han returned. That is why we speak of the **Western** and **Eastern Han**. In 184 peasants rose up in the **Yellow Turban Rebellion** against hunger and abuses. The generals who put it down became very powerful. In 220 the empire broke up into three parts.

The Han period is regarded in China as one of the most important eras. That is why the largest population group of China still calls itself the **Han Chinese**. The Chinese characters are also called **Hanzi**, that is, “Han characters”. In Japan they are called kanji, which goes back to the same word.

gewusst: Zhang Heng's seismoscope is said to have indicated a quake that nobody in the capital had felt. Days later a messenger arrived with the news.
In 81 BC officials and scholars argued in a famous debate about the salt and iron monopoly.

teile.einleitung: Attila was king of the Huns in the 5th century. He led a people of horsemen who frightened large parts of Europe. He is still a well-known figure in history and legends today.
wichtigste: Attila first shared the rule over the Huns with his brother Bleda.
Later he ruled alone.
In 451 he was stopped by the Romans and Visigoths on the Catalaunian Plains.
In 452 he met Pope Leo I in northern Italy and then withdrew.
Christian writers later called him the “Scourge of God”.
In the Nibelungenlied he is called Etzel.

abschnitte.text: The **Huns** were a people of horsemen from the steppes of Asia. They came to Europe in the 4th century. Attila first ruled together with his brother **Bleda**. After Bleda's death he ruled alone. His empire lay mainly in the area of present-day Hungary. He demanded large payments in gold from the Eastern Roman Empire.

In the year **451** Attila marched with a large army to Gaul, in present-day France. On the **Catalaunian Plains** the **Romans** and **Visigoths** stood against him. The Roman commander was called Aetius. The battle cost many lives and ended without a clear winner. But Attila had to withdraw. In **452** he marched into **northern Italy**. There he met **Pope Leo I** and then broke off the campaign.

Attila died unexpectedly in 453, and soon afterwards his empire fell apart. **Christian writers** later called him the **“Scourge of God”**. They saw in him a punishment for the sins of humankind. In the medieval **Nibelungenlied** he appears as King **Etzel**. There he is not a figure of terror, but a rather mild ruler.

gewusst: The first name Attila is still common in Hungary today.

teile.einleitung: Herodotus was a Greek writer in the 5th century BC. He wrote a great work about the Persian Wars and many peoples, and is regarded as the “father of history”.
wichtigste: Herodotus lived from about 484 to 425 BC.
He came from Halicarnassus, present-day Bodrum in Turkey.
His work is called the “Histories”, which means roughly “inquiries”.
The Persian Wars are at its centre.
Cicero called him the “father of history”.
He collected a great deal of information on journeys and in conversations.

abschnitte.text: Herodotus was born around **484 BC** in **Halicarnassus**. The city in **Asia Minor** is now called **Bodrum** and lies in Turkey. At that time it was ruled by the **Persian Empire**. Later Herodotus lived for a long time in **Athens**. He died around 425 BC. So he wrote only a few decades after the events he reported.

The great work of Herodotus is called the “**Histories**”, which means roughly “inquiries”. He wanted to record what people had done so that it would not be forgotten. The **Persian Wars**, the struggles of the Greeks against the Persian Empire, are at its centre. They include battles such as **Marathon**, **Thermopylae** and **Salamis**. Later scholars divided the work into **nine books** and named each after one of the nine **Muses**. The first book is called Clio.

Herodotus travelled a great deal, among other places to **Egypt** and the **Black Sea**. He questioned people and wrote down what they told him. Sometimes he added that he did not himself believe everything. Of Egypt he said that the country was a “**gift of the river**”. By this he meant that the **Nile**, with its yearly flood, brought fertile mud.

Herodotus described not only wars but also the **customs** and ways of life of many peoples. In the fourth book he tells in detail of the **Scythians**, a people of horsemen north of the Black Sea. He also reports on the unsuccessful campaign of the Persian king **Darius** against them. So his work is an important source for the history and ethnography of ancient times.

The Roman orator **Cicero** called Herodotus “**pater historiae**”, that is, father of history. Herodotus was one of the first to collect events, arrange them and ask about their **causes**. Some of his stories are regarded today as legends or exaggerations. Even so, researchers still read his work today, because it contains a lot of knowledge about his time.

gewusst: The word “history” goes back to the title of Herodotus' work.
Herodotus describes Babylon in detail, but does not mention the famous Hanging Gardens.

teile.einleitung: **Stratigraphy** is the study of the layers in the ground. Archaeologists and geologists read the layers like the pages of a book. From them they can tell what came about earlier and what came later.
wichtigste: In undisturbed deposits, the lowest layer is as a rule the oldest.
This rule is called the law of superposition.
Nicolaus Steno was the first to describe it, in the 17th century.
Stratigraphy alone gives a relative dating.
The vertical wall of an excavation is called a section.
The Harris matrix shows the time sequence of all layers.
Because digging destroys layers, everything is documented exactly.

abschnitte.text: Over time, layers are deposited in the ground: earth, sand, ash or rubbish. What was there first lies at the bottom. What is added later lies above it. So in an **undisturbed** deposit, the **lowest layer is the oldest**. This rule is called the **law of superposition**.

The Danish natural scientist **Nicolaus Steno** was the first to describe this law of the sequence of layers, in the **17th century**. He observed layers of rock and recognised that they had been formed one after another. His ideas are still a foundation of geology and archaeology today.

Stratigraphy tells which layer is **older** and which is **younger**. But it gives no dates in years. This is called a **relative dating**. To know how old a layer is in years, other methods are needed in addition, for example radiocarbon dating or the tree rings of wood.

In an excavation, archaeologists cut a vertical wall into the ground. This wall is called a **section**, and in it you can see the layers like stripes. The **Harris matrix** is a diagram that shows the time sequence of all **layers and features** clearly. Because excavation **destroys** the layers, every layer is documented exactly with **drawings, photographs and measurements**.

gewusst: Pits, graves or animal burrows can disturb the sequence of layers, and archaeologists have to watch out for this especially.
The Harris matrix is named after the archaeologist Edward Harris, who developed it in the 1970s.

teile.einleitung: The Library of Alexandria was the most famous library of ancient times. It stood in the city of Alexandria in Egypt and collected writings from many countries. Important scholars carried out research there.
wichtigste: The most famous library of ancient times stood in Alexandria in Egypt.
It was founded by the Ptolemies, the Greek rulers of Egypt.
The texts were written on papyrus scrolls.
Papyrus is made from a plant.
Books on ships that arrived in Alexandria were copied.
The first head was Zenodotus, and the poet Callimachus compiled a huge catalogue.
The old library is lost; in 2002 a new large library opened.

abschnitte.text: After the death of Alexander the Great, Greek kings, the **Ptolemies**, ruled in Egypt. In the 3rd century BC they founded a great library in **Alexandria**. It belonged to the **Museion**, a research centre for scholars. The kings wanted to collect as much of the world's knowledge as possible. They spent a great deal of money on it.

The texts were not bound into books but written on **papyrus scrolls**. **Papyrus** is made from a **plant** that grows along the Nile. The pith was cut into strips, laid crosswise on top of each other and pressed. Exactly how many scrolls the library owned is not known. Ancient sources speak of hundreds of thousands.

Alexandria was an important **port city**. One story tells that when a ship arrived with books, they were seized and **copied**. The library often kept the original, and the owners got a copy. In this way the collection kept growing. Works from other languages were also translated into Greek.

The first head of the library was **Zenodotus**. He worked on reliable versions of the works of Homer. The poet **Callimachus** compiled the **“Pinakes”**, a huge catalogue of books and their authors. The scholar **Eratosthenes** calculated the **size of the Earth** with astonishing accuracy. To do this he compared the position of the Sun in two places in Egypt.

The old library has **not survived**. Exactly how it disappeared is still unclear. It was probably lost bit by bit over a long time, through fires, wars and lack of money. In **2002** a **new large library** opened in Alexandria, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina. It recalls the famous original.

gewusst: Eratosthenes was one of the first to use the word “geography”.
The roof of the new library of Alexandria is slanted like a disc rising out of the sea.

teile.einleitung: The Egyptian pyramids are huge tombs that were built over 4,500 years ago for the pharaohs. The most famous is the Great Pyramid of Khufu (Cheops) at Giza, the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still stands today. To this day, people marvel at how such mighty structures could be built without modern machines.
wichtigste: The great pyramids were tombs for pharaohs.
The oldest great pyramid is the Step Pyramid of Djoser, planned by the architect Imhotep.
The largest pyramid at Giza was built by Pharaoh Khufu.
The Great Pyramid was originally about 146 metres high.
On the Giza plateau stand three great pyramids.
Next to them lies the Great Sphinx with a lion's body and a human head.
Most pyramids stand on the west bank of the Nile.

abschnitte.text: The Egyptians believed that the **pharaoh** ascended to the gods after his death. His body was buried as a mummy in a burial chamber deep inside the pyramid. Treasures, furniture and food for life in the afterlife were placed with him. Most pyramids stand on the **west bank** of the Nile, because the sun sets there, and for the Egyptians the realm of the dead lay there. In the whole of Egypt, over a hundred pyramids are known today.

Around 2650 BC, the architect **Imhotep** planned a completely new tomb for Pharaoh Djoser at Saqqara. He stacked six ever smaller steps of stone on top of one another. In this way the **Step Pyramid of Djoser** arose, the oldest great pyramid of Egypt. Imhotep was later even worshipped as a god of healing. A little later, the Egyptians built pyramids with smooth sides.

On the plateau of **Giza** near Cairo stand three great pyramids, those of the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure. The **Great Pyramid** was finished around 2560 BC and was originally about 146 metres high. Today it is somewhat lower, because the tip and the smooth casing of white limestone are missing. It consists of over two million blocks of stone, many of them heavier than a car. For over 3,800 years it was the tallest structure in the world.

In front of the pyramids lies the **Great Sphinx**, a huge figure with a lion's body and a human head. It is about 73 metres long and about 20 metres high and was cut directly out of the rock. Many researchers believe that its face shows Pharaoh Khafre. For a long time it was buried up to the neck in desert sand.

In the past, people thought slaves had built the pyramids. Today we know that they were **organised workers** who received pay in the form of bread, beer and meat. Archaeologists found their living quarters, bakeries and graves near Giza. The blocks of stone were moved with sledges and **ramps**, and on the Nile, stones came by boat from distant quarries. Exactly what the ramps looked like is still being researched.

The Great Pyramid is the oldest and only still standing of the **Seven Wonders of the Ancient World**. The pyramids of Giza have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 1979. Every year, millions of people from all over the world visit the site. Very close by, the Grand Egyptian Museum was built, in which the treasures of Tutankhamun are shown.

begriffe.erklaerung: The king in ancient Egypt, who was regarded as divine.
A pyramid made of several steps stacked on top of one another, like a giant staircase.
A figure with a lion's body and a human head that stands guard.
Seven especially famous structures of antiquity that were already marvelled at then.

gewusst: The sides of the Great Pyramid are aligned almost exactly to north, south, east and west.
The pyramids were already ancient for Cleopatra: she lived closer in time to us than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
Work gangs scribbled their team names on stones in the pyramid, such as Friends of Khufu.

teile.einleitung: The Helvetii were a Celtic people who lived in the area of today's Swiss Plateau. In 58 BC they left their homeland to look for new land in the west of Gaul. The Roman general Julius Caesar stood in their way.
wichtigste: The Helvetii left their homeland in 58 BC.
They wanted to move to western France.
Before setting off they burned down about 400 villages, according to Caesar.
They took their families and their cattle with them.
Julius Caesar stood in their way.
They were defeated near Bibracte.
Afterwards they had to return to their homeland.

abschnitte.text: The **Helvetii** were a **Celtic** people. They lived between the Jura, the Alps, Lake Constance and Lake Geneva, so roughly in today's **Swiss Plateau**. They were farmers, craftsmen and traders, and lived in villages and fortified settlements. Their territory was bounded by mountains, lakes and rivers. So the Helvetii were looking for larger and more fertile land.

In **58 BC** the Helvetii set off. Their goal was the west of Gaul, present-day **western France** on the Atlantic. According to Caesar, they first **burned down** their towns and **about 400 villages**. That way nobody would want to turn back. They took their **families**, their **cattle** and supplies with them on wagons. Caesar gives very high numbers of emigrants, which many researchers think are exaggerated.

The Roman general **Julius Caesar** was at that time governor of the Roman provinces north and south of the Alps. He did not want the Helvetii to cross Roman territory. At **Geneva** he had the bridge over the Rhone destroyed. The Helvetii chose a different route through the Jura. Caesar followed them with his troops.

A battle took place near the Celtic town of **Bibracte** in Burgundy. The Romans **defeated** the Helvetii. Caesar ordered them to **return to their homeland** and rebuild their villages. The Romans did not want the land to stay empty and Germanic peoples to settle there. Later the territory of the Helvetii became part of the Roman Empire.

Almost everything we know about the exodus comes from **Caesar** himself. He wrote about it in his book on the **Gallic War**. Because he wanted to present himself as the victor, some of his statements should be read with caution. The name of the Helvetii lives on in Switzerland: the Latin name of the country is **Confoederatio Helvetica**, shortened to **CH**.

gewusst: The abbreviation CH on cars and in internet addresses goes back to the Helvetii.
The female figure Helvetia on Swiss coins is named after them.

teile.einleitung: The Capitoline Wolf is a famous bronze figure in Rome. It shows a she-wolf with the twins Romulus and Remus and is a landmark of the city.
wichtigste: The Capitoline Wolf is made of bronze.
The real figure stands in Rome in the Capitoline Museums.
It is named after the Capitoline, a hill of Rome.
Beneath her sit the twins Romulus and Remus.
The figures of the children were only added around the 15th century.
In Latin the she-wolf is called “Lupa”.

abschnitte.text: The Capitoline Wolf is a figure made of **bronze**. Bronze is a metal made of **copper** and **tin**. The she-wolf stands on her **four legs** and looks watchfully to the side. Beneath her belly sit **two babies**, the twins **Romulus** and **Remus**. In Latin the she-wolf is called **Lupa**.

The real figure stands in a **museum in Rome**, the **Capitoline Museums**. These lie on the **Capitoline Hill**, one of the hills of Rome. The she-wolf is named after this hill. Copies of the figure exist in many places in the world. Rome has, for example, given such copies to other cities.

abschnitte.titel: The legend of Romulus and Remus
abschnitte.text: According to the legend, the twins Romulus and Remus were abandoned as babies in a basket in the river **Tiber**. The basket caught on the bank. A **she-wolf** found the two and looked after them. Later a shepherd found them and raised them. As adults the brothers founded a city. Romulus became its first king, and it is named after him, **Rome**.

The she-wolf and the children are **not the same age**. The two figures of the children were only added around the **15th century**. The she-wolf herself is older. For a long time it was thought to be a work of the **Etruscans** from around 500 BC. But recent studies suggest that it was only cast in the **Middle Ages**. Among experts this is still **disputed**.

The she-wolf with the twins is a **symbol of the city of Rome**. It recalls the **founding legend**. In Rome it can still be seen in many places, for example on the city's signs and as a **coat-of-arms emblem**. The football club AS Roma also carries the she-wolf in its badge.

gewusst: According to the legend, Rome was founded in 753 BC.
Romulus and Remus are said to have been sons of the war god Mars.

teile.einleitung: The Gallic War was a war that Julius Caesar waged from 58 to 50 BC. At the end all of Gaul, present-day France and its surroundings, was under Roman rule.
wichtigste: Caesar fought the war from **58 to 50 BC**.
It was set off by the emigration of the **Helvetii**.
In 58 BC Caesar also defeated the Germanic leader **Ariovistus** in Alsace.
In 55 BC Caesar had **a bridge over the Rhine** built in ten days.
At **Gergovia** Caesar suffered a defeat against Vercingetorix in 52 BC.
At **Alesia** Vercingetorix had to surrender in 52 BC.
Caesar wrote about himself in the **third person**.

abschnitte.text: In 58 BC the **Helvetii** from the area of present-day Switzerland wanted to emigrate west into Gaul. Caesar was at that time governor of the nearby Roman provinces. He refused them passage and pursued them. At **Bibracte** he defeated the Helvetii and sent the survivors back to their homeland. With that the **Gallic War** began.

Still in 58 BC, Caesar defeated the Germanic leader **Ariovistus** in Alsace. Later he wanted to show the Germans the power of Rome. In 55 BC he had **a bridge over the Rhine** built in only ten days, as he reports himself. He crossed over briefly and then had the bridge taken down again. In 55 and 54 BC he also crossed over to **Britain**.

In 52 BC the Arvernian chief **Vercingetorix** united many Gallic tribes against Rome. At **Gergovia**, a town of the Arverni, Caesar had to accept a **defeat**. Soon afterwards Vercingetorix withdrew to the fortress of **Alesia**. Caesar had the town enclosed with ramparts. After a long siege Vercingetorix had to **surrender**.

Caesar himself wrote an account of the war, which is called **“De bello Gallico”**. In it he writes about himself in the **third person**, that is, “Caesar did” instead of “I did”. This makes the text seem objective, although Caesar wanted to present himself well in it. The book begins with the famous sentence that all Gaul is divided into three parts. To this day many pupils read it in Latin lessons.

gewusst: The Gallic War made Caesar very rich and powerful, which later contributed to the civil war in Rome.
Caesar's account is one of the most important sources about the Helvetii.

teile.einleitung: The Karnak Temple is one of the largest temple complexes in the world. It lies in present-day Luxor in Egypt and for many centuries was the most important sanctuary of the country.
wichtigste: Karnak lies on the east bank of the Nile in present-day Luxor, ancient Thebes.
The main temple was dedicated to the god Amun-Re.
The goddess Mut and the god Khonsu were also worshipped here.
The great hypostyle hall has 134 mighty columns.
For about 2,000 years pharaohs kept building on the complex.
A long avenue with sphinx figures leads to the Luxor Temple.

abschnitte.text: Karnak is not a single temple but a whole **temple precinct** with many buildings. It lies on the east bank of the Nile in present-day **Luxor**. In ancient times the area belonged to the city of **Thebes**, which for a long time was the capital of Egypt. Today very many people visit the ruins every year. Together with other sites of Thebes, Karnak is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The main temple was dedicated to the god **Amun**. He was joined with the sun god **Re** into one god and was then called **Amun-Re**. He was regarded as king of the gods and protector of the whole kingdom. In the temple precinct his consort **Mut** and his son **Khonsu** were also worshipped. Only priests were allowed to enter the innermost rooms.

Especially famous is the **great hypostyle hall** with 134 columns. The twelve middle columns are about 21 metres high. Many columns are covered with pictures and hieroglyphs. At the entrance of the temples stand huge gate towers called **pylons**. A pylon consists of two tapering towers with a gate between them. Karnak has several such pylons.

abschnitte.titel: Sacred lake and avenue of sphinxes
abschnitte.text: The precinct includes an artificial **sacred lake**. There the priests purified themselves before the rituals. From Karnak an almost three-kilometre-long **processional way** led to the Luxor Temple. It was lined on both sides with sphinx figures. This **avenue of sphinxes** has been uncovered again in recent years.

From the **Middle Kingdom** to the **Ptolemaic period** many rulers kept building at Karnak. Each pharaoh wanted to give the gods something new and show his own glory. So temples, courts, statues and obelisks were added. In all, building went on for about **2,000 years**. That is why the complex looks today like a huge puzzle made up of many eras.

gewusst: The middle columns in the hypostyle hall are about as tall as a house with seven storeys.
Karnak is regarded as one of the largest temple complexes ever built.

teile.einleitung: Children in ancient Rome also liked to play, often with very simple things. Nuts, knucklebones, hoops, spinning tops, balls and dolls were among their favourite toys.
wichtigste: Nuts were a very popular toy.
“To leave the nuts behind” meant to grow up.
In the knucklebones game people used small foot bones of sheep or goats.
Dolls were made of clay, wood, bone or cloth.
Hoops were driven with a stick, spinning tops with a small whip.
Balls were made of leather and stuffed with hair or feathers.

abschnitte.text: Roman children especially liked to play with **nuts**. They threw them at a target, rolled them or built small towers from them. Whoever hit a tower could keep the nuts. Nuts were so typical of childhood that people said that anyone who grew up **“left the nuts behind”**. By this they meant: he stops playing children's games.

In the **knucklebones game** people used small foot bones of sheep or goats. They were thrown and caught. Each side of the knucklebone had a different value, similar to a **die**. The game was popular with children and also with adults. Later such game pieces were also made of bronze or glass.

Roman **dolls** were made of clay, wood, bone or cloth. Some had movable arms and legs that were attached with small pins. There were also small animal figures and toy dishes. Some dolls were found in graves. That is how we know today what they looked like.

Outside, children drove a **hoop** of metal or wood along the street with a stick. A **spinning top** was kept moving with a small whip. **Ball games** in a group were also very popular. The balls were made of leather and stuffed with hair or feathers. Children still know many of these games today.

gewusst: The knucklebones game lives on in some countries to this day, for example as a game with five small stones.
So spinning tops and hoops are toys at least 2,000 years old.

teile.einleitung: The Constitutio Antoniniana is a decree issued by the Roman emperor Caracalla in AD 212. With it, almost all free inhabitants of the Roman Empire received Roman citizenship. It was one of the most important changes in the law of the empire.
wichtigste: The Constitutio Antoniniana was issued in AD 212.
Emperor Caracalla issued it.
Almost all free inhabitants of the empire received Roman citizenship.
According to the surviving text, the dediticii were excluded.
Cassius Dio gives higher tax revenue as the motive.
The name comes from the emperor's official name Antoninus.

abschnitte.text: Before 212, not everyone in the empire was a **Roman citizen**. Many inhabitants of the provinces had only the rights of their own city. In **AD 212** Emperor **Caracalla** issued the **Constitutio Antoniniana**. With it, **almost all free inhabitants** received Roman citizenship. The people in the area of present-day Switzerland also became Romans in this way. Slaves were not affected.

Parts of the text survive on a **papyrus** from Egypt. According to it, the **dediticii** were excluded. Exactly who was meant by this is disputed among researchers. The historian **Cassius Dio** lived at the same time. He thought that Caracalla mainly wanted **higher tax revenue**. For certain taxes, such as those on inheritances, only Roman citizens had to pay.

The name **“Constitutio Antoniniana”** comes from the emperor's official name **Antoninus**. Caracalla is only a nickname. It comes from a Gallic hooded cloak that the emperor liked to wear. Many new citizens took the family name **Aurelius**, which was also part of the emperor's name. That is why this name is found on many inscriptions afterwards.

gewusst: Part of the text survives on only a single papyrus, which is kept today in Giessen in Germany.

teile.einleitung: Democritus was a Greek philosopher who was born around 460 BC. He thought that everything in the world is made of tiny, indivisible particles: atoms.
wichtigste: Democritus came from the city of **Abdera** in Thrace.
He lived from about 460 to 370 BC.
His teacher **Leucippus** is regarded as a co-founder of atomic theory.
According to Democritus, everything consists of **atoms** and **empty space**.
“Atomos” means **indivisible** in Greek.
Because of his cheerful nature he was called the **laughing philosopher**.

abschnitte.text: Democritus came from **Abdera**, a Greek city in Thrace in the north of Greece. He is said to have travelled widely and to have been interested in almost every field of knowledge. He wrote many books about nature, mathematics and the good life. Unfortunately only fragments of them survive. What we know about him often comes from reports by later writers.

Together with his teacher **Leucippus**, Democritus developed **atomic theory**. He imagined that you cannot divide a thing endlessly. At some point you reach tiny particles that cannot be broken down any further. He called these **atoms**, from the Greek word “atomos”, which means **indivisible**. According to his teaching, atoms differ in shape, size and position.

According to Democritus, between the atoms there is **empty space**. In it the atoms move constantly. When a thing comes into being, **atoms join** together. When it passes away, they **separate** again. The atoms themselves never come into being or pass away. In this way Democritus explained changes in nature without needing gods as a cause.

Democritus was seen as a cheerful and calm person. That is why he was given the nickname **the laughing philosopher**. He taught that a calm and contented mind is the goal of a good life. Living in moderation mattered more to him than wealth. These ideas later also influenced the philosopher **Epicurus**.

gewusst: Today's atoms are named after Democritus' idea, although we now know that they are made of even smaller particles.
Democritus already suspected that the Milky Way is made up of very many stars.

teile.einleitung: A domus was the town house of a rich family in ancient Rome. It was built inwards, with rooms around a bright inner courtyard.
wichtigste: **A rich family** lived in a domus.
The central reception room was called the **atrium** and had an opening in the roof.
The **impluvium** was a basin for collecting rainwater.
In the **triclinium** rich Romans ate lying down.
The inscription “Cave canem” means **Beware of the dog**.

abschnitte.text: Only wealthy Romans could afford a **domus**. Most people in the city lived in cramped apartment blocks called **insulae**. A domus had hardly any windows facing the street. Often there were small shops at the front, which were rented out. Life took place inside, around open courtyards.

Through the entrance you came into the **atrium**, the central reception room. In its roof there was an opening through which light and rain came in. Below it, in the floor, lay a shallow basin, the **impluvium**. It was used **for collecting rainwater**, which often flowed into a cistern. In the atrium the master of the house received his visitors in the morning.

In the **triclinium**, the dining room, the guests lay on couches around a low table and **ate lying down**. Many houses had a garden with a colonnade further back, the **peristyle**. Walls were often painted in bright colours, and floors were decorated with **mosaics**. In **Pompeii**, a mosaic with the inscription “Cave canem” warns at the entrance of one house, in English: **Beware of the dog**.

gewusst: In **Augusta Raurica** near Basel there is a rebuilt Roman house where you can see how Romans lived.
Pompeii was buried by Vesuvius in AD 79, which is why many houses there are well preserved.

teile.einleitung: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman politician, orator and writer. He is regarded as the greatest orator of Rome, and his texts are still read in Latin lessons today.
wichtigste: Cicero is regarded as the greatest orator of Rome.
He was a “homo novus”, the first of his family in the highest office.
In 63 BC he was consul.
As consul he uncovered the conspiracy of Catiline.
He received the honorary title “Father of the Fatherland”.
His Philippics were directed against Marcus Antonius.
In 43 BC Marcus Antonius had him killed.

abschnitte.text: Cicero came from a family of the **equestrian order** from **Arpinum**. None of his ancestors had held a high office in Rome. Such a climber was called a **“homo novus”**, a “new man”. Through his gift as an **orator** and lawyer Cicero became famous all the same. He reached the **consulship** for the year **63 BC**, a great success for a newcomer.

As consul Cicero uncovered the **conspiracy** of **Lucius Sergius Catilina**. Catiline was planning a coup. Cicero exposed him in his famous **speeches against Catiline**. From them comes the cry **“O tempora, o mores!”**, that is, “O the times, O the customs!”. For saving the state Cicero received the honorary title **“pater patriae”**, Father of the Fatherland.

Cicero wrote a great deal. Numerous **speeches**, **letters** and **philosophical writings** survive. His Latin is regarded as especially beautiful and clear. That is why his texts are still read in **Latin lessons** today. Through his letters a great deal is also known about life in Rome in his time.

After the death of Julius Caesar, Cicero fought with words against **Marcus Antonius**. He delivered the **Philippics** against him. He took the name from the speeches of the Greek **Demosthenes** against King Philip. From this comes our word **“philippic”** for a speech of denunciation. Marcus Antonius put Cicero on the list of enemies of the state, and in **43 BC** he was killed while fleeing.

gewusst: Later the Roman emperors also bore the title “Father of the Fatherland”, which Cicero had received as one of the first.
Over 800 letters of Cicero survive.

teile.einleitung: Greek tragedy is a form of theatre that arose in ancient Athens. It shows serious stories in which people make hard decisions and often fall into misfortune.
wichtigste: Tragedies were performed in Athens at the **Dionysia**.
The three great tragedians are **Aeschylus**, Sophocles and Euripides.
**Aeschylus** is the oldest of them.
Aristotle credits Sophocles with **the third actor**.
Sophocles wrote **“Oedipus the King”** and “Antigone”.
**Euripides** wrote “Medea”.
According to Aristotle, tragedy brings about **a cleansing through pity and fear**.

abschnitte.text: Tragedies were performed in Athens at the **Dionysia**, a great festival for the god Dionysus. There was a competition. Several poets each presented three tragedies and a cheerful satyr play. A jury chose the winner at the end. The performances took place in the open air in front of thousands of spectators.

Every tragedy included a **chorus**, which sang, danced and commented on the action. The actors wore **masks** and often played several roles. **Aeschylus**, the oldest of the three great tragedians, introduced a second actor. According to Aristotle, **Sophocles** added **the third actor**. This made the conversations on stage livelier.

**Sophocles** wrote **“Oedipus the King”**. In it a king learns that without knowing it he has killed his father and that a terrible prophecy has come true. In **“Antigone”** a young woman buries **her brother Polynices**, although King **Creon** has forbidden it. She follows her conscience and the laws of the gods. For this she has to pay dearly.

**Euripides** was the youngest of the three great tragedians. His characters often show strong feelings and inner doubts. In **“Medea”** a woman is abandoned by her husband. Out of rage and despair she takes a terrible revenge that also strikes her own children. The play is still among the best-known tragedies today.

The philosopher **Aristotle** wrote about tragedy in his **“Poetics”**. It is meant to arouse **pity and fear** in the audience. This leads to a **cleansing** of the emotions, in Greek **catharsis**. The old tragedies are still performed today, including on Swiss stages.

gewusst: Of the many tragedies by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, only a little more than 30 survive.
The word “tragedy” literally means something like “goat song”.

teile.einleitung: Genava is the old name of Geneva. The settlement where the Rhone flows out of Lake Geneva was already important more than 2,000 years ago, because a bridge crossed the river here.
wichtigste: The Celtic tribe of the **Allobroges** lived in Genava.
In Geneva the **Rhone** flows out of the lake.
In 58 BC Caesar had **the bridge** destroyed to stop the Helvetii.
Genava is first mentioned **in Caesar's “Gallic War”**.
The name Genava became today's name Geneva.

abschnitte.text: Genava lay where the **Rhone** flows out of Lake Geneva. Here the river was easy to cross, which is why there was a **bridge**. The place belonged to the Celtic tribe of the **Allobroges**. The Allobroges were already under Roman rule at that time. So Genava was a border town facing the territory of the Helvetii.

In 58 BC the Helvetii wanted to emigrate west. One route led across the bridge at Genava. Caesar hurried to Genava and had **the bridge destroyed** to stop the Helvetii. He reports this in his book on the **“Gallic War”**. There Genava is mentioned for the first time.

abschnitte.titel: From village to the city of Geneva
abschnitte.text: In Roman times Genava grew into a small town with a harbour and trade. Later the place became the seat of a **bishop**. From the name Genava developed today's name **Geneva**, in French Genève. Archaeologists have found many traces from this early period beneath the old town.

gewusst: Beneath the Cathedral of Saint-Pierre in Geneva you can visit excavations from Roman and even older times.
