teile.einleitung: The early horse is an early ancestor of our horses. It lived about 50 million years ago in warm forests and was only as big as a fox.
wichtigste: The early horse was about as big as a fox.
It had four toes at the front and three at the back.
Today's horses walk on a single toe in the hoof.
The early horse lived in the forest and ate leaves and fruit.
It lived about 50 million years ago, after the dinosaurs.
Famous finds come from the Messel Pit in Germany.

abschnitte.text: Whoever thinks of a horse imagines a large animal. The **early horse**, however, was only about as big as a **fox**. Only over millions of years did horses grow larger. The early horse lived about **50 million years ago**. The great **dinosaurs** were already extinct by then, and humans were a very long way off.

The early horse had **four toes** on its forelegs and **three** on its hind legs. With them it walked well over the soft forest floor. Today's horses walk only on **one toe**. It sits inside the hard **hoof**. The other toes became smaller and smaller over the course of evolution and almost completely disappeared.

At that time it was much warmer on Earth than today. The early horse lived in warm **forests**, for wide grasslands hardly existed yet. It ate soft **leaves** and **fruit**. Later, when more grassland spread, horses adapted: they became larger and faster and ate grass.

In the **Messel Pit** near Darmstadt in Germany, very well-preserved early horses were found. Sometimes even outlines of the body and remains of the stomach contents can be seen. So we know what the animals ate. The Messel Pit is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, because so many fossils from this period lie there.

gewusst: An early horse found in the Messel Pit bears the scientific name Propalaeotherium.
The evolution of the horse is one of the best-known examples of how animals change over a long time.

teile.einleitung: Euclid was a Greek mathematician who taught in Alexandria around 300 BC. His work the “Elements” was the most important textbook of geometry for more than two thousand years.
wichtigste: Euclid taught around 300 BC in **Alexandria**.
His main work is called the **“Elements”** and consists of **13** books.
He is called the “father” of **geometry**.
He proved that there are **infinitely many prime numbers**.
With the **Euclidean algorithm** you calculate the greatest common divisor.
The **parallel postulate** led to non-Euclidean geometries in the 19th century.

abschnitte.text: Very little is known about Euclid's life. It is certain that around 300 BC he taught in **Alexandria** in Egypt. This city was then a centre of science. Euclid gathered the mathematical knowledge of his time and arranged it anew. That is why he is often called the “father” of **geometry**.

His famous main work is the **“Elements”**, which consists of **13 books**. Euclid begins with definitions and a few basic principles that he calls **postulates**. From these he derives many theorems step by step, with **proofs**. This strict structure became the model for all of mathematics. The “Elements” are among the most widely distributed books in history.

Euclid proved that there are **infinitely many prime numbers**. The **Euclidean algorithm** is also well known: with it you find the **greatest common divisor** of two numbers. You keep dividing with a remainder until the remainder is zero. For 1071 and 462 this gives **21**. Euclid also found a formula for **perfect numbers**. For p equal to 3 it gives **28**, because 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 makes 28.

One of Euclid's postulates is about lines that never meet. It is called the **parallel postulate**. For centuries many mathematicians tried to prove it from the other principles, without success. In the **19th century** it was discovered that you can build a meaningful geometry even without this postulate. That is how the **non-Euclidean geometries** arose, which are important for curved surfaces, for example.

gewusst: The “Elements” were still used as a textbook in schools in the 19th century.
It is said that Euclid told a king that there was no “royal road” to geometry.

teile.einleitung: Cyrus II, also called Cyrus the Great, was a Persian king. He founded the Achaemenid Empire, the first great Persian empire, and conquered Lydia and Babylon, among other places.
wichtigste: Cyrus is regarded as the founder of the Achaemenid Empire.
Around 550 BC he defeated the Median king Astyages.
He defeated King Croesus of Lydia, who was famous for his wealth.
In 539 BC he took Babylon almost without a fight.
According to the Bible he allowed the people of Judah to return to Jerusalem.
His tomb stands in Pasargadae in present-day Iran.

abschnitte.titel: From petty king to great empire
abschnitte.text: Cyrus first ruled over a small Persian kingdom. Around **550 BC** he defeated the Median king **Astyages**, who is said to have been his grandfather. He took over the empire of the **Medes**. That was the first great step towards the great Persian empire. Cyrus is therefore regarded as the founder of the **Achaemenid Empire**, which later stretched from Egypt to India.

In **Lydia** in Asia Minor, King **Croesus** ruled in the city of **Sardis**. He was famous for his wealth. According to the historian **Herodotus**, he asked the **Oracle of Delphi** whether he should attack Cyrus. The answer was that he would destroy a great empire. Croesus attacked and did indeed destroy a great empire, namely his own.

In **539 BC** Cyrus entered **Babylon** almost without a fight. With that the last great Mesopotamian empire fell to Persia. On a clay cylinder, the **Cyrus Cylinder**, he describes his rule in **cuneiform**. In it he presents himself as a just ruler who spares temples and inhabitants. The cylinder is today in the **British Museum** in London.

According to the Book of **Ezra**, Cyrus allowed the people of **Judah**, who had been deported to Babylon, to return home to **Jerusalem**. There they were allowed to rebuild their temple. In the Book of **Isaiah**, Cyrus is even called the **Lord's anointed**. This title was otherwise borne only by Israelite kings. That is why Cyrus is portrayed very positively in the Bible.

According to Herodotus, Cyrus fell in **530 BC** in battle against the **Massagetae**, a people of horsemen in Central Asia. Their queen **Tomyris** is said to have led the fight. His tomb stands in **Pasargadae**, the first capital of the Persian Empire in present-day **Iran**. The simple stone tomb survives to this day.

gewusst: Because Croesus was so rich, a very rich person is still called a “Croesus” today.
The tomb of Cyrus in Pasargadae is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: The Code of Hammurabi is one of the oldest known collections of laws in the world. King Hammurabi of Babylon had it written on a large stone pillar about 3,700 years ago. Today it stands in the Louvre in Paris.
wichtigste: Hammurabi was king of Babylon.
The code is written in the Akkadian language in cuneiform.
The famous stele is made of diorite, a very hard rock.
Many rules follow the principle of retaliation, “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth”.
The punishment often depended on the social rank of the offender and the victim.
The Elamites carried the stele off to Susa in the 12th century BC.
French archaeologists found it in 1901/02 in Susa; today it stands in the Louvre.

abschnitte.text: **Hammurabi** ruled the city of **Babylon** in Mesopotamia in the 18th century BC. He turned Babylon into a large empire. Towards the end of his reign he had laws collected and written down. In the **prologue** he explains his aim. He wanted to make sure that **the strong do not oppress the weak**.

The laws stand on a **stele** more than two metres high, made of **diorite**. Diorite is a dark and very hard rock. At the top, a picture shows Hammurabi before the sun god Shamash, the god of justice. Below follow the laws in the **Akkadian** language and **cuneiform** script. There are about 280 rules, covering for example trade, work, property and punishments.

Many rules follow the principle of **retaliation**. It means that the punishment should match the deed, “**an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth**”. One example: if a house collapsed and killed its owner, the **builder** faced the **death penalty**. But the punishment often depended on the **rank** of the offender and the victim. Different rules applied to free people, dependants and slaves.

In the **12th century BC** the **Elamites** conquered parts of Mesopotamia. They carried the stele off as **war booty** to their capital **Susa**, in present-day Iran. There **French archaeologists** found it in **1901/02**. The stele was taken to Paris. Today it is displayed in the **Louvre**.

The Code of Hammurabi shows how people lived together almost 4,000 years ago. It is not the oldest collection of laws, but the best known and best preserved. The idea that laws should be **written down** and visible to everyone is still important today. In Switzerland too, all laws are public and anyone can look them up.

gewusst: Casts of the Hammurabi stele stand in various museums around the world, for example in Berlin.
The laws were copied by scribes over the centuries and learned in schools.

teile.einleitung: **Thermoluminescence dating** is a method for determining the age of fired pottery and heated stones. It measures a faint light that is released when a sample is heated. From its amount, you can calculate how long ago the last heating was.
wichtigste: Firing the clay sets the “clock” to zero.
In the laboratory, the light released on heating is measured.
Age = palaeodose divided by the annual dose rate.
Mainly quartz and feldspar are examined.
In OSL, sunlight resets the clock.
Heated flints can be dated too.
In the art trade, it is used to expose forgeries.

abschnitte.text: In the ground there is a faint natural **radiation** everywhere. It also hits tiny crystals of **quartz** and **feldspar** in clay or rock. In the process, electrons are stored there in “traps”. The longer the radiation acts, the more energy builds up. So the crystal works like a clock.

When clay is strongly heated during **firing**, the stored electrons are released. The clock is then back **at zero**. After that, new energy slowly builds up. In the **laboratory**, a small sample is heated once more. It then gives off the stored energy as a faint **light**. From the amount of this light, the total radiation absorbed is determined, the **palaeodose**.

The age is obtained like this: **palaeodose divided by the annual dose rate**. An example: a potsherd has absorbed 6 gray, and 3 milligray are added per year. 6 gray is 6,000 milligray. 6,000 divided by 3 gives **2,000 years**.

Besides pottery, you can also date **flints heated in a fire**, for example from Stone Age camps. In **optically stimulated luminescence** (OSL), sand and other sediments are measured. Here **sunlight** resets the clock before the sand is covered over. In the **art trade**, thermoluminescence is used to check whether a clay figure is really old, and so **forgeries** are recognised.

gewusst: The gray is the unit for the amount of radiation absorbed and is named after the British physicist Louis Harold Gray.
Only a few milligrams of material are needed for the measurement, so even valuable pieces can be examined.

teile.einleitung: In Greek colonisation, Greeks founded new cities around the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. This happened mainly between about 750 and 550 BC. Many of today's cities go back to such foundings.
wichtigste: The great colonisation took place **from about 750 to 550 BC**.
An important reason was **too little farmland at home**.
The city from which a colony set out was called the **metropolis**.
Southern Italy and Sicily were called **Greater Greece**, in Latin **Magna Graecia**.
Greeks from Phocaea founded Massalia, present-day **Marseille**, around 600 BC.
**Corinth** founded Syracuse in Sicily around 733 BC.

abschnitte.text: Greece is mountainous and has little fertile land. As the population grew, there was **too little farmland at home**. Trade, quarrels in one's own city or a taste for adventure also led to emigration. Many settlers first asked the **Oracle of Delphi** for advice. Then they set off in ships and founded a new city.

The city from which a colony was founded was called **metropolis** by the Greeks, that is, “mother city”. The new settlement was usually independent, but stayed linked to it. They shared gods, festivals and often laws too. So **Corinth** founded the city of **Syracuse** in Sicily around 733 BC. Settlers from the island of **Thera** founded **Cyrene** in North Africa around 630 BC.

Especially many Greek cities arose in **southern Italy and on Sicily**. That is why this area was called **Greater Greece**, and by the Romans **Magna Graecia**. One city there was called **Neapolis**, “new city”. This became present-day **Naples**. On the Black Sea too, Greeks founded many colonies, such as **Byzantion**, later Istanbul.

Around 600 BC Greeks from **Phocaea** in Asia Minor founded the city of **Massalia**, present-day **Marseille**. From there they traded with the Celts, among other routes along the Rhone. In this way Greek goods reached the area of present-day Switzerland. A well-known example is the **Hydria of Grächwil**, a Greek bronze vessel that was found in the canton of Bern.

gewusst: Many cities on the Mediterranean still bear names that come from Greek.
Through the colonies, the Greek alphabet and Greek culture spread far beyond Greece.

teile.einleitung: The Circus Maximus was the largest racetrack in ancient Rome. Mainly chariot races took place here, which were very popular with the Romans. It lay in a valley between the Palatine and Aventine hills.
wichtigste: Mainly horse-drawn chariot races took place in the Circus Maximus.
A quadriga was pulled by four horses.
Usually the race was seven laps.
A long wall in the middle separated the two sides of the track.
The racing teams were told apart by their colours.
The turns were dangerous, because chariots could tip over.
The winner received a palm branch; today the Circus Maximus is a large meadow.

abschnitte.text: The **Circus Maximus** lay between the **Palatine** and **Aventine** hills. It was about 600 metres long. The stands had room for well over a hundred thousand people. That made it one of the largest buildings for spectators that ever existed. Mainly **chariot races** took place here.

The racing chariots were pulled by **horses**. The **quadriga**, a chariot with **four** horses, was especially popular. Usually the race was **seven laps**. In the middle of the track stood a long wall, the **spina**. It separated the two sides of the racetrack. On it stood statues, columns and an obelisk from Egypt.

At both ends of the spina the chariots had to turn tightly. These **turns** were especially dangerous. The light chariots could **tip over** or collide. The drivers, the **charioteers**, needed a lot of courage and skill. Successful charioteers became rich and were famous all over Rome.

The racing teams were told apart by their **colours**: red, white, green and blue. Each colour had its own fans, rather like football clubs today. The spectators cheered on their team loudly. The winner of a race received a **palm branch** as a sign of victory. Often there was money too.

Almost nothing is left of the great stands. Today the Circus Maximus is a **large meadow** in Rome. Its long shape still shows where the racetrack ran. The area is used for concerts and big celebrations. An obelisk that once stood on the spina now decorates the Piazza del Popolo in Rome.

gewusst: The word “circus” comes from the Latin “circus”, which means circle or racetrack.
The starting gates of the chariots were called “carceres”, which actually means prisons.

teile.einleitung: The Huns were a people of horsemen from the steppes of Asia. Around 375 AD they moved west and so set off the Migration Period. Their best-known ruler was Attila.
wichtigste: The Huns were a people of horsemen who came from the steppes.
Around 375 AD they defeated the Alans and the Ostrogoths.
In doing so they set off the Migration Period.
They were feared for their powerful recurve bow.
In the 5th century their centre lay in the Great Hungarian Plain.
After Attila's death in 453 the Hunnic empire soon fell apart.

abschnitte.text: The Huns came from the wide **steppes** east of Europe. Where exactly they came from is still disputed. They lived as **nomads**, that is, they moved about with their herds. They spent almost their whole lives on **horseback**. Roman writers described them as strange and terrifying.

The Huns were feared for their **recurve bow**. It was short and made of **wood**, **horn** and **sinew**. This made it very powerful. With it the Huns could even shoot from a **galloping horse**. Their swift cavalry attacks took many opponents by surprise.

abschnitte.titel: The start of the Migration Period
abschnitte.text: Around **375 AD** the Huns moved west. They defeated the **Alans** and the **Ostrogoths**. As a result many Germanic peoples, such as the Visigoths, fled into the **Roman Empire**. This was the beginning of the **Migration Period**, a time when many peoples moved across Europe. It helped bring about the later fall of the Western Roman Empire.

In the 5th century the centre of the Huns lay in the **Great Hungarian Plain** on the Tisza. From there they attacked the Eastern and Western Roman Empires. Their best-known king was **Attila**. In **451** he fought on the **Catalaunian Plains** in Gaul against an army of Romans and Visigoths and had to withdraw. After Attila's death in **453** the Hunnic empire soon fell apart.

gewusst: In the Nibelungenlied, Attila appears under the name Etzel.
The name of the country Hungary does not come from the Huns. The Hungarians descend from the Magyars, who only arrived centuries later.

teile.einleitung: Confucius was a Chinese teacher and thinker. He lived about 2,500 years ago and thought about how people can live together well and justly.
wichtigste: Confucius lived from about 551 to 479 BC.
He came from the small state of Lu in what is now Shandong Province.
His Chinese name Kong Fuzi means “Master Kong”.
He taught respect for parents and elders.
He is the source of the rule: do not do to others what you would not want done to you.
His pupils wrote down his conversations and sayings.

abschnitte.text: Confucius lived from about **551 to 479 BC**. He was born in the state of **Lu**, in present-day **Shandong** Province. China was then split into many **small states** that often quarrelled with each other. Confucius wanted to show how order and peace could return. His Chinese name **Kong Fuzi** means “Master Kong”, and from it came our “Confucius”.

Confucius became famous above all as a **teacher**. He taught many pupils and also took in some from ordinary families. He is regarded as one of the first **private teachers** of China. He thought **learning** very important, and for the whole of life. Whoever learns becomes a better person, he thought.

For Confucius the **family** was the foundation of society. Children should **honour their parents** and **respect their elders**. Rulers too should be just and set a good example. If everyone does his task well, he thought, the community lives in peace.

A well-known rule of Confucius runs: **“Do not do to others what you would not want done to you.”** So one should not do anything to others that one would not want oneself. This rule is also known from many religions. It is often called the **Golden Rule**.

Confucius himself wrote no great book. His **pupils** wrote down his conversations and sayings. This collection is called the **“Analects”**. From his thoughts arose **Confucianism**. It shaped thinking in China and other countries of East Asia for many centuries.

gewusst: Confucius lived at roughly the same time as the Buddha in India.
In his home town of Qufu there is a large temple in his honour that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: The Akkadian Empire arose over 4,000 years ago in Mesopotamia, the land between the Euphrates and the Tigris. Its founder was King Sargon of Akkad. Many see in it the first great empire in history.
wichtigste: The Akkadian Empire is often regarded as the first great empire in history.
It was founded in the 24th or 23rd century BC by Sargon of Akkad.
Akkadian belongs to the Semitic languages.
Sargon's grandson Naram-Sin was the first Mesopotamian ruler to have himself worshipped as a god.
Sargon's daughter Enheduanna is regarded as the first author known by name.
The fall of the empire is linked with the mountain people of the Gutians.
The capital Akkad has still not been found with certainty.

abschnitte.text: A **birth legend** tells about Sargon's youth. According to it, he was set adrift as a baby in a **basket** on the river and found by a gardener. Later he is said to have been **cupbearer** at the court of King Ur-Zababa of Kish. A cupbearer handed the king his drinks and was a person of trust. Sargon became king himself and conquered many city states. In this way an empire arose that stretched from Mesopotamia far into the neighbouring lands.

**Akkadian** belongs to the **Semitic languages**, as do Hebrew and Arabic later. It was written in **cuneiform** on clay tablets. Before it, Sumerian was important in southern Mesopotamia. Akkadian remained in use for a long time after the end of the empire. Babylonians and Assyrians spoke and wrote forms of it.

Sargon's grandson **Naram-Sin** expanded the empire further. He was the first ruler of Mesopotamia to have himself worshipped as a **god**. His famous victory stele shows him with a horned crown, a sign of the gods. Sargon's daughter **Enheduanna** was priestess of the moon god in the city of Ur. She composed hymns and is regarded as the first **author** known by name in world history.

After about a century and a half, the empire fell apart. Uprisings and attacks from outside weakened it. In particular, the mountain people of the **Gutians** from the Zagros Mountains is linked with its end. The capital **Akkad** has still **not been located with certainty**. Researchers suspect it in present-day Iraq, but nobody has so far excavated it clearly.

gewusst: The victory stele of Naram-Sin stands today in the Louvre in Paris.
The story of the baby in the basket recalls later tales about other famous people.

teile.einleitung: Hippocrates of Kos was a famous Greek physician of ancient times. He and his pupils looked for natural causes of illnesses and observed the sick closely. That is why he is regarded as the founder of scientific medicine.
wichtigste: Hippocrates lived from about 460 to 370 BC.
He came from the Greek island of Kos.
He taught that illnesses have natural causes.
Treatment began first with diet and way of life.
The theory of the humours distinguished four bodily fluids.
About 60 writings make up the Hippocratic Corpus.

abschnitte.text: Hippocrates was born around **460 BC** on the island of **Kos** and died around 370 BC. He lived in the golden age of classical **Greece**. On Kos there was an important **school of physicians** and a sanctuary of the god of healing, **Asclepius**. Hippocrates also travelled through Greece as a physician. But little is known for certain about his life.

Many people at that time believed that illnesses were **punishments from the gods**. The Hippocratic physicians rejected this explanation. They looked for the causes in **diet**, **way of life**, **climate** and surroundings. They examined the sick carefully and wrote down the **course** of the illness. In this way they could make predictions and pass on their experience.

Treatment often began with **dietetics**. This means a healthy way of life: suitable food, exercise, sleep and rest. Only when that did not help did the physicians turn to **medicines** or operations. An important principle runs: the physician should **help** the sick or at least **not harm** them. This principle still applies in medicine today.

The **theory of the humours** distinguished **four bodily fluids**: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and **black bile**. Health meant a **balance** of these fluids. Illness was seen as a disturbance of this balance. This teaching shaped medicine in Europe until modern times. Today we know that it is not correct. The word **melancholy** literally means “black bile”.

About **60 medical writings** have been handed down under the name of Hippocrates. They are called the **Hippocratic Corpus**. They come from various authors from several generations. Which ones Hippocrates wrote himself is unclear. They include the **Hippocratic Oath**, a promise for physicians. Doctors still take pledges today that go back to this idea.

gewusst: The term “Hippocratic face” for the appearance of seriously ill people goes back to a description in these writings.
Words such as diagnosis, prognosis and therapy come from Greek.

teile.einleitung: Carthage was a powerful trading city on the north coast of Africa. For a long time it was the great rival of Rome, until the Romans destroyed it in 146 BC.
wichtigste: Carthage lay in present-day Tunisia, near the capital Tunis.
The city was founded by Phoenicians, according to legend by Queen Dido.
The Carthaginians lived mainly from trade across the sea.
Rome and Carthage fought three Punic Wars against each other.
The general Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants in 218 BC.
In 146 BC the Romans destroyed Carthage.

abschnitte.text: Carthage lay on the north coast of **Africa** on the Mediterranean. The ruins are today near **Tunis**, the capital of **Tunisia**. The city was founded by **Phoenicians**, a seafaring people from the eastern Mediterranean. According to legend, **Queen Dido** fled from her homeland and founded the new city on this coast. From Carthage it was not far to the island of Sicily.

The Carthaginians lived mainly from **sea trade**. Their ships carried goods all over the Mediterranean. Famous was the **circular naval harbour** with an island in the middle. All around lay berths for many warships. So Carthage was for a long time the strongest sea power in the western Mediterranean.

The most important god of the city was **Baal Hammon**. Besides him the Carthaginians worshipped above all the goddess **Tanit**. They had brought their religion with them from their old Phoenician homeland. The Romans called the Carthaginians **Poeni**, and that is where the name of the later wars comes from.

Rome and Carthage fought three **Punic Wars** for supremacy. In the second war the general **Hannibal** crossed the Alps in 218 BC with his army and **war elephants**. He wanted to attack Rome from the north and won several battles. In the end, however, he was defeated. In Rome the politician **Cato** repeatedly demanded that Carthage must be destroyed.

At the end of the Third Punic War the Romans captured the city in **146 BC** and destroyed it. Later they built a new **Roman city** on the same spot. It became large and important again for the Roman province of Africa. Today the ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: Cato is said to have ended his speeches in the Senate with the sentence that Carthage must be destroyed, even when they were about something quite different.
The name Carthage means “new city” in the language of the Phoenicians.

teile.einleitung: The Kingdom of Judah was the southern kingdom of the Israelites with its capital Jerusalem. It lasted longer than the northern Kingdom of Israel and gave the Jewish people their name.
wichtigste: The capital of Judah was Jerusalem.
According to the Bible, kings from the House of David ruled.
King Hezekiah had a water tunnel built around 700 BC.
After the fall of Jerusalem many people of Judah were deported to Babylon.
This period is called the Babylonian Exile.
The word “Jews” derives from the name Judah.

abschnitte.titel: Jerusalem and the House of David
abschnitte.text: Judah was the smaller **southern kingdom**. Its capital was **Jerusalem**, the seat of the kings and of the **Temple**. According to the **Bible**, descendants of King **David** ruled until the end of the kingdom. An ancient inscription from **Tel Dan** also mentions a “House of David”. It is one of the oldest pieces of evidence for this royal family outside the Bible.

Around **700 BC** the **Assyrians** threatened to attack Jerusalem. King **Hezekiah** therefore had a **water tunnel** dug through the rock. The **Siloam Tunnel** is over 500 metres long and led spring water into the city. So the inhabitants had water even during a siege. The tunnel survives to this day and can be walked through.

Later the **Babylonians** conquered Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple. Part of the upper class of Judah was deported to **Babylon** and lived there for decades. This period is called the **Babylonian Exile**. It shaped the Jewish religion strongly. Only after the victory of the Persian king **Cyrus** were people of Judah allowed to return.

The name of the tribe and kingdom of **Judah** became the name for the whole people. From it came the English word **“Jews”**. The word **Judaism** for the religion also goes back to it. So an old kingdom's name still recalls this history today.

gewusst: In the Siloam Tunnel an inscription was found that describes how the two gangs of workers met in the rock.
The workers dug the tunnel from both ends at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Venus figurines are small female figures from the Old Stone Age. They have been found in many countries of Europe, including in Switzerland on Lake Neuchâtel.
wichtigste: Venus figures are small female figures from the Old Stone Age.
The best known is the Venus of Willendorf from Austria.
It is about 11 centimetres tall and made of limestone.
It stands in the Natural History Museum Vienna.
The Venus of Hohle Fels is carved from mammoth ivory.
At Monruz near Neuchâtel, tiny figures of black jet were found.

abschnitte.text: **Venus figures** are small figures of women that people carved or shaped in the **Old Stone Age**. Researchers gave them the name much later, after the Roman goddess Venus. Such figures have been found from France to Russia. What they were used for is not known for certain. Perhaps they were lucky charms, pendants or figures for religious belief.

The most famous figure is the **Venus of Willendorf**. Willendorf is a place in the **Wachau** on the Danube in **Austria**. The figure is only about **11 centimetres** tall and fits easily in one hand. It was carved from **limestone** and painted with red **ochre**. For a long time it has belonged to the **Natural History Museum Vienna**.

In the **Hohle Fels** cave in the Swabian Jura in Germany, a very old figure was found. It was carved from a **mammoth's tusk**, that is, from mammoth ivory. It is about **35,000 to 40,000 years** old. This makes it one of the oldest known depictions of humans.

In Switzerland too there are Venus figures. At **Monruz** on **Lake Neuchâtel**, tiny female figures came to light during the building of the motorway. They are made of **jet**, a black, shiny stone. The largest figure is only **1.65 centimetres** long. Perhaps it was worn as a **pendant** on a string.

gewusst: The figures of Monruz are so small that several would fit on a fingertip.
Many Venus figures have no worked-out face.

teile.einleitung: Alexander the Great was a king from Macedonia who, in only about ten years, conquered a huge empire from Greece to India. He lived from 356 to 323 BC and was only 32 years old. To this day he is regarded as one of the most famous generals in history.
wichtigste: Alexander came from Macedonia, a kingdom in the north of Greece.
His father was King Philip II, and his teacher the thinker Aristotle.
At about 20 years old, Alexander became king.
He defeated the mighty Persian Empire.
In Egypt he founded the city of Alexandria.
With his army he marched as far as India.
He died at the age of 32 in Babylon.

abschnitte.text: Alexander was born in 356 BC in **Pella**, the capital of Macedonia. His father was King **Philip II**, who made Macedonia a strong power. As a boy, Alexander was taught by the famous thinker **Aristotle**, among other things in philosophy, medicine and natural history. He loved the stories of Homer, especially that of the hero Achilles. According to a well-known tale, as a boy he tamed the wild horse **Bucephalus**, which then became his favourite horse.

In 336 BC, Philip was murdered, and Alexander became king at about 20 years old. First he secured his power in Greece. In 334 BC he marched with his army to Asia Minor, to present-day Turkey, to attack the **Persian Empire**. In the city of Gordium he is said to have simply cut through the cleverly knotted **Gordian Knot** with his sword. A legend said that whoever undid the knot would become ruler of Asia.

Alexander defeated the Persian king Darius III in great battles, in 333 BC at **Issus** and in 331 BC at Gaugamela. In between he conquered Egypt, where he was welcomed as pharaoh. There in 331 BC he founded the city of **Alexandria**, which later became one of the most important cities of antiquity. After that he conquered the Persian capitals Babylon, Susa and Persepolis.

Alexander wanted to go even further east and marched as far as **India**, into the area of present-day Pakistan. At the River Hydaspes, in 326 BC, he fought against King Porus, who used war elephants. After many years far from home, the exhausted soldiers refused to go any further. Alexander had to turn back. On his campaigns he founded many cities that bore his name.

In 323 BC, Alexander died in **Babylon** at only 32 years old, probably of an illness. His generals, the **Diadochi**, divided the huge empire among themselves and fought over it for a long time. Through his conquests, the Greek language and culture spread as far as Asia and Egypt. This period is called the **Hellenistic age**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An ancient kingdom north of the Greek heartland.
A very tangled knot, today an image for a difficult problem.
The successors of Alexander, who divided his empire after his death.
The time after Alexander, in which Greek culture spread widely.

gewusst: When you solve a difficult problem today with a bold step, people say you have cut the Gordian Knot.
Alexander named a city in India after his horse Bucephalus.
The famous Alexander Mosaic from Pompeii shows Alexander in battle against Darius III.

teile.einleitung: The Würm glaciation is the last Ice Age in the Alpine region. At that time, huge glaciers covered large parts of Switzerland and shaped many of the landscapes we know today.
wichtigste: The last Ice Age is named after the River Würm in Bavaria.
About 20,000 years ago, the annual average was 12 to 15 degrees colder than today.
The Rhine Glacier reached as far as the area of Schaffhausen.
At Bern, the Rhône Glacier and the Aare Glacier joined.
A moraine of the Linth Glacier dams Lake Zurich at Zurich.
Louis Agassiz made the idea of a great Ice Age known in 1837.

abschnitte.text: Researchers named the Ice Ages of the Alps after rivers in the Bavarian Alpine foreland. The youngest is called the **Würm glaciation**, after the **Würm**. Its greatest advance was about **20,000 years ago**. At that time, the annual average was about **12 to 15 degrees** colder than today. The summers were around 8 to 10 degrees cooler.

Huge glaciers flowed out of the Alps into the **Central Plateau**. The **Rhine Glacier** filled the Lake Constance basin and reached as far as the area of **Schaffhausen**. In the **Bern** region, the **Rhône Glacier** and the **Aare Glacier** met. A tongue of the Rhône Glacier flowed north-east along the foot of the Jura and scoured out the basins of **Lake Biel** and **Lake Neuchâtel**.

During its retreat, the **Linth Glacier** stayed for a time at Zurich. It deposited a bank of debris, a **moraine**. Today it dams **Lake Zurich**. Beneath the flowing ice, **drumlins** also formed, elongated hills such as in the **Zurich Oberland**. Their long axis shows in which direction the glacier flowed.

In front of the glaciers flowed great **meltwater rivers**. They deposited huge amounts of **gravel** and **sand**. Many gravel deposits in the Swiss Central Plateau come from this. This gravel is quarried today and used for building, for example for concrete. In the gravel layers there is often also valuable **groundwater**.

abschnitte.titel: The discovery of the Ice Age
abschnitte.text: In the past, people could not explain why large blocks of rock from the Alps lie in the middle of the Central Plateau. **Ignaz Venetz** and **Jean de Charpentier** suspected that glaciers had carried them. The researcher **Louis Agassiz**, working in Neuchâtel, presented his **Ice Age theory** in 1837 and made the idea world famous.

gewusst: In the Würm glaciation, a layer of ice several hundred metres thick lay over present-day Bern.
Large blocks of rock that glaciers have carried far are called erratic boulders.

teile.einleitung: Christianity is a religion based on Jesus of Nazareth. It arose in the 1st century AD in the Roman Empire and today, with more than two billion believers, is the largest religion in the world. In ancient times it grew from a small, partly persecuted group into the state religion of the Roman Empire.
wichtigste: Christianity goes back to Jesus of Nazareth.
According to the Gospels, Jesus was crucified under the governor Pontius Pilate.
The apostle Paul spread the faith on many journeys through the Roman Empire.
Christians were at times persecuted because they did not worship the emperor as a god.
In AD 313 Emperor Constantine allowed Christians to practise their faith freely.
Under Emperor Theodosius, Christianity became the state religion in AD 380.
The fish was an early sign by which Christians recognised each other.

abschnitte.text: **Jesus of Nazareth** was a Jewish travelling preacher who lived in Galilee, in present-day Israel. He spoke of God's love and of love for one's neighbour, and gathered disciples around him. Around AD 30 he was crucified in Jerusalem under the Roman governor **Pontius Pilate**. His followers believe that he rose from the dead and is the Son of God. The four **Gospels** in the New Testament of the Bible tell of his life.

After Jesus' death his followers, the **apostles**, spread the new faith. **Paul** was especially important: on several journeys through Asia Minor and Greece he travelled as far as Rome. He founded communities and wrote them letters, which are now in the Bible. Thanks to good roads and the shared Greek language, Christianity spread quickly through the Roman Empire.

Christians refused to worship the **emperor** as a god and to make sacrifices to the Roman gods. For this reason they were at times **persecuted**, for example under Emperor Nero and later under Emperor Diocletian. As a secret sign they used a **fish**. The Greek word for fish, Ichthys, can be read as an abbreviation for Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour.

abschnitte.titel: From forbidden faith to state religion
abschnitte.text: In AD 313 Emperor **Constantine**, with the Edict of Milan, allowed everyone to practise their faith freely. He supported Christianity and had large churches built. Under Emperor **Theodosius**, Christianity became the **state religion** of the Roman Empire in AD 380. Soon there were bishops and churches in many cities.

There were Christians even in Roman times in the area of present-day Switzerland. According to legend, Saint **Maurice** and the Theban Legion were killed at Saint-Maurice in the Valais because the soldiers did not want to deny their faith. An abbey stands there that has existed without a break since the year 515. In Zurich, the siblings **Felix and Regula** are said by legend to be the city's patron saints, and the Grossmünster and the Wasserkirche recall them.

Today there are many Christian churches, for example the Roman Catholic, the Orthodox and the Protestant Reformed churches. The Reformation in the 16th century, with Huldrych Zwingli in Zurich and John Calvin in Geneva among others, shaped Switzerland strongly. Important Christian festivals are **Christmas** and Easter. Around 2.4 billion Christians live in the world today.

begriffe.erklaerung: An account of the life and teaching of Jesus; the word means good news.
A messenger who carried the Christian faith onwards.
A religion that a state officially declares to be its own.
A handed-down story about holy people that is not proven in all its parts.

gewusst: Our way of counting years, before and after Christ, was only introduced by a monk about 500 years after Jesus.
The coat of arms of the town of Saint-Maurice and many churches bear the sign of Saint Maurice.
In old pictures Felix and Regula carry their own heads in their hands, as the legend tells.

teile.einleitung: Knossos on the island of Crete was the largest palace of the Minoans, a Bronze Age civilisation. The winding complex is linked with the myth of the Labyrinth of the Minotaur.
wichtigste: Knossos lies on Crete, not far from the present-day city of Heraklion.
The palace was the centre of Minoan civilisation.
From 1900 the British archaeologist Arthur Evans excavated the palace.
A famous fresco shows young people bull-leaping.
The legend of the Minotaur in the Labyrinth is set in Knossos.
Unlike Mycenaean citadels, the palace had hardly any walls.

abschnitte.text: The **Minoans** lived on Crete in the **Bronze Age**. Their name comes from the legendary **King Minos**. Knossos was their largest palace. It consisted of hundreds of rooms, stairs and passages around a large **central court**. In storerooms stood huge clay jars for oil, wine and grain.

From the year **1900** the British archaeologist **Arthur Evans** uncovered the palace. He found frescoes, vessels and clay tablets with written signs. Evans had parts of the palace rebuilt and painted using **concrete**. In this way visitors can better imagine the complex. But these reconstructions are still **disputed**, because not everything certainly looked like that.

The walls of the palace were painted with colourful **frescoes**. The famous **bull-leaping fresco** shows young people jumping over a charging bull. The **bull** played an important role in Minoan religion. Other pictures show plants, animals and dolphins.

According to the Greek legend, in a **labyrinth** on Crete lived the **Minotaur**, a creature half man, half bull. The hero **Theseus** defeated him and found his way out again with the thread of **Ariadne**. The many rooms and passages of Knossos may have inspired this myth.

Minoan palaces such as Knossos had **hardly any defensive walls**. They were open complexes around a court. The later **Mycenaeans** on the Greek mainland, by contrast, built mighty citadels with thick walls. Researchers suspect that the Minoans on Crete felt safe for a long time.

gewusst: The hill of Knossos was already settled in the Neolithic, long before the palace was built.
At Knossos clay tablets were found in the script Linear B, an early form of Greek.

teile.einleitung: The Etruscans were a people who lived in central Italy before the Romans. They built rich cities, decorated their tombs with paintings and strongly influenced the early Romans.
wichtigste: The Etruscans lived **in Italy**, mainly in central Italy.
The region of **Tuscany** is named after them.
In its early days **Rome** was ruled by Etruscan kings.
They painted **their tombs** with colourful pictures.
Their language is **still not fully understood** today.
Their language was probably related to that of the **Rhaetians** in the Alps.
The **Romans** took over a lot from the Etruscans.

abschnitte.text: From about the 8th century BC the Etruscans lived in **Etruria**, an area in central Italy. The present-day region of **Tuscany** is named after them, because the Romans called them “Tusci”. The Etruscans did not form a single state. They lived in independent city-states, which sometimes joined together in a league. Through trade by sea many cities became rich.

In its early days **Rome** was ruled by Etruscan kings. According to Roman tradition, the Romans drove out their last king around 509 BC. Later the Romans conquered all the Etruscan cities one by one. But before that they had **taken over a great deal from the Etruscans**, for example symbols of power, building methods and religious customs. Gradually the Etruscan people merged into the Roman Empire.

The Etruscans laid out large cemeteries that looked like cities for the dead. Many **tombs** were **painted in bright colours** inside. The pictures show feasts, music, dancing, games and hunting. The tombs of **Tarquinia** and **Cerveteri**, which are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites, are famous. From the tombs we learn a great deal about the life of the Etruscans.

The Etruscans wrote with an alphabet that they had taken over from the Greeks. So their texts can be read and pronounced. But **the language is still not fully understood**, because it is related to hardly any known language. Most likely it was related to the language of the **Rhaetians**. The Rhaetians lived in the Alps, including in the area of present-day Graubünden.

The Etruscans were especially skilled **at working bronze** and other metals. They made figures, mirrors and vessels that are still admired today. Their priests tried to discover the will of the gods. For this they examined, for example, **the livers of animals**. The Romans also took over this art of prediction.

gewusst: A bronze model of a sheep's liver, the “Liver of Piacenza”, was probably used to teach liver reading.
The Latin alphabet in which we write today came to the Romans through the Etruscans.
